News.title: NATO warplanes scrambled and airports shut down as Russia launches major attack
News.content:
NATO warplanes scrambled and airports shut down as Russia launches major attack

Poland's air navigation services agency confirmed the airports in Lublin and Rzeszów have suspended operations as a result of NATO aircraft being scrambled

View 2 Images Military aircraft are operating in Polish airspace this morning (file) (Image: JAKUB KACZMARCZYK/EPA/Shutterstock)

NATO aircraft have once again been raised over Poland, with two airports closed following a fresh Russian attack on western Ukraine.

‌



‌



The Polish armed forces confirmed that the "necessary forces and resources" have been activated this morning. Ground-based air defence systems and radar reconnaissance have also been prepared.

‌



The command said the measures are "preventive" and were put in place to secure the protection of Polish airspace. The situation is being monitored.

‌



A statement from the Polish armed forces reads: "Attention. In connection with strikes by the Russian Federation on targets in the western part of Ukraine, conducted using unmanned aerial vehicles, military aviation is operating in Polish airspace.

Content cannot be displayed without consent

Donald Trump halts massive sanctions on Russian goods just days before they take effect READ MORE :

"In accordance with applicable procedures, the Operational Command of the Armed Forces RSZ, through the Air Operations Center – Air Component Command, has activated the necessary forces and resources at its disposal. Ground-based air defense systems and radar reconnaissance have reached a state of readiness.

‌



"These actions are preventive in nature and are aimed at securing and protecting Polish airspace, especially in areas adjacent to the threatened regions. The Operational Command of the Armed Forces RSZ is monitoring the current situation, and subordinate forces and resources remain ready to respond."

Poland's air navigation services agency also confirmed airports in Lublin and Rzeszów have suspended operations as a result. A statement reads: "In connection with the need to ensure freedom of operations for military aviation, the airports in Lublin and Rzeszów have suspended flight operations."

View 2 Images The situation is being monitored (file) (Image: Anadolu Agency via Getty Images)

‌



This is only the latest incident affecting a NATO country in eastern Europe in recent months, as countries like Romania, Bulgaria and the Baltic states have repeatedly reported drone intrusions into their airspace. Last week, a suspected Russian drone strike targeted two ships off the coast of Bulgaria in the Black Sea, sinking one of them.

Russian attacks across Ukraine killed at least 10 civilians and injured 73 others in the 24 hours leading up to October 18, according to regional authorities. Three western Ukrainian regions were targeted on the morning of October 18, with Moscow's recent campaign against critical infrastructure continuing across multiple parts of the country.

Ukraine also launched a drone attack on Russia overnight, sending hundreds of unmanned aerial vehicles towards Moscow and St Petersburg. A major oil terminal in St Petersburg was struck, alongside a large data centre, with footage circulating online appearing to show fires breaking out.

Article continues below

Around 1,015 Ukrainian drones have been shot down across Moscow and several western regions, Russia's defence ministry claims.

News.title: Love Island star almost dies and rushed to hospital after falling into fire
News.content:
Love Island star almost dies and rushed to hospital after falling into fire

Love Island star Trent Woolman almost died after falling into a bonfire in a terrifying accident

View 3 Images (Image: Nine)

A Love Island star has been airlifted to hospital after a fall into a bonfire left him near death. Trent Woolman, who was in series five of the Aussie version of the dating show, had to crawl back to his sister's house after being engulfed by flames.

‌



‌



Trent, 28, suffered third degree burns to his arms, mouth and airways. His family were left terrified when his medical team added that he had cysts on his brain, as well as brain bleeds, and they needed to delay surgery to graft skin onto his arms.

‌



View 3 Images Trent Woolman on Love Island Australia (Image: Nine)

‌



Traitors Maya Jama exit 'sealed' at hands of EastEnders legend Ross Kemp READ MORE :

To see more of the stories you love from The Mirror and to find them easily in Google then make us your preferred source. Free and easy-to-do, just click on the link here to find more from The Mirror at the top of your feed.

The star, 28, has been in hospital for two weeks and is expected to stay there for at least a couple more. He told the Daily Mail: "[It's] been traumatic and the worst time of my life".

He also made it clear that he was sober when he fell into the bonfire. The accident occurred when he was cleaning up a paddock at his sister's property in the rural area of Inverleigh, Victoria. He was alone at the time and had to crawl back to the house to get help.

‌



Trent praised his sister for rushing to his aid as soon as she saw him. He said she was "amazing" and "so brave", calling an ambulance and staying calm during the emergency.

Though Trent's graft surgeries had to be delayed for several days, he has now had them and must wear bandages on his arms and face, as well as mesh net, to keep the bandages on.

View 3 Images Trent has been taken to hospital with third degree burns (Image: Nine)

‌



Third-degree burns are a serious wound that damages all three layers of your skin and can destroy the nerve endings in the affected areas.

It's understood Trent will now undergo multiple skin grafts, where a piece of unburned skin is surgically removed to cover the burned area. Despite the new skin being unburned, patients can often be left with severe scarring.

This comes just after it was revealed that Trent would be making a cameo appearance in the upcoming season of Married At First Sight Australia. The reality star was spotted at a filming location, attending the wedding of his Love Island co-star and podcast co-host Zac Nunns, who was paired with TikTok influencer Vanilla Milla for MAFS.

Article continues below

In pictures, Trent could be seen in a white shirt and black suit trousers. He and Zac shared a podcast called the Trent and Zac Show, where they spoke about Love Island gossip.

Since leaving Love Island, Trent, who was a tower crane operator, appears to have gone back to his normal life. Though he has over 30,000 followers on Instagram, he made the account private and doesn't seem to be pursuing the influencer lifestyle. Similarly, he has obtained over 20,000 followers on TikTok, but has not posted since late 2025.

News.title: CFB Wainwright fire: Soldiers killed in explosion at Canadian military base named
News.content:
Dozens more were injured after the tragic incident at the CFB Wainwright Canadian Forces Base in Alberta, which reportedly occurred after a gas line or gas well was hit during a live-fire training exercise

Major fire at Canada military base: What we know so far

Four service members killed following a major fire at a military base in Canada have now been identified.

Speaking from Ottowa on Sunday night, Prime Minister Mark Carney said the situation is "evolving rapidly". "The nation is in mourning for those brave members of our armed forces who we have lost," he added.

The blaze started near the CFB Wainwright Canadian Forces Base in Alberta at around 4pm local time on Saturday and "spread rapidly due to high winds". Those who died have been named as Sergeant Morgan Wong, Private Shaun Farrell, Private Aidan Goulding and Private Hayden Lykkemark.

Canadian TV network Global News reported the incident happened when a gas line or gas well was hit during a live-fire training exercise, citing unnamed military sources.

Dr Warren Thirsk, an emergency department physician at the Royal Alexandra Hospital in Edmonton, said: "This number of patients would overwhelm the city of Edmonton and that is why we are clearing our decks and mobilizing to respond as if it was our own city. It is more patients than any of us want to count right now. It's a disaster. It’s a one in every 15 to 25-year disaster."

News.title: EasyJet flight from Tenerife declares mid-air emergency as its met by fire engines at Gatwick
News.content:
EasyJet flight from Tenerife declares mid-air emergency as its met by fire engines at Gatwick

The flight declared an mid-air emergency at nearly 30,000 ft near London before being met at the UK airport by fire engines and emergency vehicles

View 2 Images The emergency was declared at nearly 30,000 ft (Image: Jam Press)

An EasyJet flight from a popular tourist spot declared a mid air emergency before landing at a UK airport.

‌



‌



Flight EZY58XM/U28040 from Tenerife to Gatwick squawked a 7700 general emergency code at 29,900 feet near London, before landing at Gatwick Airport.

‌



The emergency was declared on the approach as per Flight Radar, due to a technical issue.

‌



View 2 Images The flight declared the emergency before landing at Gatwick (Image: Squawk app)

According to reports on social media the Airbus A320-200 aircraft was met on the airfield by emergency ground support including fire engines.

‌



The flight took off from the Spanish island at 10.10pm local time, and took a duration of just over four hours.

The squawk 7700 alert is the universal transponder code for a general in-flight emergency.

However, the flight was not diverted and did land safely at Gatwick Airport as planned.

Article continues below

A spokesperson fro easyJet said: “Flight EZY8040 from Tenerife to London Gatwick experienced a technical issue on arrival into Gatwick this morning. The flight landed normally and was met by emergency services in line with procedures and a precautionary measure only.

“The safety and wellbeing of customers and crew is always easyJet's highest priority and easyJet operates its fleet of aircraft in strict compliance with manufacturers’ guidelines."

News.title: Macron expresses 'anger and shame' after 2,400 arrested in violent France protests
News.content:
Macron expresses 'anger and shame' after 2,400 arrested in violent France protests

Emmanuel Macron has spoken of 'anger' and 'shame' as nationwide protests in France over the cost of living crisis and school conditions turned violent this weekend

View Image Macron attributed much of the violence to far-left activist (file) (Image: Express)

French President Emmanuel Macron has voiced the nation's "anger" and "shame" over sweeping protests against soaring living costs and deteriorating school conditions, which have led to at least 2,400 arrests.

‌



‌



Mr Macron echoed fellow government officials in attributing much of the violence to far-left activists, accusing them of targeting police and public buildings in a bid to stoke disorder.

‌



"Those who looted will have to pay back for the damage, and those who sought to bring down the Republic will be held accountable," Mr Macron declared in a televised address to the country.

‌



He condemned "unrestrained violence" by "insurrectionist elements from radical far-left groups, joined by numerous criminals".

Mr Macron had earlier convened an emergency meeting with senior government figures, a day after masked groups set buildings ablaze and stormed public properties, including town halls, across several cities.

He revealed he had directed prefects to collaborate with mayors to safeguard public buildings and businesses over the coming weeks, including imposing protest bans where necessary.

‌



In the central town of Limoges, fire tore through the 19th-century City Hall, causing its roof to cave in and leaving the building on the verge of total destruction.

Hundreds of demonstrators once again gathered on Sunday at the Place de la Republique in Paris, amid a significant police presence.

Officers deployed tear gas as sporadic tensions flared across the area, with small clusters of individuals attempting to set bicycles and bins alight. "The right to protest is a fundamental right. Deliberately and collectively sowing disorder through violence is not," interior minister Laurent Nunez wrote on X, pointing to the ransacking of hundreds of businesses across cities including Paris, Marseille, Lyon and Bordeaux.

‌



Official figures put Saturday's march attendance at approximately 550,000, while organisers claimed the figure was closer to 800,000.

Protesters heeded calls from a trade union, student groups and activists seeking to reignite the "yellow vest" movement, which first emerged in 2018 as a demonstration against social inequality.

Large-scale demonstrations in France are frequently tarnished by violence on the periphery of otherwise peaceful marches, resulting in confrontations with police. The number of arrests reported on Sunday came close to the nearly 2,000 recorded across the country during a single day of yellow-vest protests back in December 2018.

‌



One individual suffered a fatal heart attack, according to a statement from Paris police, though no further details were provided. The Paris prosecutors' office confirmed it had launched an investigation.

Around Paris' Place de la République on Sunday morning, the aftermath of the unrest was plain to see, with uprooted cobblestones, smashed shopfronts and shards of broken glass littering the streets.

Reports of looting and damage emerged from around the square and several other tourist and shopping districts in the city centre.

‌



Paris police confirmed 855 arrests in the capital region, with the city's prosecutor's office stating that 557 people remained in custody. "I am actually stunned by the level of destruction and violence that was expressed," said Marie Peyreigne, a 57 year old government employee, as she tried to make sense of the chaos that had unfolded.

Surveying the wreckage, scores of Parisians photographed the partially demolished base of the central monument at Place de la Republique - a statue of Marianne, an enduring symbol of France.

Jean Foissy, 74, said he had intended to join the demonstration but encountered "a wall of riot police and fires everywhere", and turned back.

‌



"I was very scared," he said. "I've been a Parisian since I was born, so when I got here, it almost made me want to cry because I find it so bad, it hurts me."

Margaux Eude, 26, said she backs the protest movement but "didn't think it would escalate like this".

"It's the troublemakers who came, and it breaks my heart because it delegitimises the movement", she said.

‌



Political figures across the divide moved swiftly to exploit the fallout from Saturday's unrest for political gain, with one eye firmly on next spring's presidential election.

Far-right leader and presidential contender Marine Le Pen rounded on far-left rival Jean-Luc Melenchon, who had taken part in the Paris march.

"Looting, ransacking, destroying and attacking law enforcement: Rioters have again spoiled the October 17 demonstrations for the protection of purchasing power," Ms Le Pen wrote on X.

‌



Her running mate, Jordan Bardella, said on X that "if the silent majority of French decide it, we will re-establish order for the long-term". Mr Melenchon, for his part, exchanged sharp words with the prime minister, accusing Mr Lecornu of "playing with fire" and claiming that "by banking on degradation, you have only succeeded in uniting all youths and workers' unions".

Mr Melenchon stated that "my message is clear: those who share our fight have no business in looting or destruction".

US President Donald Trump posted "France is burning!" on his Truth Social platform, apparently linking the unrest to "the immigration of people from an entirely different world".

‌



"Close your borders and take control, before it is too late!" he wrote.

French authorities and police have drawn no connection between immigrants and the rioting, repeatedly attributing elements of the violence to "radical far-left groups" and opportunistic looters.

Paris mayor Emmanuel Gregoire announced the establishment of an emergency unit to help businesses evaluate the extent of the damage.

‌



"The scale of the damage is considerable and unprecedented," Mr Gregoire wrote in an open letter.

"Paris is a city of freedoms, debate and demonstrations. It must remain so. But it must also be a city where everyone can work and run a business safely."

The mayors of Paris, Marseille and Lyon, France's three biggest cities, called for an urgent meeting with the prime minister in the coming days "given the extent of the damage and the seriousness of the situation."

‌



In the southern coastal city of Marseille, demonstrators temporarily stormed the entrance hall of City Hall, while a group wearing hoods and masks vandalised a police station. In Lyon, flames erupted within a tourist office.

In Limoges, a band of "radical troublemakers" broke into City Hall while elected officials, staff, security personnel and members of the public were inside, Maurice Barate, prefect of the Haute-Vienne region, said.

"Despite the presence of so many people, they deliberately set the building on fire. It is an extremely serious and unspeakable act," he said.

Article continues below

In eastern France, the Mulhouse prosecutor's office said an investigation has been launched after a 17 year old girl sustained injuries during the protests and lost an eye.

On Saturday, another investigation was launched after a young demonstrator lost a hand in Saint-Etienne.

The injuries emerge as police face intense criticism over their deployment of grenades and other riot-control weapons during recent demonstrations.

News.title: Air Force commander plunges to death in front of horrified fans at football game
News.content:
Air Force commander plunges to death in front of horrified fans at football game

Sergeant Ian Patterson was performing a stunt as part of the pregame coin toss when he slid down a rope and hit the ground before being rushed to hospital

View 2 Images (Image: @Qu4k3r0ats/X)

An Air Force commander who fell 170 foot in front of thousands of horrified football fans has died.

‌



‌



Sergeant Ian Patterson, a Tactical Air Control Party instructor, was rappelling from the roof of the Alamodome stadium at the University of Texas game on Saturday when he slipped and plunged to the ground.

‌



The service member was part of a pregame demonstration at the school's “Salute to Armed Forces and Veterans” game.

‌



View 2 Images An airman rappels from the Alamodome stadium rafters during an earlier demonstration (Image: @UTSAFTBL/X)

Videos posted on social media appear to show the moment the man loses control and slides down the rope. He then received medical treatment on the field for around 10 minutes before being rushed to a local hospital.

UTSA staff formed a semicircle around Pattersom before he got taken off the pitch on a stretcher.

‌



He sadly died at the hospital.

“Everyone was quiet, the band stopped performing. Everybody was dead silent,” Adrian Corey, who witnessed the fall, said to KSAT .

The military demonstration was part of the pregame coin toss and featured four members carrying out the stunt, who are trained in descending from helicopters at heights over 100 feet.

‌



UTSA officials expressed concerns for the man at the time of the fall. A university spokesperson said: “We are deeply saddened by the incident that occurred at the start of tonight’s football game. Our heartfelt thoughts and prayers are with the soldier who was affected, his family and his military colleagues.

“We recognize that members of our campus community may be emotionally affected by this incident and are activating wellbeing services to support our faculty, staff and students.”

“I’ve never had to deal with anything like that before,” coach Jeff Traylor stated. “It just puts things into perspective. It really does.”

‌



The American Conference also posted a statement saying they're “deeply saddened” by the incident.

“We consulted with representatives of both participating member institutions, Alamodome management, local authorities and a working group to review the information available."

“This tragedy is felt deeply across the 57th Wing,” said U.S. Air Force Brig. Gen. Scott C. Mills, 57th Wing commander. “Tech. Sgt. Patterson and his service mattered immensely to our wing, and to the family, friends, and teammates who had the privilege of knowing and serving alongside him. Our team is now focused on standing beside Ian’s family, loved ones, and fellow Airmen as we navigate this profound loss together.

Article continues below

“Our relationship with local community partners is incredibly important to our Airmen, especially during difficult times like these,” Mills said. “We are grateful to the San Antonio community and our mission partners at Joint Base San Antonio for the care, compassion and support they have shown.”

News.title: Companies exploiting welfare system by using residents as 'cash cows', BBC finds
News.content:
Some private companies are making huge profits and exploiting the welfare system by receiving housing benefits on behalf of residents but failing to give them the support they're required to, BBC Panorama has found.

Property agents are drawing people into the taxpayer-funded system using social media videos that offer free rooms, PlayStation consoles and even holidays.

The system - called supported exempt accommodation (SEA) - is designed for people in the UK with additional needs, including former prisoners, people recovering from addiction and women fleeing domestic abuse. It provides housing along with care, support and supervision.

For many residents it works well to help them get back on their feet, but charities, politicians and residents tell us parts of the system are being exploited.

Many vulnerable people are being used as "cash cows to generate income" that goes from the Department for Work and Pensions (DWP) into "the back pocket of the landlords", said Patricia Coleman-Taylor, who runs Birmingham anti-poverty charity Narthex.

Panorama has learned the DWP paid out Â£410m for SEA in Birmingham alone in the last financial year.

The city is the epicentre of the sector, with more than 34,000 people living in SEA. For context, in London about 22,000 live in supported housing despite its population being more than seven times larger.

Labour MP Jess Phillips, whose Birmingham constituency contains large numbers of these properties, said companies spending taxpayers' money while providing a poor standard of support was "an absolute catastrophe" and bad landlords "can make loads of money".

But she added that there are some housing providers who "get this money who are absolutely providing supported accommodation".

The leader of the city council, Liberal Democrat Councillor Roger Harmer, told us that "taxpayers' money is being wasted. It's a scandal."

In Birmingham, BBC Panorama's investigation found:

Vulnerable people are being left with little to no support in often unsuitable accommodation

One big housing provider wrote off Â£1.8m because of payments to some former directors and companies they ran

Evidence that some are willing to make benefit claims for people who do not live in their properties

Supported accommodation was set up for people like Alysha.

When she escaped a violent marriage, she returned to Birmingham seeking shelter. But her family did not have room so she had to look elsewhere.

News.title: Watch: Russian saboteur working for Ukraine shares reconnaissance videos
News.content:
A Russian man secretly working for Ukraine's intelligence services has shared videos of surveillance work he says he has done for Kyiv inside Russia.

The man, who we are calling Ivan, claims to have played a role in Ukrainian drone attacks on strategic bombers and munitions factories on his home soil.

He features in a BBC World Service documentary about the shadowy world of Russian saboteurs.

Ivan was cautious about how much detail he shared, making it impossible to verify the activities he claims to have carried out.

News.title: Home sellers cut asking prices on 3,000 properties a day
News.content:
Home sellers cut asking prices on more than 3,000 properties a day on average in Britain during September, according to figures from Rightmove shared exclusively with the BBC.

The property website said the total was the highest of any month for 15 years and was driven, in part, by a glut of homes on the market and some sellers setting unrealistic expectations.

The proportion of listed homes that eventually had a price cut peaked in 2023 and has remained relatively high since.

Property portals say buyers are now having to be choosy, with many working to a tight budget as mortgage rates have risen to three-year highs.

"Once a home has been on the market for a while and then has a price reduction, some buyers start asking questions, even when there is nothing wrong with the property," said Colleen Babcock of Rightmove.

"In a market with so much choice, first impressions matter."

News.title: Watch: Inside Chicago's battle against the synthetic drugs flooding the US
News.content:
Warning: This video contains descriptions of drug-taking and distressing images

A new wave of synthetic drugs is sweeping across the United States, raising fear of a worsening drug crisis.

Earlier this year, President Donald Trump pledged a crackdown on drug cartels, proscribing many as terrorist organisations.

Drug overdose deaths have fallen from a peak of around 110,000 in 2022, down to roughly 70,000 last year.

However, America's decades-long drug crisis may be accelerating and authorities are increasingly concerned about cheaper, more powerful synthetic drugs, including an animal tranquilliser called tranq.

The BBC's Quentin Sommerville reports from the frontlines in South Side, Chicago, where communities are battling the crisis.

Camera journalist: Darren Conway

News.title: NHS bosses say smaller maternity units may have to close
News.content:
NHS bosses in England say the way maternity care is organised is "not fit for purpose" with safety at risk and warn some smaller units may have to close.

The NHS Alliance, which represents health managers, warn difficult decisions lie ahead and maternity services need to be consolidated to support safer care.

It said a government taskforce into neonatal and maternity care must tackle key issues such as a lack of specialist staff and a rise in C-sections.

The Department of Health and Social Care said every woman deserves safe maternity care, and the taskforce "will deliver the reforms needed to ensure services meet the needs of women and families now and in the future".

The NHS Alliance said there are particular pressures on smaller units in rural and coastal areas and that those delivering 1,500 to 2,000 babies each year might need to close.

The rise in C-sections was a challenge, according to the NHS Alliance, and there were inadequate operating theatres and beds in outdated and decaying buildings, posing a safety risk.

The NHS leaders' organisation also said some smaller units struggled to maintain safe staffing numbers for 24-hour care, including midwives and consultants such as obstetricians.

It goes on to say the government's taskforce must "grasp the nettle" by tackling these strategic issues, including significantly worse outcomes in deprived communities and raised maternity mortality rates for Black and Asian women.

The director of the NHS Alliance's acute and ambulance network, Matthew Hopkins, said: "Difficult decisions lie ahead, consolidating maternity services to support safer, more sustainable care."

He said any local plans had to involve NHS leaders, clinical staff, patients and communities, and that politicians "must have the courage to make the case for patient safety".

"It is time now to take a step back and consider how we should best organise maternity services across England, and where those services should be located", he said.

News.title: 'Postcode lottery' driving children's inequality in England, commissioner warns
News.content:
Middlesbrough, Hounslow, Bradford, Nottingham, Halton, Peterborough, Leicester, Liverpool, Sunderland and Medway were ranked the hardest places to grow up in England.

Cheshire East, Merton, Surrey, Richmond upon Thames, Hertfordshire, Cheshire West and Chester, Haringey, Leicestershire, Central Bedfordshire and Wokingham were described as the "least challenging places to be a child".

In some cases the difference in standard was stark.

It took six days for a child to be referred for mental health assessments in Leicester, and 118 days in Hampshire and the Isle of Wight.

In Richmond upon Thames, 70% of children got good grades in English and maths GCSE compared to 31% in Knowsley.

Just 6.7% of children in Bedford felt unsafe in their local area, compared to 24.9% of children in Croydon.

In four local council areas, spending on youth services per teenager was zero.

86% of Redcar and Cleveland's children saw a dentist in the last year compared to 39% in Hackney, which was among 25 areas where fewer than half of children saw a dentist.

General poverty was not always to blame for poor children's services, the report found, external.

Haringey in North London scored highly in an assessment of its services for children, despite having high levels of deprivation. Conversely Cambridge was ranked lower, even though it was one of the least deprived areas in England.

Dame Rachel recommended there should be a minimum set of standards for the way children were affected by levels of education, policing, health, and youth services.

"Strategic authorities", which include areas with mayors, and larger local councils, should be required to have a deputy mayor for children with responsibility for testing every policy to assess its impact, she said.

A children's emergency fund should be set up to pay for improvements in services, she added.

In a separate article for the Times, external on Monday, the prime minister promised more investment in "the success of our young people" and said the government could no longer support their "failure through the benefits system."

The Department for Education said it's working to improve childcare support and school standards, and is giving more power to "local leaders" to shape the future of their education.

"We're investing and reforming at every stage of a child's journey, from more childcare support for their earliest years and higher standards in our schools, broader community support with the rollover of our National Youth strategy and Young Future hubs, to more training and job opportunities as they approach adulthood," it said in a statement.

The government said it is opening 1,000 Best Start Family Hubs in England, which offers joined-up support for parents and children, including health, education and advice services.

News.title: Burnham says youth employment and training crisis is a 'moral failure'
News.content:
Prime Minister Andy Burnham has warned the UK faces an "economic catastrophe and moral failure" due to the nearly one million young people not in education, employment or training.

Writing in the Times newspaper, external, Burnham has laid out his case for the government to "invest in the success of our young people" rather than "pay for failure through the benefits system".

"Benefits will become the backstop, not the starting point," Burnham wrote in his piece published in Monday's paper.

Later this week, the government is expected to announce plans to give young people thousands of job opportunities. The Conservative Party has labelled the government's youth employment strategy "a disaster".

According to the latest data from the Office for National Statistics, there are almost a million people aged 16 to 24 known as Neets - not in education, employment or training.

In his opinion column, the prime minister said this reflected a "generation being denied its chance to get on in life".

"This is an economic catastrophe and a moral failure. And it must change," he wrote.

Burnham said two years of Covid lockdowns, social media that erodes "confidence and sense of belonging", an education system focused on the "university route", job markets with "too few opportunities" and failures of previous governments have all contributed to the Neets crisis.

"Today, the welfare system provides an assessment, a payment and, after that, goodbye," Burnham wrote. "Too often there is no support, no offer of skills and no opportunity to get a job."

He flagged a shift in the approach to welfare, which he said "will no longer begin by establishing which benefits a young person is entitled to" but rather "begin with their ambitions and the help they need to achieve them".

The prime minister added: "The safety net will always be there for those who cannot work. But if someone can work with the right help, the government has a duty to do everything in its power to make that happen."

Ministers are this week set to release plans for tens of thousands of new youth apprenticeships and placements in the construction industry, and at accounting, consulting and legal firms.

Shadow Business and Trade Secretary Julia Lopez said: "Labour have been a disaster for youth jobs. Their tax hikes and red tape have made it harder for businesses to hire, invest and grow, destroying opportunities for young people looking to take their first step on the career ladder."

News.title: People playing loud music on buses could face £100 fine
News.content:
Passengers who play loud music on buses in England could be fined up to Â£100 under an attempt by the government to crack down on antisocial behaviour.

The measures also seek to tackle littering, vaping and threatening behaviour to help improve journeys on all forms of public transport.

Offenders on buses could be issued with the fines under new powers for local authorities.

A national campaign asking rail passengers "share the carriage, not the noise" is also being launched. The proposed crackdown has been welcomed by campaigners, but some have questioned how it can be enforced.

"We've all been on the train when someone starts blasting music or videos from their phone. It gets on your nerves and can quickly spoil the journey," said Prime Minister Andy Burnham.

Under existing powers, those who are asked to stop and refuse could be removed from a train or fined up to Â£1,000.

The phenomenon has been given many terms - including loudcasting or sodcasting - and in recent years, Ofcom, YouGov and Transport for London (TfL) have all published polls showing the vast majority of people dislike it.

Transport Secretary Heidi Alexander said small changes in behaviour "can make a massive difference to people's experience on public transport".

The government said it had issued new guidance to local authorities on powers - which were introduced earlier this year - to help them crackdown on loud music and other antisocial behaviour on buses in England.

These new powers allow them to impose new rules on buses, but still need to be signed off by the Transport Secretary

Those who commit offences could face fixed penalties of up to Â£100.

The government says bus drivers will not be responsible for enforcing the new rules. It says authorised officers, including Transport Safety Officers and the Police, will deal with the incidents.

Commenting on how fines will be enforced, Chris McDonald, Minister for Science, Research and Innovation, told BBC Breakfast that passengers can complain to staff "or the British Transport Police if they wish".

"They don't have to tackle the individual themselves if they don't feel confident to do that," he said, adding that people can text the British Transport Police.

Meanwhile a new national campaign aims to remind rail passengers to "share the carriage, not the noise", to improve journeys for everyone

The campaign will be launched across operator websites, social media, and in carriages. The government said this would end the current "patchwork" of approaches across different rail operators, and help create "a clear, consistent message across the network".

The general secretary of the TSSA transport union, Maryam Eslamdoust, said tackling antisocial behaviour on public transport was "a step in the right direction".

However, she added that the government must also "urgently confront the violence, threats and abuse faced by passengers and transport workers".

"Increasing the budget for British Transport Police is vital to protect people, respond to incidents and bring violent offenders to justice," she said.

News.title: Chance of storms this week as Atlantic jet stream roars into life
News.content:
The UK may see its first named storm of the autumn as forecasts show the potential for a deep area of low pressure to cross the UK later this week.

A strengthening jet stream triggered by temperature contrasts across North America will cause turbulent conditions to develop.

All areas will experience rain at times, including those currently in drought, but amounts of rain will depend on the exact track of a stormy low pressure system later in the week.

After a chilly weekend, temperatures will generally remain slightly below average for mid-October.

News.title: Polanski says he will not overturn Green Party's 'Zionism is racism' motion
News.content:
Zack Polanski has said he will not overturn a motion passed by Green Party members that declared Zionism a form of racism.

The Green leader told Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg that, while he would like to make amendments, it would be party policy until 2028.

The motion, passed at the party's conference earlier this month, described Zionism as an ideology supporting "an ethnonationalist Jewish state in historic Palestine to the exclusion and/or domination of the non-Jewish population".

It divided the party and sparked a major backlash from MPs, Jewish campaigners, the government and the European Green movement, with the equality watchdog writing to the party for more information on it.

The fallout from the motion overshadowed the final days of Polanski's campaign in the Holborn and St Pancras by-election, in which he came second to Labour, and threatened his leadership.

He came under criticism for not voting on the motion which was passed by 1,022 votes to 813 - a small fraction of the party's 230,000 members - in Brighton earlier this month.

The motion also asserted the party's backing for "a single democratic state throughout historic Palestine", a full arms embargo on Israel and a commitment to Palestinian liberation.

Asked if he would now step in as leader to overturn it, Polanski said: "I'm not going to try to overturn it.

"At the first available opportunity, I do want to amend it - I want to move away from one state, towards saying that Israelis and Palestinians should decide that future for themselves."

He said this would not be until 2028 as "you can't [amend it] within the rules, so when you vote on something in our party conference that's then policy for two years".

Kuenssberg asked if he would therefore change the rules as leader, but Polanski said: "I think if members have made a decision, then I respect the democratic will of our members."

Former Green Party co-leader and current MP Adrian Ramsay responded by calling for action to be taken sooner.

"I don't think it's tenable for us to continue the next two years with this policy that's been adopted given the huge political distraction that it's been for our councillors across the country," he told the BBC News Channel.

"One way forward could be to have a ballot of all party members to establish very clearly where does the party as a whole stand - my view is we would see a different answer."

Polanski had previously said he would not have voted for the motion without two amendments.

The first of these would have avoided "determining there was a single democratic state", and the other would have specified that the motion should not be used to discipline Jewish Green members who attend synagogues that consider themselves Zionist.

Both of these amendments were voted down by members at the party's conference.

Green MPs, including Ellie Chowns, have called for the party's member-led decision-making procedures to be reviewed given how few people took part in the vote.

News.title: Suspects hunted after police officer injured in shooting
News.content:
Detectives are searching for two suspects who fled after a police officer was shot in Nottingham city centre.

Nottinghamshire Police said the officer had approached two suspects in Angel Row shortly before 04:50 BST on Sunday.

The officer is in a stable condition in hospital, where he is receiving treatment for a wound to his foot, the force added.

Detectives said a man and a woman had fled the scene and that a firearm, which could be seen within the cordon, had been found.

Angel Row remained closed by a large police scene until Sunday evening.

Police cars were parked along the road, which is lined by fast food stores and shops, and orange traffic cones had been laid out alongside items left on the road.

The cordon had also been extended to St James's Street, where an officer is standing guard.

The force said there would be a heightened police presence as the investigation continued.

News.title: Man, 80, who died in light aircraft crash near Loch Lomond named
News.content:
An 80-year-old man who died in a light aircraft crash is understood to be flying instructor Ian Haggis.

He and a 16-year-old boy died when their plane came down near Loch Lomond. The teenager's identity has not been released.

The pair had flown out from Glasgow Airport at 16:17 and stopped transmitting at 16:37, a few miles north east of the village of Drymen near Stirling.

Emergency services were called to the crash at about 16:45 on Friday.

Both of them were pronounced dead at the scene.

Temporary airspace restrictions are currently in place over the area while the Air Accidents Investigation Branch (AAIB) carries out its inquiries.

Old Drymen Road, near the scene of the crash, remains closed with vehicles being turned around and hillwalkers rerouted.

News.title: Ending corridor care in hospitals for children a priority, says health secretary
News.content:
The health secretary has asked the NHS to draw up urgent plans to speed up ending hospital "corridor care" for children.

Yvette Cooper told the BBC there would be new standards for caring for children in A&E in England, with figures collected on corridor care by age for the first time.

She was speaking on Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg where the programme highlighted the case of two-year-old Finlay Roberts who died in 2024 after spending hours in a hospital corridor before being discharged.

The health secretary has announced Â£140m to improve urgent care in England ahead of what she said would be a "more difficult" winter than usual.

The government has already pledged to end corridor care for all patients by the end of this parliament, and now Cooper has said eradicating it for children would be prioritised.

Corridor care refers to patients receiving treatment or waiting in corridors, waiting rooms or other hospital areas due to a lack of appropriate space.

The health secretary was also asked if the government would meet a key manifesto pledge that 92% of patients would start treatment within 18 weeks of booking a hospital appointment by 2029.

"That remains our manifesto commitment and of course we're going to keep working towards it," Cooper said.

Pushed further on whether the target was achievable, she replied: "The whole point about having the targets is about having something stretching that we work towards."

The 18-week target has consistently not been met for more than a decade.

Cooper said that the NHS was dealing with a number of challenges after record A&E admissions following heatwaves over the summer.

According to the latest figures for England, an estimated 7.37 million treatments were waiting to be carried out at the end of August, relating to 6.24 million patients.

On the programme the story of Finlay Roberts, was highlighted. He died after being discharged from hospital in 2024 following hours spent in an A&E corridor in north London.

Finlay's father David told the BBC the situation was a "terrible mess", with the family moved into a room with a bed before being moved back into the corridor.

"He just clung to me, as we now know, slowly dying," he said.

Liz Roberts, Finlay's mother, said corridor care "robs people of their dignity when they are at their most vulnerable". She recalled being told to administer a suppository to her son in the corridor.

Cooper apologised to Finlay's parents on behalf of the NHS, saying: "No child should be treated in a corridor. No patient should be treated in a corridor."

News.title: NHS data breaches a disgrace, health secretary says
News.content:
NHS staff accessing the medical records of the Nottingham attacks victims and possible breaches over a man killed by a tiger is a "disgrace", the health secretary has said.

Speaking to the BBC, Yvette Cooper said she expected action to be taken against staff who had breached NHS data and privacy standards.

Her comments came after Nottingham University Hospitals (NUH) NHS Trust confirmed it had sacked a total of 15 members of staff and Yorkshire Ambulance Service said William Chapman's medical records may have been accessed illegitimately.

Dr Manjeet Shehmar, NUH medical director, previously said there was "simply no excuse for accessing the records of a patient without a legitimate reason".

Speaking to the BBC's Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg, Cooper said "there's got to be proper respect for patients" from NHS staff.

"Let me be really clear about this," she said. "There are proper data and privacy standards across the NHS."

Students Barnaby Webber and Grace O'Malley-Kumar, and grandfather Ian Coates, were stabbed to death on 13 June 2023 by Valdo Calocane, who was diagnosed with paranoid schizophrenia in 2020.

NUH said in May that it had sacked 11 members of staff for inappropriately accessing the victims' medical records, and had informed the Information Commissioner's Office (ICO) and Nottinghamshire Police of the investigation.

At the time, the ICO told the BBC it would "assess any evidence provided by the trust in due course and consider our next steps", while police said there was "no criminal investigation".

In its update about further dismissals on Friday, NUH said it had taken action against "doctors, nurses, registered healthcare professionals and other staff", and that independent regulators such as the Nursing and Midwifery Council and General Medical Council, the ICO and Nottinghamshire Police had been informed.

NUH added a new system, currently under testing, was being implemented to protect patient records in future and alert the trust to potential breaches.

News.title: Two teenagers die in collision
News.content:
Two people in their late teens died in a collision involving two cars, Suffolk Police said.

Officers were first called by the ambulance service to Debenham Road near Little Stonham at 10:15 BST.

Fire crews and the air ambulance were also called to the incident that involved a red Peugeot 107 and a silver Volkswagen Passat.

Police said a male passenger in the Peugeot died at the scene. The female driver was taken to Addenbrooke's Hospital in Cambridge by land ambulance, but has since died as a result of her injuries.

The occupants of the Passat suffered minor injuries, the police spokesperson added.

The road was expected to reopen later in the evening.

News.title: West Midlands Police officer who accessed police records 2,000 times sacked
News.content:
An officer who inappropriately accessed police records more than 2,000 times has been sacked for gross misconduct.

A West Midlands Police misconduct hearing acknowledged PC Shannon Parsons felt "isolated and disconnected" due to working part-time and returning from maternity leave, but had breached standards of professional behaviour.

Parsons had claimed there was a policing purpose to her searches, the panel said, and was seeking to "keep herself up to date, informed and was often in a position to support and assist other colleagues in operational matters".

However, chair of the panel Debra Tedds concluded the searches were carried out for the officer's "own personal benefit".

As a result, Parsons was dismissed without notice and barred from future work in policing.

The searches took part over a period of about five years, the panel heard, and many included incidents near her home address.

Parsons had an otherwise unblemished career in policing in the West Midlands, lasting 13 years, but was said to show no insight or remorse "as to the potential harm that has been caused by accessing the amount of information over a significant time period," according to the panel's report.

News.title: ‘Headphone dodgers’ face new fines as Burnham launches crackdown
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

People who play music out loud on buses could face fines of up to £1,000 in strict new rules.

A campaign with the tagline ‘share the journey, not the noise’ reminding train passengers to use headphones will also be launched on Monday.

The push forms part of a wider crackdown on antisocial behaviour across public transport.

Under the new measures, people who play music out loud on buses could be hit with £100 fines.

Local authorities are being encouraged to use new powers to levy fines for nuisance behaviour on buses, including littering, vaping and listening to music without headphones.

Guidance published on Monday by the Department for Transport sets out how the new legislation can be used.

Local authorities gained the power to set and enforce their own rules on their bus networks earlier this year.

Any rules drawn up under the powers will need to be signed off by the Transport Secretary.

They will be enforced by specialist transport safety officers rather than bus drivers.

open image in gallery The prime minister's first weeks in office focussed on bus fares, pubs and high streets ( PA Wire )

Prime Minister Andy Burnham said: “We’ve all been on the train when someone starts blasting music or videos from their phone. It gets on your nerves and can quickly spoil the journey.

“So, we’re launching a nationwide campaign reminding passengers to use headphones on trains.”

He added: “It’s a simple thing, but one that will make journeys that little bit better for all of us.”

Transport Secretary Heidi Alexander said: “It is so frustrating when the actions of an inconsiderate few spoil journeys for the rest of us, whether that is vaping, littering or blasting music out loud.

“Even small changes in behaviour can make a massive difference to people’s experience on public transport.”

Antisocial behaviour on public transport has become an increasingly prominent issue.

The Liberal Democrats called for action against “headphone dodgers” last year.

Ben Plowden, chief executive of the Campaign for Better Transport, said antisocial behaviour could be “a real deterrent” to using public transport.

He said: “If these new powers are properly and visibly enforced, they should help everyone feel safe and comfortable on public transport and enjoy the ride.”

News.title: ‘I lay in pool of blood after being shot at point blank range while undercover in Northern Ireland’
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

A former member of one of the British Army’s most secret surveillance units has, for the first time, told the dramatic story of his role in an undercover operation which ended with him being shot through the stomach, his partner mortally wounded, and a wanted IRA gunman fleeing injured into the night.

The veteran, known only as Blue*, recounted how events unfolded in episode five of SAS: The Shadow War.

He was just 22 and serving with 14 Intelligence Company – the clandestine unit known simply as “the Det” – when he and another soldier set up a covert observation post beside a farm in South Derry on St Patrick’s Day, 17 March 1978.

“My gut was telling me something bad was going to go down,” Blue recalls. “The hairs on the back of my neck started to come up.”

Listen to the full fifth episode of SAS: The Shadow War here, or become an Independent Member for exclusive access to all eight episodes:

open image in gallery Member of the SAS, an elite special forces unit of the British Army, on training in 1970 ( Popperfoto/Getty )

As they hid, two armed figures emerged through a hedge. Blue initially believed they were British soldiers. Moments later, both opened fire on him.

“It was just like a hail of gunfire at a range of 12ft,” he says. “I was shot three times.”

It's the first time that Blue, now 70, has ever told his story publicly.

He had joined the Det from the Parachute Regiment as one of the undercover surveillance operators deployed throughout Northern Ireland to follow suspected Republican militants and build intelligence on their movements, contacts and weapons networks.

Their target that night was Francis “Frankie” Hughes, a 22-year-old IRA gunman already regarded by police as one of their most wanted men.

Blue says Hughes was exceptionally elusive. The surveillance team hoped that an associate living around the farm complex might lead them to him.

“We were basically tasked to track down this individual,” he recalls. “The aim was that if we watch this other individual, this individual might take us to the guy we really wanted.”

open image in gallery A British armoured car of the 17/21st Lancers moves through Strabane, Co Tyrone in April 1969 ( PA )

Blue and his partner established what the Det called a “night standing OP” — a temporary observation position relying principally on darkness rather than elaborate camouflage.

There were just two of them.

“You’re on your own, basically,” Blue says.

At about 8pm that night, the man they originally intended to follow appeared at the farm and subsequently drove away. A different surveillance element followed him so Blue and his partner stayed behind.

But a second man, the owner of the property, did not return indoors. Instead, he continued wandering around the yard.

That was when Blue began to feel something was wrong. “There’s no logical reason why this should be happening,” he recalls thinking.

Then he heard movement in the undergrowth to his left.

He saw a man emerge wearing what appeared to be military uniform: beret, combat jacket and weapon held ready. A second armed man followed in single file. They appeared to patrol like trained infantry.

Blue and his partner assumed they were fellow members of the security forces who had wandered into their covert operating area.

The area was supposed to have been declared out of bounds – but sometimes the regular army didn’t get that message. Covert operators had experienced a number of previous close calls with British patrols.

Now, the two soldiers appeared to be approaching them. Blue and his partner would soon be discovered – “compromised”.

Blue had a choice. They could silently withdraw and guarantee their own safety, but in doing so risked making enough noise for the farmer to realise someone had been hiding beside his property. It could destroy the wider surveillance operation. Blue decided to stay.

That decision would haunt him for fifty years.

He allowed the two approaching men to come within about 12 feet before whispering to them: “Stop. Security forces.”

Blue says the pair halted abruptly.

One said something in an Irish accent. For a fraction of a second that reassured him: he thought they might be members of the Ulster Defence Regiment. But then he heard weapons being cocked.

“A millisecond after that, they just opened up with everything they had.”

Both Det soldiers were hit.

open image in gallery Republican murals pictured in the Bogside area of Derry in 2017 ( BEN STANSALL/AFP via Getty Images )

One round passed through the grip and magazine of Blue’s pistol before striking him. Another tore through his sleeve. A third whipped through his abdomen, destroying his left kidney, damaging his colon and passing within about half an inch of his spine.

He was thrown onto his back.

His partner, Lance Corporal David Jones, was also shot through the abdomen. The round damaged his spleen. He was mortally wounded.

From the ground, Blue could see muzzle flashes receding as the two IRA men withdrew. They were acting like trained infantry, one firing while the other moved. Bullets passed so close to his head that he could feel their shock waves. At first he thought pieces of hedge were landing on him.

Then he realised the sensation was being caused by rounds passing inches away.

Blue hauled himself back onto his knees and fired an entire 32-round magazine towards the flashes.

“I just basically emptied the magazine,” he recalls. He later discovered he had hit both men.

Severely injured, Blue crawled towards the radio only to find that its handset cable had become disconnected. His hands were already weakening as blood loss sent him into shock.

“If you don’t connect, there’s no backup nearby,” he remembers. “You’re going to die.”

On what he told himself would be his final attempt, he managed to reconnect the radio. Blood was everywhere.

“It’s like having a shallow bath in blood,” he says. “You’re drenched in blood.”

Jones was screaming nearby. Blue forced himself to ignore the pain of his friend and to “bring down the shutters” mentally to shut out the agony and noise.

He transmitted a brief report. Then he crawled to Jones and attempted first aid. When reinforcements eventually arrived – a single Det operator – Blue refused treatment and ordered him to help Jones first.

Then he realised that he may have condemned himself to death.

open image in gallery A line of British troops stands guard in the Falls Road area of riot-torn Belfast ( PA )

“You’ve just signed your death warrant here,” he remembers thinking. “By the time he finishes working on my buddy… I’m going to have little or no blood left. So be it.”

Then there was the agonising 45-minute wait for an ambulance to arrive. It had got lost on its way to the scene. Finally at the hospital, Jones was taken into surgery first due to his injuries being considered more serious. Blue went in later.

When he woke, curtains had been drawn around his bed and he was told Jones had died.

“They said, ‘Your partner has died, and we didn’t want you to wake up and see him being pulled away,’” Blue recalls.

Jones was 23 and due to be married the following week.

The firefight had also achieved, by accident, what the surveillance operation had originally intended to do: one of the gunmen Blue had shot was Francis Hughes himself.

Hughes was found the following morning, around 500 yards from the location of the shootout, badly wounded. He was later jailed for the murder of Jones and the attempted murder of Blue, as well as other offences. He died in the Maze Prison in 1981 after 59 days on hunger strike.

open image in gallery Demonstrators protesting Britain's continued presence in Northern Ireland while Prince Charles watched a Lincoln Centre ballet show in New York City, 1981 ( Getty )

The second gunman had escaped. Blue says investigators later followed two blood trails from the firefight to the home of a local nurse whom the wounded men apparently knew.

But there was nobody home – at the time, that same nurse was treating the two British soldiers whom the IRA had shot.

The coincidence was typical of the conflict. So were the decisions that determined life and death.

Blue said he and Jones could have withdrawn. Nobody, he says, would have criticised them for doing so. Instead, they remained in place.

“That little decision – or big decision - cost my buddy’s life.”

News.title: France protests latest: French PM to hold crisis meeting after 2,400 arrested in weekend of looting and violence
News.content:
From reproductive rights to climate change to Big Tech, The Independent is on the ground when the story is developing. Whether it's investigating the financials of Elon Musk's pro-Trump PAC or producing our latest documentary, 'The A Word', which shines a light on the American women fighting for reproductive rights, we know how important it is to parse out the facts from the messaging.

At such a critical moment in US history, we need reporters on the ground. Your donation allows us to keep sending journalists to speak to both sides of the story.

The Independent is trusted by Americans across the entire political spectrum. And unlike many other quality news outlets, we choose not to lock Americans out of our reporting and analysis with paywalls.
