World.title: AI giant Anthropic commits 5% of shares to ‘public benefit’ fund
World.content:
Claude creator says fund could used for donations to NGOs and ‘direct distributions to specific populations’.

Anthropic has pledged to commit 5 percent of its shares to a new fund dedicated to the public good, with plans to increase the contribution as the artificial intelligence giant’s market value grows.

The creator of the AI assistant Claude announced the new “Anthropic Public Benefit Fund” on Sunday as tech firms face intense scrutiny over the potential dangers posed by the frontier technology.

In a blog post, Anthropic said it was committing 5 percent of company shares with immediate effect, subject to stockholder approval, with an additional 2 percent to be added “at the board’s discretion” for every 50 percent increase in the company’s value.

“Because of the way the Fund is structured, the more Anthropic grows, the larger the share of the company that can be dedicated expressly to the public good,” the San Francisco-based firm said.

“It is common practice for tech companies to offer escalating compensation awards to their executives. We are instead directing that equity to the public benefit.”

Anthropic said the fund could be used to make donations to traditional nonprofits, as well as “direct distributions to specific populations”.

It said labour market disruption due to AI could be among the causes addressed by the fund.

“Anthropic has already committed $200 million to studying and addressing this issue, but given the pace of AI progress, bolder approaches may be needed,” the company said.

“The Fund will have the versatility to pursue them.”

Anthropic, officially registered as a “public benefit corporation” in the US state of Delaware, said the fund would not be used for lobbying or political donations, either in the United States or overseas.



Founded in 2021 by former employees of ChatGPT creator OpenAI, Anthropic is preparing for what could be the largest public initial offering in history. It is expected to list on the US stock market before the end of 2026, with analysts forecasting a valuation exceeding $2 trillion.

The company’s charter requires its leadership to balance shareholder returns with responsible AI development.

The breakneck speed of AI development has prompted widespread anxiety about possible negative downstream effects on society, including the job market.

In a report published last month, consulting firm McKinsey estimated that up to 11 million American workers may need to switch careers over the next decade due to AI-driven automation.

World.title: France's government under pressure after weekend of widespread violence
World.content:
France's Prime Minister SÃ©bastien Lecornu is holding a crisis cabinet meeting on Monday to assess a weekend of violence and looting across the country, in what were some of the worst scenes of public disorder in modern French history.

On Saturday over half a million mainly peaceful protesters demonstrated against rising living costs and dwindling access to decent public services, including a good state education. But the protests turned nasty after groups of black-clad, masked activists and vandals appeared.

An estimated 1,500 shops and businesses were looted and destroyed. Riot police fired tear gas and turned water cannon on crowds. They were seen hitting people with batons in several places. France's interior ministry said about 1,000 police officers were injured on Saturday, seven of them seriously.

There had been rumours in France that President Emmanuel Macron may introduce a temporary curfew in parts of the country, or even impose a state of emergency to help calm the febrile atmosphere. In the end, he used a televised address to the nation on Sunday to call for national unity and to try to assure the French public that the perpetrators of the violence would be punished.

Macron's speech has been roundly criticised on social media forums and by political opponents for lacking concrete detail.

How will vandals and rioters now be brought to account?

How might France's towns and cities be better protected - especially since new mass demonstrations have been announced in a couple of weeks' time?

Exactly how will destroyed businesses be compensated?

And when will a dialogue be established with students and teachers' bodies on the subject of education?

World.title: Funding shortages force World Food Programme to cut aid to Gaza
World.content:
One of the main suppliers of food aid to the Gaza Strip, the World Food Programme (WFP), says that it is being forced to "drastically reduce lifesaving assistance" to the Palestinian territory due to funding shortages.

Overall, the number of people helped by the UN agency will drop by about a third - from 1.6 million to 1.1 million.

The cuts will hit as winter approaches and at a time when many families in Gaza are still struggling to feed themselves.

One effect is that the number of hot meals that are currently being provided by community kitchens will be cut from 250,000 to 150,000 each day.

Families living in hard-to-reach areas, for example near the so-called Yellow Line, which demarcates Israel's area of military control, will receive a meal every other day instead of daily.

Nearly all of Gaza's 2.1 million population remains displaced and two-thirds rely on food aid to survive.

World.title: Inside the shadowy world of anti-Putin sabotage from within Russia
World.content:
"You will get a file... from me or a colleagueâ¦ with the proposed target. The file will contain [the target's] photo, his data, his details, date of birth, age, and a description of him. There'll be information on his car, if he has one. When you go to the target, don't take a phone," he told his volunteers.

Foma was once part of the Russian elite, so he claims to have a unique set of contacts and constant flow of insider information.

He showed Mamon on his laptop how he mapped military targets.

"This shows a database... the location of storage warehouses, and military units. Where generals liveâ¦ Where the pilots of strategic bombers who shell Ukraine live.

"In order to break the system, you need to understand how it works. Then you can aim for their weak points."

He said there were about "three dozen" people in his network split between Russia, Ukraine and elsewhere in Europe, with the contingent outside Russia providing logistical support, such as tracking targets' digital footprints.

Foma stressed that the GUR suggests the targets to be surveilled, but that he and his team check for themselves that these individuals should be considered military criminals.

"As a ruleâ¦ we also check the data [on that person]â¦ Only after that we say whether we work or not."

But he argued that his team's actions were justified.

"I want people who do terrible things on behalf of Putin and Russia in Ukraineâ¦ to understand that they'll have to pay for it. I want them to get scared."

Foma stressed that he only passed on intelligence to the Ukrainians, and his network did not carry out any assassinations themselves.

Of the assassination of Gen Sarvarov, killed in December 2025, he later texted Mamon to say: "Keeping track of him took quite an effort. He lived alternately with his mistress and his colleague. Covered his tracks and constantly changed his schedule."

But Foma did not share any plans with Mamon and the BBC in advance.

Ivan, however, was tight-lipped about the work he had been involved with, even after the event.

Foma did his own digging on Ivan.

After checking with his military intelligence contacts in both Ukraine and Russia, he thought it likely that Ivan had been involved in a plan to strike Russia's largest military drone factory at Yelabuga in June last year, external. One person was reported to have been killed in the incident.

Ivan stressed that the aim is always to try to avoid harming civilians.

Operations have clearly been risky for Ivan too.

"The most serious case was when my car was stopped for inspection and I had the handmade explosives on me. The risk was very high - however as you can see, I was not detected," he said.

To mitigate the risk of being compromised, "there is no clear structure" to the work, he said, adding he had never met and did not know the identity of others he had been working alongside.

Foma has the same rule for his operatives.

"As soon as you start gathering people in groups, in general chatsâ¦ leaving a mark on the internet, with a high probability this whole group will be quickly detained or destroyed," he said.

Ivan stressed there were few people left in Russia suitable for this kind of work.

"Most of the ideological people have either left the country or are already behind bars," he said.

Many Russians involved in sabotage work on their native soil are therefore either oblivious - for example lorry drivers unaware that their cargoes have been compromised - or are individuals who have been paid, the BBC understands.

Ivan, on the other hand, says he is doing this work for ideological reasons - he used to be a member of the political opposition. As such, his movements would be expected to be monitored closely by the Russian authorities.

So it was a surprise that he managed to frequently leave Russia and return.

World.title: Major fire at Canada military base leaves four dead, dozens injured
World.content:
Four members of the Canadian military have died and dozens were injured at a base in the province of Alberta after a fire broke out in a grassy training area and spread rapidly due to strong winds.

Addressing the nation on Sunday from Ottawa, Prime Minister Mark Carney described it as "one of the worst tragedies for the forces on Canadian soil in peacetime".

The fire broke out at about 16:00 local time (22:00 GMT) on Saturday at Canadian Forces Base Wainwright, one of the country's busiest military training bases, and is now contained.

"The nation is in mourning for those brave members of our armed forces who we have lost," said Carney.

The BBC has confirmed that Sgt Morgan Wong, Pte Shaun Farrell, Pte Aidan Goulding and Pte Hayden Lykkemark have died.

Of the 39 injured people being cared for in hospital, at least 19 are in a critical condition, Alberta Premier Danielle Smith said at a press briefing on Sunday evening.

Fire and rescue teams are remaining at the scene to contain any potential flare-ups, Wainwright Mayor Bruce Pugh told the BBC.

Members of the infantry had been conducting "high-intensity combat training with live munitions" at a grenade range and attack range, where 10 soldiers practise attacking a simulated enemy, Maj-Gen Wade Rutland told reporters at the briefing.

"There was a multitude of ordnance moving through the Wainwright training area," he said, including a grenade launcher, grenades, small arms and ammunition.

A grass fire ignited about 1km (0.6 miles) away, with the cause currently under investigation, and moved toward the attack range.

"What I would say is there was multiple training activities happening throughout the training area at the time," he said. "Uncommonly strong winds caused the fire to spread rapidly and shift direction towards the range administrative area."

World.title: Trump says suspension of Russia sanctions is to keep peace negotiations going
World.content:
US President Donald Trump has said his decision to suspend several Russian sanctions is an effort to keep Moscow at the negotiating table.

"I am in the process of negotiating Peace in the war between Russia and Ukraine," Trump said on his Truth Social messaging platform, adding that he didn't want to "do anything that will drive, foolishly, Russia away from the bargaining table".

Trump blocked numerous sanctions on Russia on Friday night, two days before they were due to take effect, as a row with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky deepened.

Zelensky told NBC News on Sunday that siding with Russian President Vladimir Putin would be a "historic mistake".

Russian envoy Kirill Dmitriev has responded to Trump's order by calling it "an important and truly historic moment". He said the sanctions, which were passed by the US Congress and signed into law by the US president in September, would have inflicted "serious damage" on the US and global market.

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio has described the suspension of the sanctions as a 60-day pause during which their potential impact on the US and global economies would be analysed.

In his Truth Social post, Trump also said Zelensky "doesn't want to end this war, and probably never did", adding "he could have made a better deal two years ago than he can now".

Zelensky has pushed for an end to fighting, and has repeatedly said that Putin doesn't want peace, since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.

Relations between Washington and Kyiv frayed after the US struck a controversial deal to import Russian diesel last week.

Despite the international sanctions, Russia has still been able to export oil, much of it to China and India - often at attractive discounts. According to the think-tank Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air (CREA), China has taken about half of Russia's crude exports, with India accounting for about 37%.

In remarks to a European Union summit, after Trump announced the deal to buy diesel from Russia and said Zelensky was "more difficult to deal with" than Putin, Zelensky said it was nice to be among "real leaders".

World.title: Kenya pastor accused of ordering parents to starve their children to death faces verdict
World.content:
A Kenyan court is set to deliver a judgement in a mass murder case involving doomsday preacher Paul Mackenzie.

Mackenzie and 29 of his followers are being charged with the murder of 191 children.

His cult is alleged to have forced children to starve to death so that they could "meet Jesus". His doomsday doctrine said that education was forbidden and modern medicine was considered "evil".

Mackenzie and the 29 others have all pleaded not guilty to murder, repeatedly insisting that nobody was forced to die.

Mackenzie's former head of security, Enos Amanya Ngala, was initially accused but then entered a plea deal and became a witness for the prosecution.

Mackenzie and other leaders of the cult are facing a raft of other legal cases, including for terrorism, radicalisation and denying education to children.

But this is the first time the pastor will face a verdict on the most serious charges of murder.

Authorities said over 400 bodies were found in shallow graves in Shakahola forest near the Kenyan coast, where Mackenzie led his followers from across the country.

Seventeen men were hired from the nearby town for the horrifying task of digging up the shallow graves. Some were paid just $8 (Â£6) a day.

"Every grave we found had at least three bodies," James, one of the gravediggers, told the BBC. "Some of the remains were of children as young as a few weeks old."

"We once found 12 bodies of children in a line inside a grave. It was massive, the bodies were arranged like clothes. One on top of another."

Gravediggers described some of the bodies of children as having had their "hands and legs tied and bodies wrapped in bedsheets".

World.title: Bollywood actor Tiger Shroff survives shooting in Mumbai
World.content:
Bollywood actor Tiger Shroff has survived a shooting in Mumbai and has not sustained any gunshot wounds, according to Indian police who are investigating the incident.

The 36-year-old was shot at on Sunday evening, while he was in a car that was leaving a football club in the suburb of Juhu.

Several news outlets have published a video showing at least two gunmen firing multiple shots at close range at the front passenger seat of a car while it is slowly moving past a crowd.

The incident has heightened concern about the safety of public figures in India, with some killed or injured in targeted attacks in recent years.

"These attempts to intimidate people will not be tolerated, and we will put an end to this hooliganism," said Eknath Shinde, deputy chief minister of Maharashtra state, where Mumbai is located.

He paid a visit to Shroff after the shooting on Sunday evening, and said the actor and his mother had been left "shaken" by the attack.

Police said two people were injured in the shooting, including Shroff's driver, local media reported.

This is the latest in a string of attacks on some of the country's biggest public figures in recent years.

In 2024, police in India arrested two members of a criminal gang for a gun attack targeting the home of Bollywood actor Salman Khan.

That same year, influential Indian politician Baba Siddique was shot dead in Mumbai.

The son of two actors, Tiger Shroff made his acting debut in 2014 with the romance film Heropanti and went on to star in several films.

He is also a football enthusiast who plays for the professional football club Mumbay FC.

World.title: Bomb threat forces Israel to Austria flight into emergency landing
World.content:
An Austrian Airlines flight from Israel to Austria was forced to divert to Bulgaria after a reported bomb threat.

The Airbus A320 plane was travelling from Tel Aviv to Vienna on Sunday night but made an emergency landing in Sofia, where passengers were evacuated, the Bulgarian transport ministry said in a statement.

The Bulgarian air force scrambled a MiG-29 fighter jet to escort the airliner, the statement said. No injuries have been reported and an investigation has begun.

It comes after a pilot attempted to hijack a Flydubai flight en route to Tel Aviv last month by attacking the captain, before the flight's crew and passengers overpowered him and landed the plane safely in Saudi Arabia.

Bulgarian and Israeli media reported that a bomb threat had been made.

Austrian Airlines confirmed a threat was made, without giving further details. A spokesperson told the BBC there were 51 passengers and six crew members on board the jet.

Authorities conducted a security search of the plane after it landed in Sofia, about 30 minutes from when the alert was first raised. It was over Romania when it diverted to Sofia.

Austrian Airlines confirmed that no threat was found and the flight finished its journey to Vienna with all passengers on board.

Flight tracking data showed Austrian Airlines 82 left Ben Gurion Airport in Tel Aviv on Sunday evening before landing at Vasil Levski airport in Sofia three hours later.

Last week, Croatia and Germany both scrambled fighter jets after a commercial flight from the Greek holiday island of Corfu to the German city of Nuremberg accidentally sent out a hijacking alert.

World.title: EDITORIAL: Issues should dominate as campaigns kick-off
World.content:
Campaigns for the 2027 general elections have started. A total of 18 political parties are jostling for the most coveted office – the president of Nigeria. In functional democracies, existential challenges shape the debates and town hall meetings, going into these elections. And the soapbox usually quakes as candidates justify why they should be voted for.

Here instead, muckraking and brickbats take the centre stage. Still, incredibly, some candidates shun the debates, as if they do not owe electorates any information about or scrutiny of their purposes in seeking public office.

As the 2027 campaigns gain traction, it is not in doubt that insecurity remains the country’s greatest crisis point. This is closely followed by a high cost-of-living, the sustained looting of the public treasury, absence of quality healthcare and education, good road networks, and adequate electricity supply. These are all very disturbing national deficiencies. The candidates may have listed them as what they would tackle in their manifestos, but the missing link is usually the action plan on how to resolve the concerns. This is where debates become very crucial.

As such, Nigerians eagerly await the presidential candidates – Bola Ahmed Tinubu of the All Progressives Congress (APC), Atiku Abubakar of the African Democratic Congress (ADC), Peter Obi of Nigeria Democratic Congress (NDC), Seyi Makinde of the Allied Peoples Movement (APM) candidate, Omoyele Sowore of African Action Congress (AAC), Donald Duke of Peoples Redemption Party (PRP) and Adebowale Adebayo of the Social Democratic Party (SDP) – for their campaign responses to these burning national issues.

Atiku has set the ball rolling with his promise to restore fuel subsidy if elected. This is a volte-face from his position on the policy in 2023, as he now cites the negative impact of subsidy removal on the cost-of-living in the country. But Tinubu views the retrogression as Atiku’s “demonstration of serious ignorance of the economy and governance.”

Since then, it has become more than just a debate between the two candidates, but an incisive national conversation, animating the different divides on the issue, as other presidential candidates have equally become embroiled in it. A total of the ₦15 trillion saved as a result of subsidy removal between June 2023 and December 2025 appears not have impacted the lives of citizens positively, despite the huge monthly accurals to all the levels of government.

Tinubu had abolished that fiscal tool in his off-the-cuff “fuel subsidy is gone” declaration, during his inauguration in 2023. It earned him plaudits from economists and the Bretton Woods Institutions, who argued that the scheme was not sustainable. Yes, it was not, with the massive heist it was associated with.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

Undeniably, the spiralling inflation attendant upon market-driven fuel pricing, combined with the deregulation of the forex market, has made life largely unbearable for most Nigerians. This is evident in the surging costs of food items, transportation, medicare, house rents and social services.

Government seems to have finally got the message – at least in its preliminary campaign messaging – that the economy is now a key issue, despite the seemingly laudable GDP growth figure of 4.43 per cent in the second quarter of 2026. Hence, it announced a reductrion in transport fares from 1st October. Some CNG buses have also been rolled out, as cheaper public transport options, while a 30-day price cut in the pump price of fuel at NNPCL filling stations has been announced. The cap is now at ₦1,350 per litre at NNPCL filling stations across the country.

Ironically, three weeks into this scheme, all the designated stations have been selling petrol above the capped price. Rather unfortunately, instead of better economic engineering, all that is being witnessed is a change in nomenclature, with “discount” as the new terminology for price reduction, as pushback against the continuously questioned terms of “under-recovery” and “import differential” of old. Yet, explanations are being demanded by citizens on who really bears the cost of this new discount, whether it is a ruse that would be charged back somehow along the line when elections are over, and truly what happens at the end of this strange relief window.

However, with the surge in economic hardship, it is left to be seen, for how long Nigerians, especially the 63 per cent living below the poverty line, would be left to the vagaries of the market. Fuel sells between ₦1,380 and ₦1,500 across the country. The fear is that it could go much higher.

The official view that fuel subsidy is not sustainable due to the fraud inherent in it is becoming a lame logic, with the government’s apparent indifference to recovering the looted funds from the indicted fuel importers and oil marketers. These subsidy thieves are well-known. The paper trails are with NNPCL over the dubious payments made back in the day.

A House of Representatives ad hoc committee chaired by Farouk Lawan, and a presidential panel with Aigboje Aig-Imoukhuede as chairman, investigated the subsidy scam in 2012 and uncovered more than ₦1.7 trillion stolen from the country. Surprisingly, 21 oil firms and marketers involved failed to appear before the two panels and nothing has happened to them to date.

More curiously, the immediate Group Managing Director (GMD) of NNPC, Melee Kyari, has since July refused to appear before the Senate Public Accounts Committee to explain a ₦210 trillion expenditure, covering 2017 to 2023, which has been queried by the Auditor-General of the Federation.

Responsible political leadership and accountability matter here. Nigerians expect the presidential candidates to come up with governance frameworks that would checkmate the unabashed looting of the country’s oil resources.

Electoral campaigns are critical in democratic transitions. In the US, for instance, pressing national issues decide the outcome of its elections. The economy, immigration and abortion rights shaped the 2024 presidential campaign. And, the story should not be different here.

One issue that beggars belief is the $1.8 billion the government plans to inject into the turnaround maintenance of Nigeria’s four refineries after it had already sunk $18 billion into them in the past two decades, without any result. This is certainly a monumental loss.

Nigerians grope in the dark year-in-year-out. Industries are unable to reach their optimal operational capacity as the national electricity output vacillates between 3,000 and 5,000 megawatts. In 2025, industries spent ₦1.34 trillion on alternative power supply; and 24 companies alone spent ₦400.8 billion on gas and alternative power supply in the first quarter of 2026.

Successive governments since 1999 have failed woefully to deliver on power. Small and Medium Scale Enterprises, which should have provided jobs for thousands of unemployed youths are mainly comatose, thus fueling the involvement of this crucial demographic in criminal activities. Only short-sighted presidential candidates will ignore the need to address such a critical issue.

Kidnapping, banditry and insurgency are all youth pre-occupations, which have reached pandemic levels, turning Plateau, Benue and Zamfara states into grave yards of sorts. Consequently, a security policy shift with strategies that will reverse our two decades of tragedies is urgent. But it should not be anchored on promises, without pragmatic steps that would midwife results.

World.title: “I won’t be everywhere” as chichidodo, a maggots-loving bird, By Festus Adedayo
World.content:
The ancient wisdom of our forefathers we grew up to meet is that, no one delegates the very personal task of emptying one’s bowel to their closest acquaintance. Not even your child. “A kì í fi iṣé ìgbònsè rán ọmọ ẹni” was the ancient Yoruba wisdom in this regard. But that was when life was straightforward and hadn’t been taken over by hypocrisy. It was unimaginable for anyone, no matter how close they were to you, to qualify for a delegation of the task of forcing out your excrement to. It is a wisdom which, for centuries, curbed trickery. It is also a metaphor for setting boundaries of specificity. However, today, strange occurrences have taken over this world. The world is standing on its head, upside down.

When I heard Nigeria’s president speak at the State House Banquet Hall, Abuja last Wednesday, that poo-poo feeling came over me. The president spoke shortly after inaugurating the APC Presidential Campaign Council. He would not be everywhere campaigning for Nigerians’ votes, he said boldly without batting an eyelid.

The president wants to delegate the task of emptying his bowel to his vice, APC chairman, Nentawe Yilwatda; the man with the arrogantly irritating gruff, Nyesom Wike and the 31 governors already held captive in its penitentiary. To equally help Mr. President force out the smelly poo-poo trapped inside the narrow pipe of his buttocks is the dancing fellow in Osun State, as well as the grovelling man who sold his brother for a mess of political pottage living in Awka. Individually and collectively, that is their task.

“You have warned me and asked me not to allow the rigour of the campaign to distract me from governance. I hear you. I am in full agreement with your decision. Nigeria needs more attention now than ever before. The responsibility of this office does not pause… So, you will excuse me from going everywhere with you,” he said to a Nigerian world which was unfazed by this quixotic declaration.

Watching how feeble the president gets by the day, Nigerians predicted this day, more than two years ago, that their president would be quarantined at home during the presidential campaigns. As he belched out what was obviously a huge lie, I wish I was at the event to see whether, at that moment, Mr. President had blood encrusting his lips. He would be a nice guinea pig for testing the efficacy of Yoruba’s literal perception of lie-telling. The people take the lie-telling act as equal to “killing a lie” (pa iró) but believe that you cannot find blood on the lips of liars.

This morning, I am listening to Chief Commander Ebenezer Obey’s classic Jùjú medley track entitled, “A ńjáde L’ónìí, Elédùmarè“. It is an early morning supplication to the Owner of the universe for spiritual fortification from the arrows of this world. It asks for protection against crossing paths with misfortune (àgbákò). For decades, this song was an early morning invocation in many Yoruba homes. In their spirituality and cosmology, Yoruba do not joke with early mornings.

Sung in 1982, after that prayer to the gods of our forefathers, Obey and his Inter-Reformers Band then made a detour. “Àbòsí ti d’áyé, ònà ti jìn…” Obey sang. It is a philosophical reflection on human nature. The world is polluted by widespread evil, dishonesty and malice. That pollution by sons and daughters of perdition makes life’s journey long and arduous. The song further warns that the world is a lie, occupied by wiles in high and low places. Leaders are becoming more and more deceitful and the led, extremely treacherous. For humanity to sail through this mesh and navigate life safely, it needs extra care and divine protection, Obey’s classic track said in a serenade.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

As I listened to this man of power waddle through a cloud of obvious lies, I pitied him. In all this, you will see the almightiness of God. How does a man spend all his adult life pursuing an elephantine warthog, (Ìmàdò) only to develop toothache at meal table, when the animal had been killed and barbecued for dinner?

I am reminded of Odolaye Aremu’s famous musical line: “Ohun t’óo l’óó dà l’o dà yí o!” – “This is what you have pursued all your life…” In that line, the Ilorin bard was addressing an unnamed man of power who perhaps thought that wearing a beautiful cap was the be-it-all of manly elegance. Knowing how to wear a cap, our elders say, is the littlest of the trip of the fancy of elegance. For the cap to fit the wearer is an architecture of elegance that can only be bestowed by the Creator. Taking this life’s vanity philosophy from where Odolaye left it, Yusuff Olatunji continued. He sang of those who called for war and when this same war came, they ran away – “Ẹyin l’ẹ p’ogun tí ẹ sá f’ógun, ẹyin l’ẹ p’òtè t’ée fi s’éyìn.”

How does a man who had always wanted to be Nigeria’s president now resort to delegating one of the most fanciful apparatuses of being a president – the political campaign? Allahu Akbar!

As the 2027 elections draw near, norms collapse, rules die and the bolts that tighten us to the rest of humanity loosen. The truth is, there is a huge pall of mystery surrounding Nigerian government and politics.

Most times, when you tell a lie, you will need hundreds of other tissues of lies to panel-beat your lying thesis. To me, this is the summation of the Nigerian presidency’s almost 4-year attempt to hide behind a single leprous finger. Last week, Pope Leo XIV underwent a successful thoracic surgery at Rome’s Gemelli Hospital. For about 90 minutes, he was under the scalpel to remove a cancerous growth on his right lung. The world was even told the identity of the doctor who undertook the operation. He is Professor Stefano Margaritora.

Leo, leader of approximately 1.38 to 1.41 billion people worldwide, the world was told, is expected to remain hospitalised for about a week. He came clean with the world on his own share of life’s burden that humanity carries. The world is still on its knees praying for Leo. As our people say, if you do not hide the Ifa corpus from me, I have no reason to hide the Ọpẹlẹ, the sacred divination chain, from you as well.

For African leaders, chief among whom is the man who recently went AWOL for 30 days from Nigeria, hiding inside a hole in France, and who will yet be AWOL from his own campaign, It is high time to know that openness and accountability aren’t strictly about finance. Openness on health matters is an integral part of accountability in office. Those who framed the idea of democracy say it thrives on direct engagement between leaders and the citizens whose mandate they seek. Delegating direct interface with the people you govern, though may not be a constitutional infraction, is a symptom of deliberate retreat from direct democratic accountability.

Put correctly, it is a presidential abdication of responsibility, a moral absenteeism which insulates the leader from the lived realities and grievances of the electorate. By asking surrogates to poo-poo for him, the president cleverly avoids direct scrutiny from citizens he was elected to govern, whose harrowing cries of rising living costs, security challenges and economic reforms have risen to the highest decibel.

No matter how fluid the voice of Nentawe Yilwatda could be on the campaign podium, it cannot substitute for the soothing, though coarse voice of the man the people voted into office. Nyesom Wike’s croaky voice and his bully can rally votes, but they cannot defend presidential policy failures, nor can they articulate personal vision, or take direct public ownership of government outcomes.

Perhaps, the APC and the president assume that the campaign to the people of Nigeria is a political side-show. No, it isn’t. It is a crucial, hands-on auditing process where the leader directly faces the people who issued him an IOU in 2023. To dismissively tell this same people the bombastic lie that Tinubu would be absent on the hustings because “We have bills to pay” and because he wants to maintain focus on national development is a lie from the pit of hell. Whenever my people are face to face with a barefaced trickery as this, they draw a comparison between it and the loud swagger of an Òkóbó – the libido-challenged man – who, rather than inserting into an ancient hole, boastfully claims he could insert a thread inside the needle, even in the dark! The truth Aso Rock thinks over 200 million Nigerians do not know is that the president’s health cannot withstand the rigour of campaign. Simplicita!

By detaching from directly addressing worsening security and economic hardship, Aso Rock covertly deepens public disillusionment, eventually risking rebellion.

During the 1983 Second Republic election, President Shehu Shagari pioneered this aloofness. In the build-up to the elections, he relied on powerful party barons whom the newspaper press of the time dubbed “NPN heavyweights” in the task of running regional campaigns. He remained trapped inside the belly of the State House in Lagos. He however succeeded in creating the image of a distanced presidency, alienated from growing public dissatisfaction. People also tend to see this strategy as an attempt to shelter weak candidates from press interrogation and unpredictable public scrutiny. By the time Shagari woke up to his reality, there had been loss of legitimacy, even though he was officially announced as having secured the 1983 electoral victory.

President Jimmy Carter of America suffered this same fate in 1980. Applying what later came to be known as the “Rose Garden strategy” during his re-election campaign, Carter remained inside the White House. He claimed to be focusing rather on what he called “presidential duties,” rather than actively traveling to have a one-on-one with American voters. Carter suspended foreign travel and regular political campaigning, choosing to manage the crisis directly from the Oval Office.

Unfortunately, as these dragged on, Carter’s portrayal by the press as an isolated and ineffective leader trapped by circumstances went full throttle. The press dubbed him everything but a busy statesman. By the time Carter realized this strategy as a political waterloo and chose to eventually leave the White House on an aggressive political campaign, it was too late. He lost the 1980 election to Republican Ronald Reagan.

As the Nigerian president told that naked lie of staying at home to tackle Nigeria’s development issue last Wednesday, Nigerians laughed themselves hoarse. A man who just returned from a 30-day junket, in violation of the constitution; who didn’t bother about the suffering of selfsame national development during his AWOL period, is now all of a sudden bothered. Now that he needs to be interrogated by the electorate, he has chosen to cherry-pick the 12 states he would attend. The other question in need of answer is, if indeed Mr President is AWOL from campaign in order to handle Nigeria’s development, how come all critical persons needed to help him bring about the elusive development are already on the list of presidential campaign? I remember a line from James Hadley Chase – a liar must have a very good memory.

The president’s decision to delegate his meeting with the people who elected him to unelected campaign surrogates reminds me again of Ayi Kwei Armah’s chichidodo bird. Chichidodo came into limelight in Armah’s famous The Beautyful Ones Are Not Yet Born (1968). Chichidodo is a mythical bird that fiercely hates filth and human excrement but whose favourite food is the maggots that grow inside that very filth.

This allegory of the chichidodo has become a critical lens through which political analysts and literary commentators evaluate statecraft, accountability, as well as how leaders distance themselves from systemic realities. Armah portrays the chichidodo as a hypothetical bird which was defined by a profound, paradoxical conflict. He wrote: “The chichidodo is a bird that hates excrement with all its soul, but feeds exclusively on maggots, which grow best inside filth.” While this strange bird is rankled by dirt and corruption, its life sustenance is attached to organisms sprung forth by decay. Chichidodo struggles to keep an image of moral purity through being aloof from mess, but is kept alive by the outcome of that mess.

Like the chichidodo, Baba’s campaign strategy of delegating accountability to campaign surrogates is not only in sync with poo-poo’s thematic parallels, delegating the task of accounting for his administration’s austere achievements and shortcomings to political aides, party loyalists or campaign councils presents the president as creating a buffer. Our own chichidodo the bird cannot separate its appetite from the environment that creates its food. As the Armah bird is a symbol of a hypocritical attempt to enjoy the benefits of a situation, while pretending to be untainted by its uncomfortable realities, it explains the position our president found himself.

Overall, w ords fail me to express this misty mystery of a chichidodo Aso Rock . It beggars belief that those we give our more, in exchange, we receive less from them. They are interested in the warmth of the pool’s water but are afraid of jumping into it. By this, they ignore ancient wisdom which says, you “Don’t jump in the water, if you can’t swim.”

Festus Adedayo is an Ibadan-based journalist.

World.title: Decoupling Sovereignty Index (3): Persona, exit and the ethics of going dark, By Max Amuchie
World.content:
Last time, this column dressed the researcher for the street.

It described the Visual Assimilation Protocol, the wardrobe of the worn and unremarkable, and the deep immersion through which a scholar-journalist or researcher may, for a time, become less conspicuous inside a decoupled zone.

That idea deserves more than a cliffhanger.

A methodology that asks a researcher to live under a borrowed role creates three obligations that cannot be avoided: the role must be disciplined, the researcher must be able to leave, and the deception must be ethically justified.

The third is the hardest.

I take them in that order.

The Persona Is a Contract, Not a Costume

A wardrobe is the easy part of a persona.

The hard part is everything that comes after it.

Where are you from? Who do you know here? Why did you leave your last job? How long have you been doing this? Who taught you?

Every answer is a claim. And every claim is a thread that can unravel the persona.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

Three disciplines follow.

Keep the persona thin. The best cover story is the smallest one. Every invented detail is another fact that must be remembered, and every additional fact creates another opportunity for contradiction. A persona should remain as close to the researcher’s real experience as safety permits, with as little fiction as possible.

Do the job properly. A researcher who takes a stall, an apprenticeship or a market post must actually work it. The persona is not merely an explanation for being there. It is a social obligation to the people around it. A researcher who plays a vulcaniser’s assistant badly, or works half-heartedly, is not simply compromising the research. The researcher is becoming a bad neighbour.

Set the boundaries before entering the field. There are things the persona must never do, regardless of what circumstances appear to demand.

It must not participate in illegal activity.

It must not pass information to an armed group or other violent actor.

It must not manipulate friendships or intimate relationships simply to extract information.

And it must never assume the identity of a real person by borrowing that person’s name, documents or reputation.

These limits matter more than the sophistication of the technique.

The moment the persona begins making decisions for the researcher, the method has become a risk.

The Exit Is Designed Before the Entry

In Part 2, I described a researcher who could blend in.

What I did not say clearly enough is that the ability to leave is itself part of the method.

At the Sundiata Post Knowledge Lab (SPKL), the governing principle is straightforward:

No researcher enters a zone before the exit has been written down.

In practice, that means four things.

Someone outside knows the plan. A base contact holds the schedule, the check-in windows and the agreed procedure if a check-in is missed. Immersion is not a solo act.

Triggers are decided in advance. The point at which an assignment ends must be established before the researcher becomes emotionally or intellectually invested in completing it. These include any imminent threat to life, which the rules below treat as overriding the persona. The conditions that terminate the assignment are agreed in a calm room because they may not be assessable calmly in the field.

The departure is ordinary. A sudden disappearance can draw attention not only to the researcher but also to the people who worked beside the persona. The best exit therefore has a plain, believable explanation and leaves the community with as little exposure as possible. That ordinary explanation is itself a second, quieter lie, and it must stay consistent for as long as the people who trusted the persona remain.

The data leaves separately from the person. Field notes should be minimal. Where circumstances permit, they should be written after leaving the site rather than in it. Information should be stored so that the loss or search of the researcher’s device does not expose other people, and whatever is recorded should be safe if it is lost. On leaving, the researcher writes a method record covering what was done, how, and at what cost, without identities, for the panel to review.

Behind all four principles sits one question:

Who could be blamed after I am gone?

The researcher leaves. The market remains. The neighbours remain.

The people who trusted the persona remain. That is why the exit is not logistics. It is ethics.

The Ethics of Research in the Dark

Now to the third obligation.

By the ethics of going dark, I mean the obligations that bind a researcher who works under a borrowed identity, without the knowledge of the people observed, in places where openness would be unsafe or would defeat the research.

It asks two questions. When, if ever, is concealment justified? And what is owed to the people it touches?

The answer here has four parts: tests that decide whether to go dark at all, rules for harm witnessed or suffered, honest disclosure of the method afterwards, and duties to both the people observed and the researcher.

None of this is new ground. Research ethics has argued about covert methods for decades, and this column builds on that work rather than replacing it. Journalism has argued about it for generations. Neither has concluded that deception is never permissible. Both have established that it is never automatic.

Deep immersion is the gold standard but a gold standard is only as good as the ethics that justify it.

Deep immersion may produce the richest data. That is precisely why it faces the strictest test. Four tests apply.

Necessity. Immersion comes last in the Tri-Tiered Approach. Remote tracking comes first, rapid intercept next. If either can answer the question, immersion is not justified.

Proportionality. The knowledge gained must justify the deception used to obtain it. The bar rises with the vulnerability of the people observed. Studying a market stallholder is harder to justify than studying an official or an institution. Foreseeable harm means any harm someone who knows the community could anticipate: reprisal, stigma, lost livelihood or legal jeopardy. No one observed may face it so that the researcher can have better data.

Protection. Names, precise locations and identifying details stay out of the record unless essential. Data that cannot be protected should not be collected merely because it is interesting.

Accountability. No institution approves its own covert research. Before any immersion, a panel of outside advisers, appointed independently of the unit, reviews the case in writing. The panel’s terms are published. It can veto. Its decision is reported in the method account. And no researcher enters a jurisdiction without a legal review for that jurisdiction.

Three hard cases test these principles harder than any others.

What if the persona witnesses a crime?

The rule that the persona must not participate in illegal activity covers what the researcher does. It does not cover what the researcher sees.

Reporting may endanger the people the researcher is protecting. Silence may make the researcher complicit. The rule must therefore be set before entry, not in the moment.

Life outranks the cover. Where a life is in imminent danger, meaning likely to be lost before help or withdrawal could prevent it, the researcher warns or withdraws, even at the cost of the persona. Everything else is recorded, and the panel decides what follows.

A researcher who has not settled this in advance will settle it under pressure. That is the worst time to do so.

What if the persona is exposed?

Exposure, detention and compromise are not remote possibilities. They are possibilities the protocol plans for.

The researcher withdraws. The base contact informs the panel. The unit’s first act is to protect those who worked beside the persona. The failure is reported in the method account like any other outcome.

What if disclosure itself exposes people?

I have said the deception should end, at the latest, when the findings become public. But publication can expose the very neighbours the method was designed to protect.

So disclosure has two parts. The method is disclosed in full: what was done, how, why and at what cost. The identities are not. Details that could trace a finding back to a stall, a street or a person are altered or withheld, and the account says so openly.

The community’s consent cannot be obtained in advance, because asking would defeat the research. That is exactly why the other safeguards must be strict. Where consent is impossible, restraint must carry the weight.

The duty to the people observed.

The researcher’s protection is only half of the duty. The people observed carry risk too: reprisal, stigma, broken trust and legal exposure. They receive none of the salary, the training or the byline.

So no one observed may pay a foreseeable price for the findings. If they discover the research, they have a channel to respond, answered by someone outside the unit. Findings are returned to the community in a form it can use. And no benefit is taken from the research without sharing it.

The duty to the researcher.

An institution should never ask an individual to accept a risk it would not bear itself. Field researchers must be trained, briefed, fairly paid and free to refuse or withdraw without penalty.

A methodology that works only because someone else absorbs the danger is not a methodology.

It is an outsourcing of risk.

That is true of the researcher. It is equally true of the community.

SPKL will publish its field ethics protocol, covering legal review, data handling and the panel’s terms, so that every commitment here can be checked.

The Lie Must End. The Record Must Not.

Part 2 closed with the researcher living “a quiet lie” in order to find the truth.

I stand by the phrase. But the tests, the panel and the rules for the hard cases all lead to one condition: a lie in the field is defensible, if at all, only when the account afterwards is honest about the method.

That means being honest about what was done, how it was done, why it was done, and what it cost.

The people may be protected. The method may not.

That is the distinction between a researcher who deceives and a fraud who happens to write notes. The first accounts for the deception. The second conceals it.

The wardrobe was never the point. It was only the first layer of a much larger discipline.

The researcher must master the persona. The researcher must design the exit. The researcher must submit to the tests. And, finally, the researcher must be prepared to account for the entire exercise.

Going dark does not mean abandoning accountability. It means carrying accountability into the dark.

Part 4 turns to the question that gives this entire exercise its purpose: how does a stall in a market, a checkpoint on a road and a conversation over a recharge card or airtime become a number on the Decoupling Sovereignty Index?

Field evidence is only useful if it can be translated into a system that can be scored, tested and challenged.

The researcher may disappear into the field. The method cannot.

From the Desk to the World.

Max Nwabueze Amuchie is CEO and theorist-in-chief of Sundiata Post, lead researcher at the Sundiata Post Knowledge Lab (SPKL), and an Expert Member and Peer Reviewer in Behavioural and Social Sciences at ScienceOpen. He is the formulator of three frameworks — the Sundiata Post Model (SPM), The Insecurity Triad framework, and the Trinity of Sovereignty Decay (TSD) theory—and the creator of the Decoupling Sovereignty Index (DSI), the quantitative extension of TSD. His work develops original frameworks for understanding, explaining, and measuring insecurity, conflict, state decay, and sovereignty, with particular relevance to the Global South. World.title: Burkina Faso, Niger, Mali resume talks with ECOWAS after withdrawal from regional bloc
World.content:
Burkina Faso, Niger and Mali have resumed formal discussions with the Economic Community of West African States (ECOWAS), agreeing to work towards establishing a framework for cooperation despite their withdrawal from the regional bloc.

The three Sahel countries officially left ECOWAS in January 2025 after forming the Alliance of Sahel States (AES), amid growing disagreements with the bloc.

Saturday’s meeting, held in Dakar, is believed to be the first official ministerial-level engagement between the two sides, although discussions had been ongoing since January 2025.

In a joint statement issued on Saturday evening, both sides welcomed the discussions, citing fraternity, mutual respect and openness as guiding principles. They also emphasised the importance of good neighbourly relations and respect for national sovereignty.

The parties agreed to establish joint thematic working groups to develop a framework cooperation agreement.

Burkina Faso’s Foreign Minister, Karamoko Traore, led the AES delegation, while Senegal’s Foreign Minister, Cheikh Niang, headed the ECOWAS team.

Insecurity across the Sahel

Across the AES countries and other parts of the Sahel, armed groups continue to carry out attacks and expand towards coastal West African countries. Mali, Burkina Faso and Niger have battled jihadist insurgencies for more than a decade, with al-Qaeda- and Islamic State-linked groups exploiting weak state presence, porous borders and local grievances.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

In Mali, coordinated attacks on 25 April targeted several locations, with the violence involving Jama’at Nusrat al-Islam wal-Muslimin (JNIM), an al-Qaeda affiliate, and the Azawad Liberation Front, a separatist movement. The country’s Defence Minister, Sadio Camara, was killed during the attacks.

In Burkina Faso and Niger, armed groups have also sustained pressure on security forces and civilians, while violence has increasingly threatened northern Benin and Togo.

Also, Nigeria, the largest economy in the region, faces overlapping security threats, including Boko Haram and Islamic State West Africa Province (ISWAP) insurgencies, banditry and mass kidnappings.

With armed groups operating across borders, strained relations between Nigeria and the AES countries risk weakening intelligence-sharing and joint counterterrorism operations. Niger’s withdrawal from the Multinational Joint Task Force in March 2025 gave a clear implication of the collapsed regional cooperation.

The challenge of regional cooperation

The AES countries have pursued an independent security and political course, distancing themselves from France and strengthening ties with Russia.

READ ALSO: ECOWAS Court gets four new judges

Their withdrawal from ECOWAS has complicated regional cooperation, despite shared threats that require intelligence-sharing, effective border controls and coordinated military responses.

The diplomatic disputes have also been fuelled by allegations from Sahelian leaders that neighbouring countries and foreign powers are supporting armed groups. Such claims remain contested, and allegations should not be treated as established facts without independently verifiable evidence.

It is not yet clear whether the renewed talks envisage the AES states returning to the regional bloc. If this is not part of the agenda, it will be interesting to see how ECOWAS, which has traditionally emphasised democratic governance, navigates diplomatic engagement with the junta-led countries while addressing mounting security threats across their shared borders.

World.title: ‘Please forgive me’: Fatai Okoya begs billionaire father after 40 years apart
World.content:
More than four decades after becoming estranged from his father, Fatai Okoya has publicly appealed to billionaire industrialist Razaq Akanni Okoya for forgiveness and an opportunity to rebuild their relationship.

Mr Fatai, who identifies himself as the Eleganza Group founder’s first child, appealed in an open letter that circulated online.

He said the years they had spent apart weighed heavily on him and urged his father to allow them to make peace while they still had time.

“More than four decades have passed, and today, I write with a humble heart, putting aside all pride to say: Dad, I am truly sorry. Please, find it in your heart to forgive me,” he wrote.

The letter, signed “Your First Child, Fatai Okoya,” has generated reactions online, with some people expressing sympathy and others questioning what caused the prolonged estrangement.

‘Pain of separation’

Mr Fatai said he had made previous attempts to reach his father and resolve their differences, but the separation continued to cause him pain.

“Over the years, I have tried to reach out and make peace because the pain of our separation and the precious years we have lost weigh heavily on my heart,” he said.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

“No matter what has happened, you remain my father, and I will forever be your first child.”

He asked Mr Okoya to look beyond the events that separated them, saying they could not recover the years already lost but could decide what happened next.

“Dad, we cannot turn back the hands of time, but we can choose to make the years ahead different,” he wrote.

“Life is precious, time waits for no one, and I do not want us to lose any more opportunities to love, forgive and reconnect.”

Although Mr Fatai repeatedly referred to past pain and differences, he did not explain what caused the rift or why the separation lasted for more than four decades.

‘Let us begin again’

Mr Fatai said he wanted a chance to heal their relationship and restore their bond.

“I am simply asking for a chance a chance to heal, to make peace and to rebuild the bond between a father and his child,” he wrote.

He said he was prepared to pursue reconciliation with humility and an open mind.

“Dad, please, let love speak louder than the pain of the past. Let forgiveness open a door that has been closed for far too long. I am ready to take that step with humility, sincerity and an open heart.”

He ended the letter with another apology, saying that despite their years apart, he still wanted his father back in his life.

“I love you, Dad. I miss you, and deep down, I still long for the blessing of having my father back in my life,” he wrote.

“Dad, I am truly sorry. My heart is open, my hands are extended, and my hope for reconciliation remains alive. Please, let us begin again.”

The Okoya family

Razaq Okoya founded the Eleganza Group, a manufacturing conglomerate known for producing household and consumer goods.

He began his business career as a trader before expanding into manufacturing and establishing Eleganza in the early 1970s.

The industrialist has a large family, although the precise number of his children has not been publicly confirmed by him.

In February 2026, one of his sons, Raheem Okoya, popularly known as Siraheem, said in an interview that his father had 26 children with nine women.

The singer described himself as the 23rd child and said the eldest was about 60 years old.

However, the information available for this report does not independently establish Mr Fatai’s claim that he is the billionaire’s first child.

Mr Fatai’s mother’s identity also remains unclear. He did not name her in the letter, and PREMIUM TIMES found no reliable public record identifying her.

The circumstances surrounding the estrangement also remain unclear. Beyond saying he had previously sought peace, Mr Fatai did not provide details of his reported attempts to contact his father.

As of the time of this report, Mr Okoya had not publicly responded to the letter.

World.title: Presidency disputes Makinde’s claim of N250 billion NLNG dividends per state
World.content:
The presidency has disputed Oyo State Governor Seyi Makinde’s claim that the federal government is withholding N250 billion in Nigeria Liquefied Natural Gas Limited (NLNG) dividends meant for each state, describing the allegation as “false.”

Bayo Onanuga, special adviser to President Bola Tinubu on information and strategy, said in a statement on Sunday that the amount claimed by the governor was inconsistent with the revenue-sharing formula and the history of NLNG’s dividend payments to the Federation.

Mr Onanuga argued that a one-off payment of N250 billion to each of Nigeria’s 36 states would amount to N9 trillion, excluding the federal government, the Federal Capital Territory and the 774 local government areas.

“Under the Federation Account Allocation Committee (FAAC) formula, states receive 26.72 per cent of the distributable Federation Account revenue. For the states’ share alone to reach N9 trillion, total NLNG dividends paid into the Federation Account would have to exceed N33.68 trillion (about $25 billion) in a single declaration,” the statement read. “NLNG has never paid $25 billion in dividends to the Federation Account in a single payout.”

Mr Onanuga urged the public to disregard the claim. “Makinde’s latest claim that the Federal Government is withholding the NLNG dividend windfall is false and should be disregarded.”

However, the presidency’s statement did not provide a transaction-by-transaction reconciliation of the specific NLNG dividend proceeds referenced by Mr Makinde or a breakdown of the sums allegedly due to individual states.

The dispute followed remarks by Mr Makinde at the 2027 Budget Stakeholders’ Consultative Engagement in Ibadan on Friday, where he alleged that the Federal Government had spent the dividend proceeds instead of distributing the states’ shares.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

“They fooled us. The Nigeria LNG paid dividends to the Federal Government, which went straight into the Federation Account, but they spent it,” Mr Makinde said,

He stated that the amounts due to the states had been reconciled and that each state was expected to receive more than N250 billion.

Mr Makinde, the presidential candidate of the Allied People’s Movement for the upcoming 2027 elections, further alleged that the release of the funds had been postponed until after the 2027 general elections, questioning why political considerations should take precedence over the needs of citizens.

“Each state was supposed to get N250 billion. We had already identified projects that would expand Oyo State’s economy. But they have now said the money will not be paid until after the election. Is the election more important than the people of Nigeria?” the governor said.

Presidency’s argument

Responding, Mr Onanuga said states receive 26.72 per cent of distributable Federation Account revenue under the Federation Account Allocation Committee (FAAC) sharing formula.

He argued that for the states’ combined share to reach N9 trillion, the total NLNG dividends paid into the Federation Account would have to exceed N33.68 trillion ($25 billion), in a single declaration.

“NLNG has never paid $25 billion in dividends to the Federation Account in a single payout,” the presidency’s statement read.

According to the statement, NLNG has paid approximately $21.5 billion in dividends to the Federation over the past 25 years, with less than $3 billion realised since Mr Tinubu assumed office.

Mr Onanuga argued that the amount allegedly being withheld would therefore exceed the company’s entire historical dividend payments to the Federation.

“Therefore, any claim that a single payout exceeds the company’s entire lifetime distribution to the Federation—and is being withheld—defies basic logic and economic reality,” he said.

World.title: Protect indigenous seeds, farmers’ rights, HOMEF tells FG on World Food Day
World.content:
The Health of Mother Earth Foundation (HOMEF), an environmental advocacy organisation, has called on the federal government to protect indigenous seeds and farmers’ rights, warning that industrial agricultural practices and restrictive seed policies could undermine food sovereignty, biodiversity, and nutrition.

The organisation made the call on Friday to mark World Food Day, observed annually on 16 October, arguing that hunger and malnutrition persist in resource-rich countries because of political and economic choices that disadvantage smallholder farmers and local food systems.

In a statement made available to PREMIUM TIMES by its Media and Communications Manager, Kome Odhomor, HOMEF said food security requires more than increasing agricultural output. It called for policies that protect local seed varieties, promote ecological farming and give farming communities greater control over what they grow and how they produce food.

The organisation also called on Nigerians to pay closer attention to the origins and nutritional quality of their food, warning that climate change, economic instability, and conflict continue to threaten food production and distribution.

Food sovereignty

Nnimmo Bassey, HOMEF’s executive director, said Nigeria’s food system was overly dependent on monoculture and cash-crop production, which he noted weakened food supply chains, depleted soil health and reduced farmers’ control over agricultural production.

“World Food Day should be a day of reflection. It must also be a day of structural reckoning,” Mr Bassey said, calling for a shift from industrial uniformity towards diverse and ecologically sustainable farming systems.

He said indigenous seeds are critical to adapting to climate change because they preserve genetic diversity that can support drought resistance, pest management, and improved nutrition.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

“We must move beyond the short-sighted goal of ‘yield at any cost’ and support a transition to agroecology,” he said.

Agroecology applies ecological principles to agricultural production, emphasising soil health, biodiversity, local knowledge, and sustainable relationships between farming communities and their environment.

Mr Bassey said protecting indigenous seeds was essential to preventing biodiversity loss and sustaining ecosystems, arguing that food systems should not sacrifice environmental health for short-term production gains.

Seed laws, farmers’ rights

HOMEF’s Director of Programmes, Joyce Brown, said hunger in resource-rich African countries reflected failures in political and economic decision-making.

She said that food should not be treated merely as a commodity for profit but as a fundamental human right connected to public health, cultural identity and community livelihoods.

Ms Brown called on governments and international institutions to review policies that, she said, privilege industrial exporters over small-scale farmers who supply local communities.

She specifically raised concerns about Nigeria’s Plant Variety Protection Act, 2021, explaining that restrictions on farmers’ ability to save and reuse seeds could threaten the food and nutritional security of vulnerable communities.

The law provides a framework for protecting the rights of breeders of new plant varieties. The debate over its implementation includes questions about how breeders’ rights should be balanced with farmers’ traditional practices and access to seeds.

Ms Brown said agricultural policies should recognise farmers’ rights and ensure that communities closest to the land retain meaningful authority over what they grow and how they use their resources.

‘Industrial agriculture not the only solution’

Mariann Bassey-Olsson, deputy director of Environmental Rights Action/Friends of the Earth Nigeria, described seed-saving and exchange as essential to farmers’ independence and the preservation of cultural heritage.

She rejected the argument that industrial agriculture was the only viable way to feed the world, saying smallholder farmers had sustained communities for generations through locally adapted farming practices.

Ms Bassey-Olsson said indigenous seeds embodied generations of farmers’ knowledge and adaptation to local soils and climatic conditions.

She warned that losing control of local seed varieties could make farmers increasingly dependent on foreign corporations and weaken their ability to adapt to changing environmental conditions.

She also opposed genetically modified crops, saying it could threaten farmers’ seed rights and biodiversity and increase dependence on foreign companies.

Her position reflects HOMEF’s call for increased investment in agroecology and locally controlled food systems, rather than approaches that put industrial agricultural interests at the centre of food production.

Food security, climate change

HOMEF said future food systems should prioritise nutritional quality, environmental sustainability and farmers’ livelihoods, rather than focus narrowly on increasing yields.

It called for better access to agricultural knowledge, tools and resources for smallholder farmers and marginalised communities, warning that climate change and other socioeconomic pressures could further destabilise food supplies.

The organisation also asked governments to support diverse local food systems that can withstand climate shocks while protecting biodiversity and improving soil health.

World Food Day is an annual international observance that raises awareness of hunger and food insecurity and promotes access to safe, nutritious, and affordable food.

World.title: NCDMB, Heritage Energy train 48 Nigerians in subsea engineering
World.content:
The Nigerian Content Development and Monitoring Board (NCDMB), in partnership with Heritage Energy Operational Services Limited (HEOSL) and Global Oceon Engineers Nigeria Limited, has launched a Human Capacity Development programme to train 48 Nigerians in subsea engineering.

The kick-off ceremony took place on Friday, 16 October, in Port Harcourt, Rivers State, as part of the Board’s efforts to address critical skills gaps and strengthen indigenous technical expertise in the oil and gas industry.

The programme combines six months of classroom instruction with six months of structured on-the-job training, giving participants specialised knowledge and practical experience in subsea engineering. The curriculum covers risers and hydrodynamics engineering, offshore structures design and engineering, pipeline engineering, and computer-aided design and drafting (AutoCAD).

In his keynote address, the Executive Secretary of NCDMB, Felix Omatsola Ogbe, a Fellow of Nigerian Society of Engineers, represented by the General Manager, Human Capacity Development, Ms Emelle Alexis, said the programme would equip the trainees with the technical expertise required for complex subsea operations and the safe, efficient and reliable operation of modern oil and gas facilities.

“Today marks the beginning of a transformational journey for 48 young Nigerians in a highly specialised field that demands precision, discipline and accountability. Through intensive classroom instruction and structured on-the-job training, the participants will gain hands-on experience in subsea engineering,” he said.

Ogbe stressed that subsea operations require technical competence, professionalism and an unwavering commitment to safety.

“The competencies you acquire through this programme are critical to the safe, efficient, reliable and environmentally responsible operation of modern oil and gas facilities. Beyond technical proficiency, the training is designed to develop your problem-solving skills, teamwork, professionalism and commitment to safety,” he stated.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

The Executive Secretary urged the trainees to make the most of the opportunity and demonstrate the discipline and commitment required to succeed in the industry. He expressed confidence that they would emerge with the skills and professional standards needed to contribute to the sector.

In his remarks, the Manager, Nigerian Content Development at Heritage Energy, Felix Osiwo, reaffirmed the company’s commitment to indigenous skills development. He noted that a skilled Nigerian workforce is essential to delivering current and future energy infrastructure projects and sustaining industry growth.

Earlier in his welcome address, the Managing Director of Global Oceon Engineers Nigeria Limited, George Ebuh, represented by Ifedolapo Aderibigbe, described the programme as a strategic investment by Heritage Energy, NCDMB and Global Oceon in developing indigenous subsea engineering expertise. He noted that skilled local professionals are vital to the safe and reliable operation of offshore and deepwater infrastructure.

The trainees expressed appreciation for the opportunity to acquire specialised subsea engineering skills, identifying safety training and AutoCAD as important areas of learning. The programme is part of NCDMB’s Top 10 Field Readiness Human Capacity Development initiatives, designed to address critical skills gaps in the oil and gas industry. It supports the Board’s efforts to develop specialised Nigerian expertise for offshore and deepwater operations, facilitate technology transfer and increase local participation in high-value industry activities.

The ceremony was attended by representatives of NCDMB, Heritage Energy Operational Services Limited and Global Oceon Engineers Nigeria Limited, as well as the trainees, facilitators and other industry stakeholders.

World.title: PANDEF declares seven days of mourning for Dele Cole
World.content:
By Henry Umoru

ABUJA — The Pan Niger Delta Forum (PANDEF), the apex socio-political body of the South-South geopolitical zone, has declared seven days of mourning in honour of its leader and elder statesman, Patrick Dele Cole, who died in London at the age of 86.

Cole, popularly known as Chief PDC, died weeks after celebrating his 86th birthday, leaving behind a legacy of service in journalism, education, diplomacy, public administration and politics.

In a statement signed by PANDEF National Chairman, Ambassador Godknows Igali, on behalf of the organisation’s Board of Trustees (BoT) and National Executive Committee (NEC), the forum described Cole’s death as a painful and irreplaceable loss.

Igali said Cole played significant roles in the socio-cultural and political development of the Niger Delta, particularly in the formation and growth of PANDEF.

The late Cole served as Editor-in-Chief of the Daily Times of Nigeria, one of the country’s leading national newspapers, and later as presidential adviser on foreign affairs. He also served as Nigeria’s ambassador to Brazil.

According to Igali, Cole brought considerable intellectual depth and experience to various socio-cultural and socio-political organisations in the Niger Delta.

PANDEF directed all its chapters in Nigeria and the diaspora to suspend official social activities for seven days, beginning October 18, 2026. It also directed that Cole’s photograph be displayed on its media platforms throughout the mourning period.

Igali said Cole played a significant role in the region’s struggle for true federalism and resource control, noting that his commitment to the aspirations of the Niger Delta people remained firm even while he served as a special adviser in the administration of former President Olusegun Obasanjo.

He added that Cole’s political choices were guided by his commitment to the interests and legitimate aspirations of the Niger Delta people.

Cole’s political career included a presidential bid under the Social Democratic Party (SDP) and membership of the Board of Trustees of the Peoples Democratic Party (PDP), PANDEF said.

The forum also acknowledged his contributions as a Christian leader and advocate of Nigeria’s cultural heritage, particularly the traditions and identities of the South-South region.

Expressing condolences over his death, PANDEF extended its sympathies to his son, Rt. Hon. Tonye Cole, other members of the Cole family, the people of Abonnema in the Kalabari Kingdom, the Ijaw nation, the Rivers State Government and the people of Rivers State, as well as Nigerians across the country.

The organisation urged the bereaved family and the wider Niger Delta community to draw comfort from the distinguished life and enduring contributions of the late elder statesman.

PANDEF prayed for the peaceful repose of Cole’s soul.

World.title: Nigeria joins league of nations in global measurement pact
World.content:
By Adaobi Abimbola

Nigeria has joined the league of nations with globally recognised measurement standards following the signing of the Mutual Recognition Arrangement of the International Committee for Weights and Measures, CIPM MRA, in France.

The agreement was signed by the Director-General of the Standards Organisation of Nigeria, SON, Dr Ifeanyi Chukwunonso Okeke, at the 28th General Conference on Weights and Measures CGPM. The signing coincided with the DG’s third anniversary in office.

According to a statement made by SON’s Director of Corporate Affairs, Mrs. Ethan Talatu, Nigeria’s admission as an Associate State of the International Bureau of Weights and Measures, BIPM, took effect on June 4, 2026.

The CIPM MRA is the framework through which national metrology institutes prove that their measurement standards are equivalent and earn global recognition for their calibration and measurement certificates.

Okeke said that the arrangement would bring international recognition of Nigeria’s measurement capabilities, global acceptance of its calibration certificates and easier trade across borders. He added that it would reduce dependence on foreign metrology services, strengthen SON’s technical authority and open doors to scientific collaboration and capacity building.

Nigeria now joins Egypt, Kenya, Morocco, South Africa and Tunisia as the only African countries with full BIPM membership. For manufacturers and small businesses, products can be tested locally and trusted abroad without the cost of foreign laboratories.

World.title: FG targets $7.1bn sugar investments, 110,000 jobs in 10 years
World.content:
The Federal Government is targeting $7.1 billion in investments in the sugar industry over 10 years to boost domestic production above two million metric tonnes annually, create 110,000 jobs and save $2.1 billion in foreign exchange annually.

The programme, coordinated by the National Sugar Development Council (NSDC), is aimed at reducing Nigeria’s dependence on imported raw sugar through increased sugarcane cultivation, processing capacity and private-sector investment.

Executive Secretary of NSDC, Kamar Bakrin, disclosed the plan in Abuja, saying the initiative would strengthen local production and supporting agricultural infrastructure.

Under the programme, the council is proposing 10 integrated sugar estates across Niger, Kwara, Oyo, Kaduna, Jigawa, Bauchi, Nasarawa and Adamawa states. The estates are expected to cover 143,478 hectares, with a combined milling capacity of 55,500 metric tonnes of sugarcane daily.

According to NSDC, the proposed estates could produce 835,000 metric tonnes of sugar annually, while existing operators are expected to contribute another 1.22 million tonnes through increased output.

The projects are also expected to support ethanol production and electricity generation, creating additional opportunities for agro-processing and value addition.

To finance the programme, the council is seeking $5 billion in long-term debt and $2.1 billion in equity contributions from investors. Funding is expected to involve export credit agencies, development finance institutions and local financial organisations.

NSDC also disclosed a $1 billion agreement with Chinese engineering company Sinomach, although the associated financing arrangements are yet to be completed. It is collaborating with the Bank of Industry on a proposed N10 billion Sugar Projects Acceleration Fund to support feasibility studies and prepare projects for investment.

World.title: Manufacturing index plunges 10% as cement sector contracts – NESG
World.content:
