World.title: Africa: Every Story Is Unique, Every Journey Matters for Women's Cancers
World.content:
Raising awareness of early detection of breast cancer, at the WHO regional office for Africa.

guest column

Addis Ababa and Geneva — Leaders of the Organization of African First Ladies for Development, the African Union and the World Health Organization issue a call to accelerate action on women's cancers in Africa in this AllAfrica guest column during Breast Cancer Awareness Month

Across Africa, too many women are dying prematurely from breast and cervical cancers. In 2024 alone, 350,000 women across the continent died from these diseases, often because prevention, early detection, diagnosis and treatment came too late or were inaccessible.

Behind every statistic is a woman, a family and a community. A mother waiting too long for a diagnosis. A daughter unable to access preventive care. A family struggling to afford treatment.

These stories are unique but the responsibility to respond is shared.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

Our message to governments, policymakers and partners is clear: the time has come to accelerate action on women's cancers and move them from the margins of health policy to the centre of Africa's health, development and financing agendas.

The African Union is leading the way by placing the health and wellbeing of Africa's people at the heart of the continent's development agenda. This leadership provides an important platform for Member States to translate continental commitments on women's health, noncommunicable diseases and universal health coverage into measurable results.

Through the Organization of African First Ladies for Development (OAFLAD), African First Ladies are bringing a complementary and powerful form of leadership. They are using their voices and platforms to mobilize political attention, engage communities, challenge stigma and keep the experiences of women and families visible in national and continental discussions.

WHO, through its initiatives on breast and cervical cancer, is supporting governments and communities with the evidence, technical approaches and implementation support needed to translate political commitment into effective services.

The challenge is substantial.

Breast and cervical cancer burdens are increasing across Africa. Women still face barriers to vaccination, screening, diagnosis, referral, treatment, palliative care and survivorship support. Diagnosis frequently occurs at advanced stages, when treatment becomes more difficult, more costly and less likely to succeed. WHO's latest Global Status Report on Cancer, issued this year, provided the first global estimates of breast cancer survival and cervical cancer screening coverage. It showed that the African continent is lagging behind the progress happening elsewhere.

Yet there is hope. WHO's Global Breast Cancer Initiative and Cervical Cancer Elimination Initiative provide governments with a practical pathway to improve outcomes. Through multi-sectoral partnerships, WHO is bringing resources to implement new global standards in the prevention and care of breast and cervical cancers, already benefiting millions of women on the continent.

Current efforts alone are not enough.

Governments must integrate women's cancers into national health strategies, primary health care, essential benefit packages and domestic financing priorities. Development partners must align behind country-led priorities and invest in sustainable systems rather than fragmented interventions. Parliamentarians must support enabling legislation, adequate budgets and accountability. Survivors, civil society and communities must have a meaningful voice in shaping policies and assessing progress. Political champions must keep women's cancers visible at the highest levels of decision-making.

The respective strengths of our institutions must be pooled.

OAFLAD uses advocacy and mobilizes political attention. The African Union provides continental leadership and policy direction. WHO brings evidence, standards and technical and implementation support. Governments translate commitments into national policies, budgets and services. Partners bring catalytic financing, innovation and implementation capacity.

Together, these contributions can turn awareness into policy, policy into investment and investment into services that women can actually access.

The steps to expand this access are clear.

We must expand HPV vaccination, cervical cancer screening and breast health awareness. We must shorten the time from detection to diagnosis and treatment. We must strengthen pathology, imaging, referral pathways, surgery, radiotherapy, access to medicines, palliative care and survivorship support. We must also protect families from financial hardship caused by cancer care.

These investments can do more than strengthen cancer care for women. They will reinforce primary health care and accelerate progress towards universal health coverage.

The time is ripe to make these investments and deliver results. Africa stands at a defining moment. Through the African Union, OAFLAD, WHO, governments and many committed partners, there is today a growing momentum to advance a stronger continental agenda for women's cancers and other noncommunicable diseases.

During October's Breast Cancer Awareness Month, the theme "Every Story is Unique, Every Journey Matters" reminds us that every woman experiences cancer differently. But the need is universal for sustained leadership, financing, investment in research and accountability to deliver these solutions at scale. possible thanks to the leadership, knowledge and capacity that Africa possesses to protect women's futures from the threat of cancer. What will make these advances possible is the leadership, knowledge and capacity that Africa possesses to protect women's futures from the threat of cancer.

Access to prevention and care should never depend on geography, income or circumstance.

We call for greater investment in the prevention and care of women's cancers. We call for women-centred policies that place equity, dignity and access at the heart of cancer care. We call for reliable domestic financing, aligned partner support and stronger accountability for results. We call for greater protections from the social, physical and economic hardship that cancer can bring.

Close 

This is not only a call for greater awareness. It is a call to governments, political leaders, partners and communities to act with urgency.

Because every woman deserves the opportunity to live a healthy and productive life.

Because every family deserves more time with its mothers, daughters and sisters. And because Africa's development depends on the health of its women and girls.

For Africa, tackling women's cancers is not only a health imperative; it is a question of equity, dignity and development, and a measure of whether our health systems serve every woman.

The measure of our commitment will not be the declarations we make, but whether women can access prevention, screening, timely diagnosis and quality treatment when and where they need them.

H.E. Dr Fatima Maada Bio is President of the Organization of African First Ladies for Development; H.E. Amb. Amma Twum-Amoa is African Union Commissioner for Health, Humanitarian Affairs and Social Development; Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus is Director-General of the World Health Organization

The authors acknowledge the WHO Liaison Office to the African Union and UNECA, the UN Economic Commission for Africa, for coordinating this joint contribution.

World.title: Kenya: Mackenzie Faces Verdict Over 191 Murder Charges in Shakahola Case
World.content:
Nairobi — The High Court is set to rule on Monday whether controversial preacher Paul Nthenge Mackenzie and 30 co-accused are guilty of murdering 191 children, as families continue to seek answers over a tragedy in which the human rights commission documented 448 deaths.

Justice Diana Kavedza is scheduled to deliver the judgment at the Mombasa High Court at 9.30am, according to a Judiciary media advisory.

The case centres on deaths linked to Mackenzie's Good News International Church, whose activities came under scrutiny in April 2023 after authorities uncovered mass graves in Kilifi's Shakahola Forest, exposing an alleged starvation cult in which followers were reportedly encouraged to fast to death in the belief that they would meet Jesus.

Mackenzie charged with murder of 191 children in Shakahola



Minor, lactating mother detail deadly fasting ordeal under Mackenzie's orders

Cult leader Mackenzie stages sit-in at Shanzu court due to bullying by prison officials

The Kenya National Commission on Human Rights (KNCHR) documented 448 deaths in its Mashaka ya Shakahola report released in March 2024, while more than 600 people were reported missing.

The commission said fewer than 10 per cent of the bodies had been identified and handed over to families for burial.

The discoveries triggered a major search and exhumation operation, with forensic teams working to identify the victims and establish the circumstances surrounding their deaths.

In its investigation, the KNCHR found that the deaths were linked to starvation, strangulation, head injuries and dehydration, citing autopsy findings alongside accounts from survivors and witnesses. It also criticised state agencies for failing to act on earlier warnings about Mackenzie's activities.

The prosecution has argued that the accused were involved in a common plan that led to the deaths. doubt.

In April, Justice Kavedza ruled that Mackenzie and his co-accused had a case to answer, directing them to present their defence.

The April ruling meant the prosecution had established a prima facie case, a key threshold for further proceedings.

The trial featured testimony from survivors, relatives of victims, investigators and forensic experts. Evidence included postmortem findings and other material gathered during investigations into the deaths.

Prosecutors also relied on the doctrine of common intention, alleging that the accused acted together towards a shared objective. The defence was subsequently heard before the court reserved its judgment.

Close 

Beyond the criminal proceedings, the Shakahola tragedy prompted wider scrutiny of religious organisations and the state's response to allegations of harmful practices.

The KNCHR concluded that the state had failed to protect citizens from harm, citing missed opportunities to act on warnings, delays in investigations and shortcomings in the support provided to survivors and families.

The commission called for accountability among officials whose actions or omissions may have contributed to the tragedy, as well as improved rehabilitation and support for survivors.

World.title: Kenya: Kenya Cases Rise to 8, Spreads to 8th Congo Province
World.content:
Health workers in protective gear inside the Ebola treatment centre at Buniaâs referral hospital in Ituri province, eastern DRC, October 2026.

A senior health official in Kenya said there have now been 8 Ebola infections in the country, while in DR Congo the disease has spread to an eighth province.

Kenya's Health Ministry on Sunday confirmed another case of Ebola, bringing the number of confirmed infections in the country to eight.

News of another patient in the East African state came as health officials in Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) reported that the outbreak there had spread to an eighth province.

What Kenya's health director general said



"Today, 38 people were tested, and one tested positive for Ebola," Health Ministry Director-General Dr. Patrick Amoth said in an interview on Kenya's Citizen TV.

"He is a 49-year-old man who is not a healthcare worker. He developed fever, headache and muscle pain," Amoth said.

He went on to explain that the latest case was a patient attendant who cleaned utensils and linen and had likely been exposed to Kenya's first Ebola case, discovered earlier this month.

Amoth said patients in quarantine were being tested after developing symptoms and that the other six patients were stable after receiving supportive treatment. The first patient died on October 5.

Kenya has been on a heightened state of alert as a major outbreak of the highly contagious disease spread in Congo in central Africa.

Ebola now in 8th province in Congo

Also on Sunday, authorities in DRC said that the Ebola outbreak had spread to an eighth province in the north.

Congo's Health Ministry said that two cases including a death were recorded in Nord-Ubangi province which borders the Central African Republic (CAR).

"We see pockets of Ebola generally going down, but unfortunately geographically it's spreading out," said World Health Organization Regional Director for Africa Mohamed Yakub Janabi in an interview with The Associated Press in Beni, eastern Congo, on Friday.

It's currently the deadliest outbreak in Congo's history with authorities recording at least 9,400 cases, including over 4,500 deaths, in the outbreak declared in mid-May.

The current epidemic is caused by the Bundibugyo virus, a rare type of Ebola that has no approved vaccine or treatment.

Ebola is spread between people by direct contact with bodily fluids. It can cause fever, fatigue, and muscle pain, followed by vomiting and diarrhea. Some patients also develop internal or external bleeding.

World.title: Sudan: Drone Strikes Kill Civilians in Darfur and Kordofan As Attacks Target Eastern Sudan
World.content:
Children walk at a camp for displaced persons in Port Sudan, which is hosting families who fled violence across the country, including Darfur and Kordofan regions.

Bir Saliba / Abu Zabad Locality / El Mazroub / Wad Banda / Fouja Area / El Gedaref / Khashm El Girba / El Gedaref / El Burgeig — Drone attacks killed civilians in West Darfur and West Kordofan on Saturday, including women, while further strikes targeted military installations in eastern Sudan. A separate fire destroyed up to 80 commercial stalls in Northern State.

In West Darfur, a drone strike attributed to the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) killed several people, including six women, and injured five others in Bir Saliba, in Sarba locality. Sources said most of the victims were displaced people who had travelled to the area to work in agriculture.

The Joint Force, allied with the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF), took control of Bir Saliba in early October, while fighting has continued in surrounding areas.

Civilian lorry hit in West Kordofan



In West Kordofan, the Kordofan Observatory reported that an SAF drone strike on a civilian lorry near Ankush killed four civilians, including three women, and injured others on Saturday.

The vehicle had travelled from Abu Zabad locality, towards El Mazroub in North Kordofan. Civilians were on board, including patients travelling for medical treatment and people heading to the town to shop.

The Observatory also reported that a drone attack killed three civilians in Fouja area on Wednesday, while a separate strike on the village of El Janana, near Wad Banda, killed a child the same day.

Condemning the attacks, the Observatory said targeting civilians and civilian vehicles violated international humanitarian law and could amount to war crimes.

It called on the SAF to stop attacks on civilians in Kordofan and urged the RSF to keep away from residential areas. It also called for the incidents to be documented and those responsible held accountable.

Drone attacks target military sites in eastern Sudan

Drone attacks targeted military installations in El Gedaref, Khashm El Girba and the Upper Atbara and Setit Dam Complex on Sunday morning, according to eyewitnesses and field reports.

Air defences reportedly intercepted several drones, including three targeting the Ali Atbara Dam in El Fashaga locality and another over Khashm El Girba. Two drones targeting El Gedaref were also reportedly shot down. No casualties were reported.

Fire destroys up to 80 stalls in Northern State

In Northern State, a fire destroyed between 75 and 80 commercial stalls in El Burgeig market on Saturday evening.

Resident Shaker Abdelrahim told Radio Dabanga that people heard explosions before the evening prayer and then saw thick smoke rising from the market. The fire swept through stalls packed with goods, destroying their contents.

Initial accounts attributed the blaze to an electrical fault inside a shop. Abdelrahim said the concentration of perfume shops helped the flames spread rapidly.

World.title: Kenya: Three Years On From Kenya's Shakahola Cult Murders, Families Still Seek Closure
World.content:
A court in Mombasa, Kenya, will on Monday deliver a long-awaited verdict in the Shakahola sect murder trial. Paul Nthenge Mackenzie, a self-proclaimed pastor, is accused of forcing church members, including children, to starve themselves to death in order to meet Jesus. Three years after the tragedy, families of the victims are hoping for closure so they can finally mourn their loved ones.

In March 2023, a man reported to Kenyan police that relatives who had joined a new church had not come home. Authorities began searching the area, around the Shakahola forest, near the coastal town of Malindi - and found hundreds of shallow graves.

While a number of people were also found alive after the alert had been raised, hundreds more remain missing to this day.



Elizabeth Dzidza Mwatsuma's remains were identified through DNA profiling more than three years after she disappeared into the Shakahola forest.

In May this year, her relative Alice Mwajuma Deche was finally able to bury her.

But Deche, 66, still has 11 more members of her family to find. She lost two children and 10 grandchildren in the massacre.

"We have been through a difficult time. This was not an ordinary event. Losing 12 relatives is hard. But we are grateful that we found one of them," she told RFI.

Francis Wanje, a teacher, found his eight-year-old grandson in the forest on 17 March, 2023 after a distress call from his son.

He was the first survivor to come out of Shakahola. The boy's two younger siblings had starved to death there.

Wanje's family lost eight relatives in all, but has only been able to bury four.

Police link new bodies exhumed from Kenyan mass graves to starvation cult

Conflicting accounts

Paul Nthenge Mackenzie, leader of the Good News International church, has been charged with 191 counts of murder, manslaughter and terrorism in connection to the Shakahola deaths - charges he denies.

Thirty accomplices are also on trial in the case.

The state argues that the accused acted with a common purpose, and that children who died as a result of fasting could not have consented.

Over the course of the trial, differing accounts of what happened in the Shakahola forest emerged.

Witnesses said some of the accused worked at the site, in the role of village elders, guards, gravediggers and cooks.

One of the accused, Steven Sanga Muye, testified that people lived in Shakahola voluntarily and that fasting instructions came from the Holy Spirit, not Mackenzie.

But Lucas Owino Ogola, another co-accused, said he was forced to fast and was assaulted for refusing.

Steven Ngugi testified in April that he helped dig graves and bury the dead in good faith as a community member, according to a statement from the prosecution office.

He said the deaths were treated as spiritual rather than medical events, and that the group used "weddings" as a coded term for them.

Mackenzie, along with dozens of other suspects, faces charges of manslaughter, terrorism, child cruelty, torture and denial of education in several other cases which have yet to be tried.

Kenyan cult leader faces terrorism charges over mass starvation deaths

Stigma

By October 2023, a Kenyan senate inquiry had recorded 428 bodies exhumed, plus one suspect who died in custody. Later exhumations brought the number of bodies recovered to 446.

Of the 443 bodies and body parts held at the Malindi mortuary, only 34 have been positively identified through DNA matching.

Kilifi County executive committee member for health, Peter Mwarogo, says some families had traced their relatives but declined to collect the remains for cultural reasons.

"Some people were able to trace their relatives, but they refused to come and take the body because of the stigma," he said.

The county has given the families until mid-October to claim remains. Those left unclaimed will be buried through a court-approved process at a site near Shakahola by December, with the graves arranged so the dead can still be identified later.

Kenya's Interior Cabinet Secretary Kipchumba Murkomen said the identification process has been slowed by the condition of the remains, and difficulties obtaining DNA reference samples from relatives.

"The biggest problem is not funds. More people need to come out and give their DNA samples for matching."

Kenyan authorities should have prevented cult deaths, president says

Regulating churches

The Commission on Administrative Justice, Kenya's ombudsman, noted that there was "a gross dereliction of duty" by officials of the National Government Administration and the National Police Service, who ignored warnings about Mackenzie's activities between 2021 and 2023.

Close 

It called the deaths preventable and recommended disciplinary action for six officials.

Elema Halake, chief executive of the Independent Policing Oversight Authority, called the case a multi-agency failure.

The Shakahola tragedy has also opened a debate over how to regulate churches in Kenya without infringing on freedom of religion.

A presidential task force set up in May 2023 handed its report to President William Ruto in July 2024, recommending a separate statute and the re-registration of all religious institutions.

The resulting Religious Organisations Bill also proposed to penalise leaders who extort money through false miracles.

While cabinet approved a draft in July 2025, its application was stalled after the clergy appealed for the bill to be withdrawn.

"The laws are present, we have enough regulatory policies but they are not followed," says Bishop Francis Omondi of the Anglican Church.

But for task force chairman, Rev Mutava: "Our greatest fear is that if this is not implemented, we are likely to see another Shakahola."

World.title: Congo-Kinshasa: Ebola Vaccine Trials 'Reason for Hope' in DR Congo and Beyond
World.content:
Five months into the Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo, there is still no approved vaccine against the rare Bundibugyo strain that has now caused more than 4,000 deaths. But candidates currently undergoing trials give reason to hope, according to Emanuele Capobianco of Gavi, the global vaccine alliance.

The DRC's worst-ever Ebola outbreak has now passed the 9,000-case mark, with the number of deaths topping 4,000 at the beginning of this month.

Among the many challenges is the lack of any approved vaccines or treatments for the Bundibugyo strain of Ebola that is behind the outbreak.

The first clinical trial of a potential vaccine is expected to begin by the end of October, World Health Organization experts said on Tuesday.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

Ervebo, a vaccine already approved for use against the more common Zaire strain of Ebola, will undergo a full-scale human trial in the DRC to see if it offers any cross-protection against Bundibugyo.

Two vaccines specifically for Bundibugyo are also being developed, one by the University of Oxford and another by the US-based Moderna group. They are currently in the early stages of testing in smaller-scale clinical trials.

Capobianco, director of global health security at Gavi, told RFI they have the potential to save lives in this and future Ebola outbreaks.

RFI: What can you tell us about the development of a potential Bundibugyo vaccine?

Emanuele Capobianco: There is currently no approved vaccine specifically for this virus. However, several candidates are in development, which offers reason for hope.

Two are leading the way: one from the University of Oxford - developed with partners including the Serum Institute of India - and the one from Moderna, which uses messenger RNA (mRNA) technology. They rely on different platforms, but both target the Bundibugyo virus.

We are expecting the results of their phase 1 trials later in October. They will provide data on their safety and their ability to stimulate the immune system.

If the results are positive, phase 2 and 3 trials may begin on larger populations. These will last several months and will make it possible to evaluate their efficacy. If all goes well, a rollout could take place in the first half of 2027.

At the onset of the outbreak, Gavi mobilised $50 million (€44 million) to support the response, including access to vaccines. We are investing ahead of final results so that doses can be made available as soon as their efficacy is proven and their use is authorised.

Violence against healthcare workers in DRC hampers Ebola response

RFI: In the meantime, could the existing Ervebo vaccine help?

EC: Ervebo is approved for use against the Zaire strain of Ebola. It is safe and highly effective against this virus, but its protection against Bundibugyo has not been established.

The global stockpile contains approximately 500,000 doses of Ervebo. If it is demonstrated to be effective against Bundibugyo, we will therefore have a tool that could be deployed rapidly.

At the request of the Congolese government, 70,000 doses were released in August from the global stockpile funded by Gavi. A portion is being used for studies. Healthcare workers are also being vaccinated as part of a research protocol: they are protected against the Zaire strain, and monitoring them will make it possible to study whether this also provides protection against Bundibugyo.

RFI: What can be done before the vaccines arrive?

Ebola outbreaks have previously been contained without vaccination or specific treatment, through infection prevention, surveillance and early care. This outbreak, too, could be contained before the arrival of new vaccines.

Because of the security situation, the system is unable to detect cases early on, so we don't have have a strong surveillance system. We can't detect where the patients are, or support them as fast as required.

Seventy percent of deaths occur in communities, before patients even arrive in health facilities. A huge effort is needed to encourage people to go to health centres. We also need for health centres to get closer to people to provide the kind of support that will result in patients surviving.

By intervening early, you can reduce the number of infections from a single case. So there's a lot of work that can be done in this area.

Ebola outbreak spreads in DRC as misinformation hampers response

RFI: How can you convince people to get vaccinated, when the vaccine they got during a previous outbreak does not necessarily protect them against the current one?

First, a vaccine with proven safety and efficacy has to be available. Beyond that, healthcare workers are essential allies. They set an example and explain the benefits. Having well-informed, empathetic health professionals is a crucial first step.

Close 

Radio and television also have a role to play. However, direct, personal interaction is vital. It is important to engage with respected figures within communities - such as religious leaders, teachers and elders - who are not necessarily political figures.

These trusted individuals play a vital role in bridging what I call the final distance - the gap between the syringe and the arm. Even when the vaccine is available, administering it hinges on trust. And trust is hard to build, easy to lose.

RFI: These new vaccines may not be available until after this outbreak is over. Will the current research help regardless?

We are running a marathon. We have already covered several kilometres by nearing the end of the phase 1 trials. The results may prove useful for the current outbreak, but we must also look further ahead.

If we secure an effective vaccine against Bundibugyo, we will be able to build a global stockpile, just as Gavi did for the Zaire strain. We will then have doses available for future epidemics - not only in the DRC but in other countries too.

This article is based on an interview by RFI's Christina Okello and has been lightly edited for clarity.

World.title: Firefighters save historic 'Godfather' church from raging NYC warehouse blaze
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

Firefighters saved a historic New York City church, notable for its appearance in "The Godfather," as a four-alarm fire tore through a nearby vacant warehouse.

More than 200 firefighters and EMS personnel rushed to Mount Loretto in Staten Island after the blaze began to spread inside an empty warehouse at around 5:45 p.m. on Saturday, FDNY chief of operations Kevin Woods said at a press conference that evening.

"There is heavy, heavy damage to this structure, the roof did collapse, and right now we’re maintaining a collapse zone around that structure," Woods said.

NYC 5-ALARM FIRE INJURES AT LEAST 17 FIREFIGHTERS, OTHERS AS BLAZE DAMAGES MULTIPLE APARTMENT BUILDINGS

"Upon arrival, units encountered heavy fire throughout the building and immediately went into a defensive operation," Woods said. "We set up multiple large-caliber stream tower ladders and handlines."

The warehouse at 6581 Hylan Boulevard has been vacant for five years, but it is located near several other structures on the Mount Loretto grounds, including two schools and the historic Old Church of St. Joachim and St. Anne, which was famously featured in exterior shots of the baptism scene of the 1972 film "The Godfather."

FIRE BREAKS OUT AT HISTORIC BROADWAY THEATER THAT HOSTS 'THE BOOK OF MORMON' IN NEW YORK CITY

The ornate Catholic church was largely destroyed by a fire in 1973, though its façade survived, and it was rebuilt three years later.

Firefighters managed to control the blaze on Saturday and stop it from spreading to the other buildings. The fire was under control at around 8:30 p.m.

"It’s very windy out here tonight. Our units did a great job with many of the flying embers, preventing additional structures from going on fire," Woods said.

Woods said one firefighter suffered a minor burn injury to his leg.

The cause of the fire remains under investigation by the Fire Marshal’s office.

World.title: Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier secures state arrest warrant for Raúl Castro
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

Florida has obtained a state arrest warrant for former Cuban leader Raúl Castro on a no-bond charge of conspiracy to commit first-degree murder stemming from the 1996 Brothers to the Rescue shootdown, according to a warrant obtained by Fox News Digital.



Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier, whose office reopened the state's investigation into Castro after he took office, is expected to announce the new arrest warrant alongside Gov. Ron DeSantis at a press conference Monday morning.



The no-bond warrant, issued in Miami-Dade County, directs law enforcement to immediately arrest Castro and says a judge found probable cause to believe he conspired to commit first-degree murder in connection with the deaths of four men aboard the unarmed civilian aircraft.



The warrant marks a new front in efforts to hold Castro accountable for the Feb. 24, 1996, attack, which has long reverberated through South Florida's Cuban-American community. Castro already faces a separate federal prosecution over the shootdown.

HAVANA REGIME IN SUSPENSE AFTER CASTRO INDICTMENT WITH TRUMP PRESSURE ON, SAYS CUBAN-BORN GOP REP.

"The investigation revealed evidence of a conspiracy to kill persons aboard BTTR aircraft. The deaths of Carlos Costa, Pablo Morales, Mario de la Peña, and Armando Alejandre Jr. were the object of that conspiracy," the warrant reads.

According to the warrant, investigators allege that in 1996, the Castro regime's foreign intelligence service's plan to shoot down Brothers to the Rescue aircraft and kill their occupants traveled through the chain of command, with Raúl Castro and his brother, former Cuban leader Fidel Castro, as the final decision-makers.

"They have violated the airspace, the waters of the Republic. I made it clear that this had to be decentralized if we wanted it to do its job, and five generals were given the authority. I used to say: Try to shoot them down over our territory. But they would come into Havana and leave," Raúl Castro, now 95, said in a recorded statement months after the incident, recounting orders he gave to senior military leaders before the shootdown, according to the warrant.

"Of course, with a missile shot like that, plane against plane, what comes down is a ball of fire, and it is going to fall on top of the city. So I said: Fine, shoot them down at sea when they show up, and those who have the authority are not to consult anyone," he added in his statement.

RAÚL CASTRO MAKES FIRST PUBLIC APPEARANCE SINCE TRUMP ADMINISTRATION CHARGED HIM WITH MURDER

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

Brothers to the Rescue is a Miami-based organization that flew unarmed civilian aircraft to search for Cuban migrants stranded or lost at sea. By the mid-1990s, the group had also become involved in anti-Castro political activity, including dropping pro-democracy leaflets over Cuba.

The Cuban government has rejected the U.S. prosecution of Castro, maintaining that Brothers to the Rescue repeatedly violated Cuban airspace and that Cuba acted in defense of its sovereignty.

The warrant indicates that Florida authorities are seeking full extradition of Raúl Castro if he is arrested outside the Sunshine State, authorizing authorities to pursue his return to Florida to face the felony charge if he is arrested in another U.S. jurisdiction.

The attorney general’s Office of Statewide Prosecution will assume jurisdiction over the multi-circuit criminal conspiracy case against Castro.

World.title: NFC East nearing second straight winless week as Packers beat struggling Cowboys on 'Sunday Night Football'
World.content:
The Green Bay Packers’ win over the Dallas Cowboys, 23-13, on "Sunday Night Football" maintained a tale of two divisions in the NFC.

The NFC North is once again a very strong group to begin the 2026 season, and perhaps for the second straight week, the NFC East will be winless.

Last week, the Cowboys and Philadelphia Eagles both lost, while the New York Giants and Washington Commanders managed an overtime tie in wacky fashion.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE

After the Giants and Eagles lost in the 1 p.m. slate this Sunday, the Cowboys were routed at Lambeau Field by a Packers team that did much of the same against their divisional foe, the Chicago Bears.

That leaves the Commanders, sitting at the bottom of the division at 1-3-1, as the only team still able to pick up a victory, though it will be tough on the road against a red-hot San Francisco 49ers squad that remains unbeaten.

It’s too early to say this NFC East division has shades of 2020, when Washington won it at 7-9, but it’s been an interesting start to say the least. In recent seasons, one team usually breaks away from the pack and wins pretty comfortably, but each team has its own issues that need addressing at the moment.

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

For the Cowboys, it was the defense entering this game against the Packers. World.title: Arizona man accused of plotting mass casualty attack on religious site with 'cookbook' tied to OKC bombing
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

An Arizona man who allegedly plotted a mass casualty attack on a Jewish or Muslim house of worship is being accused by prosecutors of possessing an infamous bomb-making manual linked to the Oklahoma City bomber.

Matthew Bjornholt, 27, faces a felony count of making a terrorist threat in connection with his alleged plot to attack a religious site.

Prosecutors in Maricopa County said Bjornholt laid out a chilling blueprint for violence that involved guns, explosives and an accomplice tasked with gunning down survivors.

During an initial court appearance on Friday, prosecutor Stephen Garcia sought a $500,000 cash bond, calling Bjornholt an imminent danger to the community, according to FOX 10.

TRANS NEO-NAZI ACCUSED OF PLOTTING HINDU TEMPLE MASSACRE, WILL RECEIVE HORMONE TREATMENT IN JAIL: OFFICIALS

Bjornholt allegedly outlined detailed plans to attack a religious site, according to Garcia, who also claimed the suspect kept a copy of "The Anarchist Cookbook," a manual containing bomb-making instructions that has been linked to Oklahoma City bomber Timothy McVeigh.

Garcia alleged that Bjornholt referred to the book as his "Bible."

The alleged plot included plans to detonate bombs before an accomplice of Bjornholt's would begin "picking off people" with firearms, according to prosecutors.

Investigators later seized three guns and ammunition from Bjornholt’s home.

Bjornholt’s defense attorney, Chad Schell, pushed back against the allegations, claiming that the charges are based solely on unverified hearsay from a disgruntled former acquaintance, according to FOX 10.

Schell told the court that the tip came from a "homeless alcoholic" whom Bjornholt had briefly let crash on his couch before kicking him out late last month.

PENNSYLVANIA MAN ACCUSED OF PLOTTING ISIS ATTACK ARRESTED WITH RIFLE AND 190 ROUNDS OF AMMUNITION: DOJ

Schell said federal authorities had already investigated the claims weeks ago. Schell said the FBI executed a search warrant at Bjornholt’s home on Sept. 29 and that Bjornholt voluntarily provided investigators with his electronic devices and passwords.

According to Schell, federal investigators found no evidence of terrorism or bomb-making materials and did not pursue federal charges before county authorities took over the case a couple of weeks later.

"There is no evidence he's a danger to the community. What is the evidence that he's a danger to the community? Some hearsay statements from some dude — that my client kicked out of his house two days before September 29," Schell told the court.

"Again, the FBI served a search warrant, got all of his electronic devices. He gave them access, gave him his passwords to those devices. They went through all of those electronic devices. They didn't see anything about terrorism. And FBI cut him loose," he continued.

Schell also argued that the three seized guns were lawfully possessed, adding that Bjornholt's civil rights were restored after completing a previous sentence on a drug charge stemming from a closed first-degree murder case. According to Schell, the murder charge against Bjornholt was dropped because of a lack of evidence.

The ammunition found inside the home, Schell said, was no more than standard magazine loads.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

Fox News Digital has reached out to the Maricopa County Attorney’s Office and FBI Phoenix for comment.

Despite prosecutors citing Bjornholt's criminal history in arguing for a larger bond, the judge said the state's preliminary evidence relied heavily on hearsay and set Bjornholt's bond at $100,000, according to FOX 10.

The judge nevertheless found enough probable cause to move the case forward.

It remains unclear whether specific houses of worship were targeted in the alleged plot or whether there was a specific accomplice.

Bjornholt is scheduled to return to court on Oct. 22 for a status conference and then later for a preliminary hearing on Oct. 26.

World.title: Strait of Hormuz crisis traps 6,000 sailors as attacks on ships mount, UN maritime chief says
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

Thousands of sailors remain stranded near the Strait of Hormuz amid escalating attacks on commercial ships, the United Nations' top maritime official warned Sunday after Iran accused the U.S. military of using an international emergency radio channel to threaten civilian crews.

The warning also came amid reports that 24 ships had been attacked on the waterway over roughly two weeks, underscoring growing concerns about maritime safety in the region, according to Financial Times.

"The situation continues to be severe and critical when it comes to international shipping," International Maritime Organization (IMO) Secretary-General Arsenio Dominguez told Fox News Digital.

"There is a double blockade and too many vessels have been attacked, particularly in recent days.

'VAST MAJORITY' OF IRAN'S ATTEMPTED ATTACKS ON STRAIT OF HORMUZ ARE UNSUCCESSFUL, CENTCOM SPOKESMAN SAYS

"Seafarers have continued to perish in these attacks and around 6,000 seafarers remain trapped since the beginning of the conflict," he warned, adding that his message was not to transit the Strait of Hormuz or put seafarers at risk "until we have guarantees."

Dominguez's warning followed an Oct. 9 letter to the IMO in which Iran alleged that the U.S. military used VHF Channel 16, an internationally designated maritime distress and safety channel, to intimidate Iranian crews in the Persian Gulf.

"VHF Channel 16 has been repeatedly occupied for prolonged periods by the United States military forces operating in the Persian Gulf," the letter stated.

TRUMP OPENS HORMUZ UNDER FIRE WITH ‘PROJECT FREEDOM’ AS IRAN WARNS OF ATTACKS

"During such transmissions, Iranian seafarers have been addressed in Persian with threatening, abusive and provocative language and in certain instances urged to abandon their vessels."

In a statement to Fox News Digital, U.S. Central Command defended its enforcement of the naval blockade of Iranian ports.

"The U.S. naval blockade has been in place for months and is professionally communicated to all international mariners," CENTCOM said.

"Vessels that refuse to comply with blockade enforcement receive multiple warnings, with ample opportunity to comply.

"American forces remain highly vigilant, focused, and professional while fully enforcing the naval blockade against Iran."

Iran's complaint was submitted by Seyed Ali Mousavi, its ambassador to the IMO, and circulated to member states on Oct. 9, according to a copy reviewed by Fox News Digital.

Tehran also accused American forces of turning the maritime safety channel into an "instrument of military intimidation and psychological pressure against civilian crews."

The letter cited commercial vessels, shipping companies and maritime operators but provided no recordings, transcripts or specific details of the alleged exchanges. Fox News Digital could not independently verify the accusations.

IRAN THREATENS TO HALT RED SEA TRAFFIC IN RESPONSE TO US MILITARY BLOCKADE OF PORTS

"Seafarers are not trained for combat, and they are not guilty of any conflicts that are happening around the world," Dominguez said.

"And we have seen this in several parts of the world where Channel 16, that should not be used for this kind of communication, starts receiving messages that may be perceived as actually threatening or that are outside the remit of why it was created."

Iran also asked the IMO to raise its allegations with member states and relevant international organizations, potentially including the International Telecommunication Union.

Dominguez said the IMO could review its regulations and procedures to determine whether stronger safeguards are needed, though he did not announce a formal investigation.

"Our role here at IMO is that when those situations take place, we will then look into any technical measures or any operational aspects that we may need to clarify further within our regulatory framework," he said, stressing that member states have equal rights to raise concerns, regardless of the conflict.

"We have a responsibility, and I have a duty as well, to circulate letters and notes that the countries actually put forward when they're also being affected."

WHO CONTROLS THE STRAIT OF HORMUZ RIGHT NOW? HERE'S WHAT THE SHIP TRAFFIC ACTUALLY SHOWS

"We take all that information, meet at the level of different meetings of the organization and have the discussions," Dominguez added.

"If it's demonstrated that we probably need to improve our rules in order to avoid communications issues, or that we need to enhance the knowledge of how these channels should be used, that is a role for us."

The IMO had recorded 100 confirmed maritime incidents across the region as of Oct. 9, with 24 seafarers killed since the conflict began Feb. 28. Dominguez also warned that fraudulent ship registrations and false flags have become major contributors to the danger.

"What we've also seen right now is an increase in fraudulent registries with false flags that are taking the risk and acting as shuttle tankers in order to bring goods in and out," he said. "That's one of the reasons that we're seeing an escalation.

"And it's the irresponsible shipowners that are taking the risk in order to actually be able to trade and move some of the goods and the cargoes."

WHITE HOUSE SILENT ON IRAN-OMAN HORMUZ PLAN TEHRAN SAYS WOULD BAN US WARSHIPS

"For me, any single case, any vessel that is attacked, any life of a seafarer that is lost, is a critical situation for me, because they are all relevant, they are all important."

Despite the confrontation, Dominguez said diplomatic channels with Iran remain open, though he has no direct contact with the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps.

"I have communications with all the member states of IMO, and that includes the Islamic Republic of Iran," he said.

"Of course, that's through the diplomatic channels. I don't have direct contact with the IRGC.

"I have conversations with them and they respond to my messages. You know, the information flows. What is difficult is to get final decisions because of the conflict that is ongoing."

Fox News Digital has reached out to the Iranian embassy for comment.

A late-night crash has thrown a Massachusetts Republican’s statewide campaign into turmoil just weeks before voters head to the polls.

Shawn Oliver, 42, the Republican nominee for lieutenant governor and a New Bedford city councilor, suspended his campaign on Sunday. The move came after Oliver was arrested following a rollover crash that involved five parked vehicles, police confirmed to Fox News Digital.

Officers responded around 11:40 p.m. Saturday to 448 Dartmouth St., where a vehicle had overturned after striking multiple parked vehicles, the New Bedford Police Department said. Two of the five parked vehicles sustained extensive damage.

Oliver, identified by police as the driver, was taken to St. Luke’s Hospital for treatment of his injuries.

Following an investigation at the scene and at the hospital, officers arrested Oliver and charged him with operating under the influence of liquor, negligent operation of a motor vehicle, a marked lanes violation and speeding, police said.

DEMOCRAT CANDIDATE SEEN SOBBING, PRAYING IN PATROL CAR AFTER DUI ARREST: VIDEO

Republican gubernatorial nominee Mike Minogue publicly called on Oliver to suspend his campaign.

World.title: Poll: Americans are anxious, pessimistic and deeply unhappy with Trump ahead of the midterms
World.content:
Weeks ahead of Election Day, 71% of U.S. adults think the country is on the “wrong track.” It’s the highest share yet in President Donald Trump’s second term, illustrating the grim national mood his party faces in the midterm elections, according to a new NBC News Decision Desk Poll powered by SurveyMonkey.

Poll respondents expressed deep unhappiness over economic conditions and widespread distrust toward both major political parties, but Trump and Republicans bore the brunt. For the first time in Trump’s second term, the poll has found the “right track” sinking into the 20s. A majority of Americans view the president’s administration as uniquely corrupt, even as they look skeptically at corruption in both parties. And they say Trump is failing to improve their material financial conditions.

Trump’s approval rating slipped to 34% among U.S. adults, a second-term low in this poll, while his disapproval rating rose to 66%. In another warning sign, the poll found a majority (51%) of respondents “strongly disapprove” of his performance, a second-term high.

Trump’s approval rating is slightly better among registered voters, 39%-61%. Registered voters said they prefer Democrats over Republicans to control Congress by a 55%-45% spread, another sign that the GOP’s House and Senate majorities are in danger in the Nov. 3 election.

Yet despite the sinking ratings for the party in power, Americans continue to hold a negative view of Democrats, too. Among adults, just 43% view the Democratic Party favorably, while 57% hold an unfavorable view.

The survey found that 37% have a favorable opinion of the Republican Party, while 63% view it unfavorably.

The president’s approval rating is 76% with Republican adults. That represents a drop from his previous numbers among members of his own party, fueled by a decline among Republicans who consider themselves more a supporter of the party than a supporter of the MAGA movement. Meanwhile, Trump’s approval rating sits at 21% with independents.

Among men under 30 — a group Trump won by 1 point in 2024 exit polling — his approval rating sits at 28%. And among Latinos, who also shifted toward Trump in 2024, his approval rating is 31%.

The poll highlights the tricky balancing act facing Republican candidates in competitive states and districts as they simultaneously try to energize GOP voters who continue to support Trump without alienating Americans who disapprove of the administration.

Among adults, 58% said Trump’s policies are hurting the country, while 28% said they are helping the country. Another 14% said they aren’t making a difference.

When broken down by issues, Trump’s approval rating is 27% on handling the cost of living, 29% on handling the war with Iran and 33% on his handling of AI. On his best issue, border security and immigration, 43% of adults approve.

Economic concerns are at the center of the sour national mood, with the economy once again topping the list of most important issues at 31%. While 18% of Americans said their financial situation is better off today than a year ago, 38% said it’s about the same and 44% said it’s worse now.

The results provided detail on how rising inflation, which last month rose to 3.7% year over year, has weighed on Americans’ daily lives.

Gas prices were described as a “very serious” or “somewhat serious” problem by 67% of respondents. Majorities said economic conditions have caused them to change what groceries they buy to live within their means and to cut back on spending to afford necessities.

Pluralities also said they’ve cut back on electricity use, changed or canceled travel plans or delayed a major purchase as a result, according to the poll.

Trump has sought to appeal to voters by promising $5,000 payments if Republicans win the 2026 midterms. But the new poll showed that most U.S. adults aren’t buying it: Just 14% said they “definitely” or “probably” expect to receive such a check if the GOP keeps control of Congress, while 71% think they “definitely” or “probably” won’t.

Self-identified Republicans are among those who don’t appear to buy the president’s pledge, with 47% saying they don’t expect to receive the $5,000 payment Trump promised, while 28% do.

Corruption also registered as a major concern, with Americans harboring skepticism about both parties.

More than half (52%) of U.S. adults said in the poll that they find his administration “more corrupt” than previous administrations, while about 1 in 4 said it’s less corrupt and another 1 in 4 said the current administration is about as corrupt as predecessors.

A 56% majority also said corruption is equally bad in both parties, while another 25% said it’s a bigger problem inside the GOP and 17% said it’s worse among Democrats.

The dissatisfaction may be reshaping what Americans want in a politician. In another edition of this poll one year ago, Americans said by a 16-point margin they prefer an insider with the experience to get things done over an outsider who shakes up the system. That margin narrowed to 4 points in the new poll.

Among Democrats, the survey also found indicators of diminishing trust in the party’s establishment and an openness to different kinds of candidates.

When asked to pick one or the other, 52% of self-identified Democrats said they’re more of a supporter of progressive causes and the progressive movement, while 48% said they’re more of a supporter of the Democratic Party.

Among Democratic-aligned adults, 42% said they consider themselves to be democratic socialists, while 58% said they do not.

And despite Trump’s unpopularity, the country was split almost evenly on whether a potential Democratic-led House should begin impeachment proceedings: 52% said it should, while 48% said it should not go down that path.

The NBC News Decision Desk Poll powered by SurveyMonkey surveyed 19,135 adults online from Sept. 28 to Oct. 12 and has a margin of error of plus or minus 2.6 percentage points.
