World.title: NASA Satellites track warming Pacific waters as El Niño develops
World.content:
NASA Satellites track warming Pacific waters as El Niño develops

By Zoila Palma: NASA satellites are tracking signs of El Niño in the Pacific Ocean, including rising sea surface temperatures and changes in ocean levels and colour.

According to NASA, one of the first indicators appeared in January 2026, when a wave of warm water known as a Kelvin wave was detected near Micronesia in the western Pacific. By early April, the waves had reached the eastern Pacific, contributing to warmer ocean temperatures and rising sea levels in some areas.

Kelvin waves transport heat across the Pacific Ocean, helping trigger a chain reaction that weakens the trade winds and allows warm water to accumulate farther east. NASA reported that sea levels in parts of the eastern Pacific rose by approximately 1 to 1.3 feet, while levels around Indonesia and northern Australia were 6 to 8 inches below normal.

NASA data also show that sea surface temperatures in the eastern Pacific are approximately 3 degrees Fahrenheit, or 1.7 degrees Celsius, above the long-term average, with the possibility of further warming in the coming months. These temperature changes are significant because ocean heat influences atmospheric conditions, affecting rainfall and weather patterns around the world.

Another sign of El Niño is a change in the ocean’s colour as populations of microscopic marine plants known as phytoplankton decline in some equatorial Pacific waters.

NASA says that its scientists will continue monitoring El Niño through its fleet of Earth-observing satellites to better understand the phenomenon and its potential effects.

World.title: INSIDE THE SLIGOVILLE STAND-OFF
World.content:
Police are seen on the road leading to the house off the Sligoville main road in St Catherine where three men were killed in an alleged shoot-out with members of the security forces last Friday morning.

“POLICE, we a go pull the door, just wait nuh. Mi nuh waan dead enuh!”

One of the children inside the ill-fated house in the Five Miles area off the Sligoville main road in St Catherine shouted these words as she and two other occupants of the premises seemingly negotiated with law enforcers to cease their gunfire so they could exit the house last Friday amid a stand-off with alleged gunmen inside the building.

A video recording seen by the Jamaica Observer captured some of what was happening inside the house while law enforcers were outside. The 18-minute 25-second video was captured during a WhatsApp video call with relatives during Friday morning’s daring gun battle. The video cuts out for much of the recording, with an onscreen notification saying “video paused”, but the audio can still be heard.

The child, who the Sunday Observer has been told is the 10-year-old girl who was injured in the incident, is heard appealing to one of the occupants of the house to open the door.

At another point in the recording, the child is heard saying to law enforcers: “Police, yuh see me, right? Do not shoot me, yuh hear?”

A voice, seemingly from outside, confirmed.

“Do not shoot me family dem either, yuh hear?” the child added.

Reports from the police are that members of the Jamaica Constabulary Force’s Specialised Operations Branch came under gunfire after going in search of a high-risk target identified as Kenroy Willis, who operates out of the St Andrew North Police Division and is wanted for four murders.

The police, who returned gunfire, said men barricaded themselves inside a house with a woman and children. During the stand-off, the men indicated that they wanted to surrender, and reportedly used one of the children to signal their willingness to lay down their illegal firearms, by holding a “child out the door”.

“When the police approached, seeking to retrieve the child, fire was opened upon those policemen,” senior communications strategist at the Jamaica Constabulary Force Dennis Brooks told journalists metres from the shooting scene on Friday.

According to the Independent Commission of Investigations (INDECOM), 10 people, including two minors, three police officers, and one member of the Jamaica Defence Force (JDF), sustained gunshot wounds. Three men — Errol Hussey, his son Malique Hussey, and nephew Javoun Cogle, said to be the gunmen — were also fatally shot.

Two of the policemen have since died, with Corporal Trevoy Shaw succumbing on Friday and Constable Devoney Rose of Thomas Road in Ewarton, St Catherine, succumbing to his injuries on Saturday.

The police have also reported that two firearms, including a rifle, were seized.

However, a relative of the alleged gunmen is accusing the police of murder while calling for an independent investigation into the deaths of Corporal Shaw and Constable Rose.

That relative, who lives overseas, said she was on a WhatsApp call with one of the now-deceased men during the reported stand-off.

She told the Sunday Observer that her family members were in the process of surrendering to the police when they were killed.

“We were watching them because we are on WhatsApp video, we have our little family group…we on WhatsApp video and we a watch them a surrender,” the relative told the Sunday Observer on Saturday.

She said the WhatsApp call was disconnected when they went outside, but related what happened next based on reports from another occupant of the house.

“Him have [the child] in his hand, she [alleged eyewitness] said, and him say, ‘Don’t kill [the child] enuh.’ Dem take the baby from him, beat him and kill him in front [the child], kill mi other [relative], and then [Errol] now weh deh a the door a come out — him nuh have no firearm — him run back in, not fi nuh firearm, because him done surrender the one gun weh dem have,” the relative said.

According to the relative, Errol was kneeling by a bed when he was killed.

Admitting that the elder Hussey was not innocent because he did, in fact, have an illegal Glock firearm, the relative who spoke to the Sunday Observer is insisting that one Glock pistol could not have done the damage that is being described by the police.

She is also contending that the policemen were killed by their colleagues.

“Mi nah say [Errol] never have a gun, so there was a gun inna the house. But fi him fi use that one gun and shoot two police, now mi need fi know what gun dem say him did have. It was not a rifle, it was a Glock; they had no rifle.

“The whole story is not true. If they investigate, you will find out that is police bullet hit police,” she said, adding, “So they got so emotional because a police died… that even when they surrendered and went out[side], dem beat them and kill dem out a door.

“And a nuh dem drag dem out… they came out, because we were on the phone with them,” the relative said.

She is insisting that the narrative from the police cannot continue.

“It is not right, and they continue to do these things and paint people like a big shoot-out,” she said.

In the video seen by the Sunday Observer, while no faces were visible, the voices of the men and a child are heard. The recording starts with two men on the floor of a section of the house, with glimpses of a dresser in another room and the legs of someone, dressed in military garb and holding what appears to be a shield, can be seen just outside a doorway in the other room.

“Come out now, come out now, rude boy, yuh good,” said the voice from just outside the next room.

“Dem a say, ‘Don’t go out deh, don’t go out deh,’ ” responded one of the men from inside the house.

The man just outside the door replied: “A me a control yah suh and a me a tell yuh fi come out.”

Another voice is heard assuring the man inside that he is “good” and can exit the room as they were seeing his hand.

The occupant of the house queried whether “sojie” is the one talking to him, declaring that he’d prefer to talk to the soldier. A soldier seemingly confirmed that he was in fact speaking to a member of the JDF.

The man inside the house explained that he was not the one firing a gun. The dialogue continued and gunfire can be heard.

“Woi, officer, the baby, mi nah nuh gun officer!” said one of the men inside. Another voice could be heard adding: “We a di door nah nuh gun; two a we nah nuh gun… a one man a shoot.”

As the occupants continue to appeal to those outside the house not to shoot and declare that they are coming out, a child’s voice is heard: “Don’t shoot.”

“Sojie, we a come out, we swear, but a nuh we a fire,” said one of the men inside the house. “Yuh see the two smaddy weh nah fire, we a come out with the baby, yuh hear?”

The man inside then questions if they want to kill everyone inside and the baby before shortly declaring that he is going to stand up, but what he is holding in his hand is a phone.

The video then pauses around three minutes and 40 seconds, but the audio can still be heard. They continue to seemingly negotiate with the law enforcers in order to exit the building, with them being ordered to throw the gun outside and show their hands. At five minutes and 47 seconds, gunfire rings out.

“The man weh have the gun, him nuh wan come out,” shouted one of the men inside the house. “A nuh we a fire the shot enuh, a nuh we a fire the shot.”

The video then resumes at six minutes and four seconds. Three pairs of feet are visible, two seemingly sitting on the floor and the third suspended from an area above the frame of the video.

There is a glimpse of a handgun in one of the men’s hands. They all appear to be behind a door, including a child seemingly sitting in the lap of one of the men on the floor.

The men inside continue to declare that they are going to exit the house. Occasional gunfire can be heard, and the men continue to declare that they are not the ones shooting.

The child is then heard saying: “Police, we a go pull the door, just wait nuh. Mi nuh waan dead enuh!”

The video is paused again at eight minutes and 28 seconds. The men are heard declaring that their hands are empty and that they were going to open the door, while also making it clear that the baby is also at the door. They also asked if the law enforcers were looking at the door.

During this exchange between the men inside the house and the law enforcers, the child is heard saying repeatedly: “Daddy, stop!”

A voice from outside is heard asking: “Yuh a work with me?”

The occupants inside the house, including the child, responded: “Yea, we a work with yuh.”

The audio continues. When it gets to 11 minutes and 57 seconds, a voice from outside is heard saying: “Come, man. Nobody fire.”

Inside, the child is heard saying, “Pull the door.”

They continued to plead their case that they were not shooting, with one of the men asking what guarantee they had that they wouldn’t still be killed. One of the men is heard declaring that he is 21 years old and just had a child so he does not want to die.

At about 17:52 seconds, gunfire is again heard. The men in the audio declare: “A nuh we, a nuh we. We nah fire nuh shot. A nuh we… God know!”

The child is also heard saying: “A nuh we.”

The gunfire continues.

“A nuh we fi true. Mi fada dung deh,” said one of the men before the audio and recording end at 18 minutes and 25 seconds.

The relative who spoke to the Sunday Observer said she could speak for one of the deceased men, Javoun, and she knows he is not involved in anything gun-related.

“We have the audio, but we don’t have the video of them going out. [It was] at the door when they surrendered and reached out to them then the phone shut off.

“It was a blatant murder,” she said.

The relative added: “The way the house look now, yuh can’t recognise the house the amount a shot, and is one Glock they had, so you know a nuh dem do that…

“This is not right. They can’t keep doing this… the truth must be told… Mi really want see if a really [Errol] shoot the police dem because, based pon weh me a hear, shot dem just a guh, guh, guh from two sides; dem nuh must shoot each other,” she claimed.

World.title: Integrity advocates support State funding for CAFFE, but with guardrails
World.content:
MUNROE... it is essential for Jamaica’s taxpayers to provide a budgetary allocation to help sustain CAFFE, possibly through a line item in the budget for the Electoral Commission of Jamaica

SOME governance integrity advocates believe that the Jamaican Government could provide a financial lifeline for Citizens Action for Free and Fair Elections (CAFFE), but offered differing positions on how State subvention should be administered.

As the electoral watchdog group continues to seek private sector assistance amid financial challenges following the withdrawal of US funding, Dr Trevor Munroe, founding director of National Integrity Action and former vice-chair of CAFFE, argued that Government funding could be a crucial source of support to its survival.

Speaking with the Jamaica Observer last Monday, Munroe noted that CAFFE plays an integral role in safeguarding the integrity of Jamaica’s polls, and warned that inadequate funding could undermine the country’s democratic process.

“The recent narrowing of the funding base of CAFFE potentially weakens our citizens’ critical role in maintaining the electoral foundation of Jamaica’s democracy. It also undermines the important role that the organisation can and is seeking to play in building public awareness on the importance of voting as well as in the exercise of our other democratic rights,” he said.

CAFFE, established in 1997, has monitored seven general elections, seven local government polls, and several by-elections and re-run elections. Since 2025, however, the watchdog group has faced severe financial challenges following the Donald Trump Administration’s withdrawal of United States Agency for International Development (USAID) funding from non-governmental organisations globally.

The frozen funding has heightened concerns about CAFFE’s capacity to monitor future elections.

“In these circumstances it is essential for Jamaica’s taxpayers to provide a budgetary allocation to help sustain CAFFE, possibly through a line item in the budget for the Electoral Commission of Jamaica (ECJ),” Munroe reasoned.

While acknowledging that ethical concerns could arise from the executive arm of government interfering in the operations of neutral bodies, Munroe argued that CAFFE’s integrity depends on its ability to maintain impartiality towards political affiliations.

“For example, alertness to ethical concerns is always demanded when neutral regulatory bodies, like the NEPA [National Environment and Planning Agency] and the judiciary — the latter an independent co-equal branch of the Jamaican State — are financed by the Jamaican taxpayer through the Government budget,” he pointed out.

“If and when Government oversteps its bounds, it is an alert citizenry and robust neutral bodies’ resistance that deters and blocks interference, thereby putting Government back in its proper place,” said Munroe.

He added that he does not anticipate CAFFE facing such complications, noting that its funding from USAID had been channelled through the executive branch of the US Government without influencing the organisation’s performance.

“It was up to CAFFE and USAID to ensure that the conditions of, and the actual dispensation of funds did not violate CAFFE’s independence nor neutrality in the exercise of its responsibilities. So it must [also] be with funding provided by other international partners [eg the European Union] or by the Jamaican Government,” he argued.

“In this latter case the funding would come through the ECJ budget, and CAFFE would have to ensure that its utilisation would be consistent with independent election monitoring — excluding political considerations and being mindful of ethical concerns,” Munroe said.

Meanwhile Jeanette Calder, executive director and founder of the Jamaica Accountability Meter Portal, argued that while Government subvention to neutral agencies is not a foreign concept, it must be instituted at no risk to CAFFE’s autonomy.

Calder argued that if Government funding is considered, then it should not be the observatory group’s main or only source of financing.

“CAFFE serves an important, independent monitoring role of the State’s elections processes. State funding can assist but [should] not be [the] sole or primary source, in order to protect and preserve independence. State funding would best be for CAFFE’s discretionary use where it determines best,” she said.

Attorney and former politician Ronald Thwaites shared similar sentiments, stating that it is “perfectly reasonable” for the Government to subsidise CAFFE’s monitoring and surveillance operations.

Expanding on his position, Thwaites told the Sunday Observer that it was embarrassing for CAFFE to have relied on international funding rather than support of the Government and private sector.

“I would also want to hope that Government’s interests would not be singular, and that the private sector and all of us, in different ways, would want to support CAFFE.

“I’ve been a little embarrassed that we were depending on foreign sources to help us to keep our elections clean and fair, so the moment has come now where we have to take care of our own interests. And that should be a combination of Jamaican donations — no doubt including people from the Diaspora and also, very appropriately, a subvention from Government,” he argued.

Addressing concerns that State funding could compromise a neutral body, Thwaites said other independent public interest organisations receive Government support while remaining autonomous, provided that proper accountability safeguards are maintained.

“The Integrity Commission does that. Various other bodies that are for the public good but are not connected with any State agency also receive those monies. The question of the ethical considerations would only apply in terms of the use of the private sector, and it is not beyond us to ensure that we give proper accounting,” he said.

World.title: Larry McDonald’s journey
World.content:
Larry McDonald

FOR nearly seven decades, the heartbeat of Jamaican music has echoed through the hands of one extraordinary musician: Lawrence “Larry” McDonald.

A master percussionist, cultural ambassador, and living legend, McDonald has devoted his life to preserving, celebrating, and sharing the rich rhythmic traditions of Jamaica with the world.

On Monday, October 19, 2026 his remarkable journey will receive national recognition as he is awarded the Badge of Honour for Meritorious Service in the field of Entertainment, acknowledging his tremendous contribution to Jamaica’s musical heritage and cultural identity.

For McDonald, whose hands have helped shape the sound of ska, rocksteady, reggae, jazz, and countless other musical traditions, the honour represents more than personal achievement. It is a celebration of Jamaican culture, its ancestral rhythms, and the generations of musicians who have carried those traditions across the globe.

Born on June 11, 1937, in Port Maria, St Mary, McDonald’s musical journey began long before he stepped onto an international stage.

Growing up immersed in Jamaica’s vibrant cultural traditions, he was deeply influenced by the powerful African-derived rhythms of Kumina, Burru, and Jonkannu. These traditions, rooted in the island’s history and ancestral heritage, became the foundation of his musical identity.

As Jamaican popular music evolved through the 1950s and 1960s, McDonald emerged as one of the percussionists helping to define its distinctive rhythmic character.

Working alongside pioneering musicians such as Carlos Malcolm, Count Ossie, and Toots and the Maytals, he brought the expressive power of traditional hand drumming into the developing sounds of ska, rocksteady, and reggae.

At a time when the drum kit, bass, and guitar were becoming central to Jamaican popular music, McDonald helped establish the conga as an equally compelling musical voice. His playing added depth, texture, and a connection to Jamaica’s African heritage.

After relocating to the United States in 1973, he became an influential presence in an international musical community, collaborating with some of the most celebrated names in reggae, jazz, blues, soul, and spoken-word performance.

His remarkable list of collaborators includes Bob Marley and the Wailers, Peter Tosh, Bunny Wailer, Lee “Scratch” Perry, Taj Mahal, The Skatalites, and the groundbreaking poet and musician Gil Scott-Heron.

His association with Scott-Heron, spanning nearly three decades, was particularly significant. Together, they helped create music that combined rhythm, poetry, social consciousness, and powerful cultural commentary.

Whether performing before thousands or contributing the subtle rhythmic details that elevate a recording, McDonald has always approached percussion as something greater than accompaniment.

In 2009, after decades of lending his extraordinary talents to the music of others, McDonald released his first album as a leader, Drumquestra.

The album was both a musical achievement and a cultural statement.

Bringing together an exceptional gathering of Jamaican musicians and vocalists, including Sly Dunbar, Toots Hibbert, Mutabaruka, Bob Andy, Bongo Herman, and members of the Mystic Revelation of Rastafari, Drumquestra placed percussion at the centre of the musical conversation.

Rather than treating the drum as a supporting instrument, McDonald presented it as the foundation of an entire orchestra of rhythm.

The project celebrated Jamaica’s African musical inheritance while demonstrating the extraordinary possibilities of traditional percussion in contemporary music.

At 89 years old, he continues to embody the spirit of creativity, resilience, and cultural pride that has defined his life’s work.

Far from slowing down, McDonald remains an active and dynamic presence on the international music scene, continuing to tour and perform with The Skatalites, David Hillard and the rocksteady 7, The NYC Ska Orchestra and Subatomic Sound System.

Whether introducing new generations to the infectious rhythms of ska and reggae, or sharing the stage with musicians decades younger than himself, McDonald continues to demonstrate that great music knows no age limits.

In January 2026 he was selected to deliver the keynote address at the University of California, Santa Cruz’s 42nd annual Martin Luther King Jr Convocation, a recognition of his extraordinary artistic journey and his enduring connection to music, history, and social consciousness.

Although his name may not always have appeared in the brightest lights, his rhythms have been heard alongside some of the most important voices in modern music.

He belongs to that exceptional generation of Jamaican musicians whose artistry helped transform a small Caribbean island into one of the world’s most influential musical nations.

World.title: New private high school in St James working to create global citizens
World.content:
Founder and Director Natalie Morris speaks with students (from second left) Marissa Hylton, Natoya Williams and Zavoya Forbes at the recently opened Integrated School of the Arts Jamaica.

MONTEGO BAY, St James — Founder and director of Integrated School for the Arts Jamaica (ISAJ) — the newest educational institution in the western end of the island — Natalie Morris says the plan is for the school to develop global- ready students.

Just weeks after the private high school opened its doors for the 2026/2027 academic year, Morris told the Jamaica Observer in an interview that it is already making progress towards that goal.

“Global citizens, that’s our motto. It means regardless of your ability, we want you to — even if you’re living locally — you should be thinking global…As we are living in a world where artificial intelligence is shaping the way we do business and the way we learn, I want our students to be thinking in that realm,” said Morris.

She said the varied nature of the student population is already helping to bring that vision to life.

“We have a diverse school even though it’s so small. We have Spanish speakers, we have Mandarin speakers, we have English speakers,” explained Morris, who pointed out that the school has already started establishing international connections — including one expected to provide students with opportunities to travel overseas.

“Just right now, we were identified by Marnix College in Curaçao…they are coming… to Jamaica next year to partner with us as a language exchange programme.

“We want to get the students to be thinking that we are not just in a local space, we are in a global space, and that’s how we have been pushing the school,” Morris told the Sunday Observer.

Located at the Blue Diamond Shopping Mall in Ironshore, on the outskirts of Montego Bay, ISAJ currently has 45 students enrolled in grades seven to 10.

The grade 10 cohort will progress to grade 11, in which students will be guided in preparing for the Caribbean Secondary Education Certificate (CSEC) examinations.

Morris shed some light on the school’s origin.

“I was a consultant to Naz Children’s Centre where I actually assisted them to implement a high school programme,” she explained.

Naz Children’s Centre offers tailored learning programmes for children who may have special educational needs.

“Naz, as most persons would know, it would be from preschool to elementary, and I implemented a high school programme there in 2018,” Morris explained.

“Fast-forward to 2026, on February 28 this year, the owner of Naz Children’s Centre called me and said… the programme is doing well there, but she really wants to refocus and go back to core —and that is how she said, ‘I am giving you back your baby,’ “ she recounted.

Taking a leap of faith, Morris said she stepped down from her corporate job at Harbour City Mall in Montego Bay to establish the school. Nearly 30 students from Naz Children’s Centre were transferred to her care to continue their secondary education.

Morris said she felt prepared to take on the challenge, given her background in teaching.

“My journey started about 20-something years ago in the classroom as a primary school teacher. I have taught in Jamaica and in The Bahamas,” she said.

Despite her experience, she admitted that she was uncertain about how things would unfold, particularly as she had to find suitable premises to accommodate the school.

“I am saying it’s nothing short of a miracle, because I’ll tell you this, when I got that call, I didn’t have a building. I didn’t have any idea how anything was going to work, and this moment has been a faith walk for me.

“I remember the day when we were looking for a venue and we’re looking at another venue, and it was not approved by the Ministry [of Education], and the same day I called the owner of Blue Diamond and he said, ‘You know, ironically, one of our tenants is moving,’ “ she told the Sunday Observer.

The tenant was Nexus Tours, a tourism-based company that was relocating its operations to the grounds of Sangster International Airport.

“I can say that Nexus Tours was here and they were our first funding partner. Nexus contributed a large percentage of our furniture. They started us with everything, most of the things that you’re seeing here are from Nexus Tours,” said Morris.

“All of what you are seeing in form, is like God placed all of this and so we were able to organise to start school in six months. We met the students on June 1, and from June to September we were able to transition and to start school with 44 children here,” she stated.

Despite the progress, Morris said the school’s long-term goal is to secure premises of its own, although she remains grateful for what has been achieved so far.

She explained that the small class sizes were intentional, allowing teachers to provide greater support to students, particularly those who require additional assistance.

“Our class right now is standard 10 to 15 [students], but our largest class right now is 12, and we are able to do a more personalised learning or differentiation learning experience and that is part of the unique nature of this,” said Morris.

She pointed out that although ISAJ has a focus on the arts, its curriculum extends beyond that field.

“We do try to use a STEAM [science, technology, engineering, the arts, and mathemat-ics] based approach. So, in the mornings, mostly, we do all the academic stuff, but in the afternoon we do arts-based subjects. We have drumming as a part of the curriculum, we have robotics, we have all of those things,” said Morris.

World.title: BEYOND THE LENS
World.content:
In this file photo Samantha Hall competes in the women’s discus throw Group B qualification during the World Athletics Championships in Tokyo . (Photo: AFP)

WHEN Dominica’s Olympic champion Thea LaFond and Trinidadian journalist Dennis Allen first discussed the new European broadcast guidelines, they pointed out a tricky puzzle: While tight, suggestive camera angles objectify female athletes, those same viral moments often help competitors build a following and secure paying sponsor deals.

Published by the European Broadcasting Union (EBU) and European Athletics, the Raising the Bar guidelines instruct camera operators to avoid extremely low-angle shots from behind, limit unnecessary slow-motion replays during athlete preparations, and use wider shots that focus on technical execution over physical body parts.

For the women inside and around the sport every day, this debate goes much deeper than camera angles. It touches on what they describe as a frustrating double standard — a female athlete’s financial survival often depends on her looks, even when her hard work and talent should be doing all the talking.

Reigning Commonwealth Games champion and national discus thrower Samantha Hall knows this struggle first-hand. She sees a clear gap in how male and female athletes are treated.

“I understand both sides of the argument,” Hall told the Sunday Observer. “As athletes we do like to see ourselves — especially for field events, we can see where we went wrong with our technique based on pictures — but at the same time, we don’t want to be seen as sexual figures. I hate that for women, this is how we have to earn money — that we have to look sexy, and not for our talents. For men, they don’t really have to do much; it’s just about their talents. They’re getting paid for their talents but for women, it’s not enough. You have to have that image with it.”

Hall’s words point to a wider issue in sports. While male athletes build their careers purely on distances, times and medals, women are expected to win medals and meet a specific standard of beauty.

Long before the cameras zoom in on the field, female track stars face non-stop public criticism over their appearance—from make-up and hair to body art. Criticism male athletes rarely hear.

“I’ve seen it for other athletes, especially like Elaine Thompson-Herah and Ashanti Moore, because they have tattoos in various places on their bodies,” Hall said. “I’ve seen comments like, ‘Why do they have these tattoos? It’s the reason why they can’t perform well.’ And I’m like, ‘That has nothing to do with their performances.’ But yeah, you always have people criticising females based on how they look — like their make-up is off, ‘Her hairstyle doesn’t look neat on her’, ‘Her outfit doesn’t fit her’. They’re always judging female athletes based on their looks.”

Even off the screen, off-hand comments can be intrusive. Hall shared that people sometimes approach her to talk about her physique rather than her throws.

Yet Hall handles this pressure with incredible grace. Rather than letting outside noise get to her, she chooses to own her style and feel confident on her own terms. “It does affect me, but not in a negative way,” she said. “I want to impress my fans, so if this is what the fans want then I have to dress to impress them. At the end of the day, it’s all about fashion; they like your sense of style. For Shelly-Ann [Fraser-Pryce], it’s all about her wigs; they like her style of wigs. For me, if they talk about my bottom it doesn’t really affect me in any way. I don’t feel bad about it. I try to dress appropriately, but at the same time I want to feel sexy as well.”

Hall says other broadcasters around the world will eventually adopt Europe’s cleaner camera rules by 2028, to keep athletes respected and comfortable. But media experts say changing camera angles won’t fix deep-rooted cultural habits overnight.

Melena Helias, a Kingston based French sports journalist who has covered track and field for both local Jamaican outlets and France’s premier sports newspaper L’Équipe, welcomes the new European guidelines as a solid first step.

“My first reaction was quite positive,” Helias told the Observer. “That said, it’s a shame that it has come to the point where a guide on this is needed but I commend EBU Sport for their work. It won’t solve the problem of the sexualisation of sportswomen, or of inequality and stereotypes in sport, but it’s a good start.”

Helias reminds us that women have had to fight for basic space in sports history. Because track and field doesn’t offer massive multimillion-dollar contracts like football or basketball, athletes often have to rely on their public image to survive financially.

“A male athlete attracts sponsors thanks to his results and his personality, among other things,” Helias said. “A female athlete, on top of her results, needs to be perceived as beautiful. That’s precisely the paradox: There isn’t that much money in athletics compared to other sports so you have to capitalise on what sells. And I certainly don’t blame female athletes who use their assets or their beauty on social media to attract sponsors; it’s actually quite logical. I’d just like appearance to be a less omnipresent criterion in the way women are perceived.”

Speaking up against objectification isn’t always easy, either. Even inside the press box Helias admits that as a woman in a heavily male-dominated career, finding the courage to call out inappropriate remarks can be a challenge.

“Unfortunately, no,” Helias said when asked if she feels she has a safe platform to speak out. “I’d even say that I’ve heard, more than once, remarks that outraged me — comments about female athletes — but I didn’t dare say anything. It’s not always easy to find your place in sports journalism; we’re still very much a minority. It’s one thing to have confidence in your abilities and knowledge but it’s another to assert yourself, stand up for yourself, and express your opinions. I’m hopeful that all of this will improve, but it won’t happen overnight.”

When asked if Caribbean broadcasters will follow their European peers, Helias says protecting young athletes — especially minors competing in high school meets — should be a top priority. Ultimately, she believes that while better camera rules help, the real change has to happen inside the minds of the people watching.

“We can change the guidelines but social norms, mentalities, what is or isn’t acceptable, that’s another matter.”

World.title: Restoration & Resilience: The Hermitage
World.content:
Achance encounter led SO to the story behind The Hermitage located in Bluefields, Westmoreland, related by Bluefields Bay Villas CEO Debbie Moncure…

My husband Braxton and I arrived at Bluefields in 1981 beginning our family’s journey of what I often say has been a creation of “our own world”. However, that is not entirely true, as our work in so many ways channelled the Jamaican world that existed in previous days — and before the current trend of white boxes with too much glass and too little ventilation. But first a little history of how The Hermitage came to be: In March of 1989, we attended a Washington, DC function honouring former Jamaican Prime Minister Michael Manley who had just been the first foreign dignitary to meet with President George H W Bush. As we left and after a long and lovely discussion with then Foreign Affairs Minister David Coore, I was struck by a drunk driver and sustained a head wound that rendered me unconscious and unable to remember. I worried that I would never be the same again. After recuperating for three months and with our two small kids in tow, we travelled to Bluefields, Jamaica, where I designed the basics of The Hermitage in a mere two weeks. I have always felt this villa was my saviour.

Construction began in October 1989, about seven years before phone lines reached Bluefields. Wonderful local builder Lloyd Crooks (still doing projects for us!) provided tilers who laid floors with then available Hellshire marble, masterful masons who clad insides of block walls with local limestone, and careful carpenters who cut cedar stair balusters and more on trestles set up in the outside yard. I am so glad those exist as they were my version of what was in Black River but are now gone after Hurricane Melissa. Outside treatment of concrete block walls was my method of having them resemble large building blocks and not need painting. Splendid 8’ curved-top doors, louvre windows, and built-in mahogany armoires were originally done by a Mr Barrett of Savanna-la-Mar, now deceased, who retired in Jamaica after a career in London working for Harrods. Hurricane Melissa tore out most of those doors and windows that happily have now been replaced.

After 16 months of construction and furnishing, our first guests arrived in January 1991. My husband Braxton, who passed away last April, was a masterful collector of antiques and adored what he found in Jamaica. The Hermitage, as well as our other villa properties, feature antique four-poster canopy beds, mahogany sideboards, and all the rest of what had been in Jamaican great houses. As nearly all The Hermitage’s roofs were blown away in Melissa, much of its large antiques collection got destroyed or badly damaged. Thankfully, Jamaica still has an incredibly talented furniture restorer, notably Wayne Nasralla, of Kingston, who put most of those possessions back into usable order.

Post-Melissa, growth of gardens was so supercharged in Bluefields that new visitors would not know that hurricane had happened even though it hit us with 185mph winds. By March, guests were able to stay in the villa and again lounge on cobblestone patios made from the sea-smoothed stones collected below the home, back in 1990. We are extremely proud of the fabulous work done by so many persons to help put “our world” back together again. It is a true testimonial to the resilience of the Jamaican people — and yet another reason why our Moncure Family chose to settle in and become citizens of this wonderful country.

World.title: Manchester dad charged in suspected revenge killing of two men over daughter’s murder
World.content:
File photo of the crime scene in Land Settlement, Manchester where two men were gunned down in March 2026.

MANCHESTER, Jamaica – A Manchester father has been charged with conspiracy to murder in relation to the killing of two men in the parish in March that is believed to have been a reprisal for the shooting death of his daughter a month earlier.

Charged is 37-year-old Kumar Obrien, otherwise known as ‘Frazzle’, of Melrose Drive, Land Settlement.

The deceased have been identified as 29-year-old farmer Yakieni Shaw, also known as ‘Yankee’, of Comfort District, Manchester, and 21-year-old Damien Edwards, otherwise known as ‘Damie’, of Melrose Gardens, Williamsfield, in the parish.

Reports from the Mandeville Police are that Obrien allegedly conspired with other men to kill Edwards and Shaw, who were gunned down about 3:50 pm on Saturday, March 14, 2026.

The shooting is believed to have been a reprisal for the fatal shooting of Obrien’s four-year-old daughter, Saniyah Obrien, on Sunday, February 8, while they were seated in his Voxy motor car in the parish.

An investigations led to Obrien being apprehended, interviewed, and subsequently charged. He is scheduled to appear before the Manchester Parish Court on Wednesday, October 21.

World.title: Adam Stewart, Sheryl Lee Ralph honoured at AFJ Hummingbird Gala
World.content:
Sandals Resorts Executive Chairman Adam Stewart and Emmy Award-winning actress Sheryl Lee Ralph pose with their awards after being honoured at the American Friends of Jamaica (AFJ) Hummingbird Gala at The Plaza in New York on Friday, October 16, 2026.

Sandals Resorts Executive Chairman Adam Stewart and Emmy Award-winning actress Sheryl Lee Ralph were honoured at the American Friends of Jamaica (AFJ) Hummingbird Gala, held at The Plaza in New York on Friday,

Stewart received the International Achievement Award in recognition of his contribution to Caribbean tourism, business and philanthropy, while Ralph received the International Humanitarian Award for her achievements in entertainment and longstanding advocacy, particularly in HIV/AIDS awareness.

Prime Minister Andrew Holness and Tourism Minister Edmund Bartlett were among the guests at the annual fundraising gala, which brought together business leaders, philanthropists and members of the Jamaican diaspora in support of AFJ’s work across Jamaica, including ongoing Hurricane Melissa recovery efforts.

World.title: Trump’s Russia rethink — and Europe’s response
World.content:
Donald Trump’s latest moves on Russia and Ukraine have alarmed Kyiv and European capitals alike. But rather than scrambling to contain the fallout, EU leaders are keeping their cool. Zoya Sheftalovich and Nick Vinocur explore Europe’s strategy for weathering Trump’s midterm storm — and what it means for Ukraine.

Then, France reels from a weekend of violent protests, with more than 1,800 arrests and widespread destruction. As political leaders trade accusations, we look at how the unrest is shaping the battle ahead of the 2027 presidential election from Paris.

World.title: Deutschland braucht wieder mehr Spielraum für Wachstum
World.content:
Deutschland muss Wachstum wieder stärker ins Zentrum seiner Wirtschaftspolitik rücken. Doch bevor wir darüber sprechen, wo wir 2030 sein wollen, sollten wir genau hinschauen, wo unsere Unternehmen heute stehen.

Prof. Dr. Robert Mayr, © DATEV

Seit mehr als zwei Jahren beobachten wir mit dem DATEV Mittelstandsindex eine wirtschaftliche Entwicklung, die weniger einem plötzlichen Einbruch als einer schleichenden Erschöpfung gleicht. Die Umsätze kommen nicht nachhaltig in Schwung, während Löhne und andere Kosten weiter steigen. Die Beschäftigung, lange ein Stabilitätsanker des Mittelstands, gerät zunehmend unter Druck. Der Mittelstand hält sich, aber er ist nicht im Aufschwung.

Wenn Erlöse über einen langen Zeitraum kaum wachsen und gleichzeitig die Kosten steigen, schrumpfen die Spielräume für das, was unser Land dringend braucht: Investitionen und wirtschaftliche Erneuerung. Deshalb müssen wir die Bedingungen verbessern, unter denen wirtschaftliche Dynamik entstehen kann.

Investitionen schaffen Zukunft

Viele Unternehmen konzentrieren unter den aktuellen Rahmenbedingungen ihre verfügbaren Mittel zunehmend darauf, den Bestand zu sichern. Investiert wird in Ersatz und Erhalt, während Erweiterungen, neue Technologien oder zusätzliche Kapazitäten schwieriger zu finanzieren sind. Das hat langfristige Konsequenzen. Digitalisierung, künstliche Intelligenz, klimaneutrale Produktion oder neue Geschäftsmodelle entstehen nicht allein durch politische Zielsetzungen. Sie müssen in Unternehmen konkret umgesetzt und finanziert werden. Dafür brauchen Unternehmen wirtschaftlichen Spielraum.

Wenn Erlöse über einen langen Zeitraum kaum wachsen und gleichzeitig die Kosten steigen, schrumpfen die Spielräume für das, was unser Land dringend braucht: Investitionen und wirtschaftliche Erneuerung.

Gerade aus kleinen, dynamischen Unternehmen können disruptive Innovationen und damit die großen Unternehmen von morgen entstehen. Doch Unternehmen können Risiken nur eingehen, wenn sie über ausreichende Reserven verfügen und darauf vertrauen können, dass sich langfristige Investitionen am Standort Deutschland lohnen. Statt unternehmerische Dynamik vor allem mit neuen Förderprogrammen erzeugen zu wollen, sollten wir Unternehmen wieder mehr Raum, bessere Rahmenbedingungen und mehr Planungssicherheit für eigene Entscheidungen geben.

Deutschland braucht einen schlankeren Staat

Zu guten Standortbedingungen gehört auch ein leistungsfähiger Staat. Genehmigungsverfahren, Berichtspflichten, Steuerverfahren und Verwaltungsprozesse kosten Zeit und binden Personal. Das trifft auch große Konzerne, kleine und mittlere Unternehmen aber besonders stark, weil sie regulatorische Anforderungen nicht auf große Fachabteilungen verteilen können.

Gleichzeitig ist der Staat selbst immer größer geworden. 2025 lag die Staatsquote bei über 50 Prozent. Das ist keine Kennzahl, mit der wir uns abfinden sollten. Deutschland braucht einen schlankeren Staat – nicht als Selbstzweck, sondern weil ein Staat, der immer mehr Ressourcen bindet, diese Mittel und Arbeitskräfte dem privaten Sektor entzieht. Wir sollten eine unbequeme Wahrheit aussprechen: Deutschland hat kein Einnahmenproblem. Die entscheidende Frage ist, was wir mit den vorhandenen Mitteln machen und welche Aufgaben der Staat tatsächlich übernehmen muss. Immer neue Einnahmen zu mobilisieren, während Unternehmen unter hohen Kosten und schwachen Umsätzen leiden, ist keine Wachstumsstrategie.

Das gilt auch für zusätzliche steuerliche Belastungen. Ein höherer Spitzensteuersatz trifft nicht nur gutverdienende Privatpersonen. Er trifft unmittelbar viele mittelständische Unternehmen. Für Personengesellschaften und Einzelunternehmen ist die Einkommensteuer die Unternehmenssteuer. Wer diesen Unternehmen zusätzliche Mittel entzieht, darf sich nicht wundern, wenn anschließend das Geld für Investitionen fehlt.

Europa darf deshalb nicht nur ein großer regulierter Markt sein. Es muss auch ein großer Markt für Wachstum werden.

Auch der Staat selbst steht vor dem demografischen Wandel. Digitalisierung und künstliche Intelligenz bieten die Chance, staatliche Aufgaben künftig effizienter zu erfüllen. Ein schlankerer Staat darf dabei kein schwächerer Staat sein. Er muss sich auf seine Aufgaben konzentrieren und diese schneller und verlässlicher erfüllen.

Europa muss Wachstum ermöglichen

Deutschland kann seine wirtschaftliche Stärke dauerhaft nur in einem wirtschaftlich starken Europa sichern. Der europäische Binnenmarkt ist einer unserer größten Vorteile. Im Alltag erleben Unternehmen Europa aber noch zu häufig als fragmentiert. Unterschiedliche Verfahren, zusätzliche Dokumentationspflichten und nationale Sonderwege erschweren grenzüberschreitendes Wachstum. Besonders sichtbar wird das bei jungen, erfolgreichen Unternehmen, die den nächsten Wachstumsschritt gehen wollen. Für sie muss Europa zum gemeinsamen Markt mit besseren Bedingungen werden, um zu wachsen und Kapital für die nächste Entwicklungsstufe mobilisieren zu können.

Europa darf deshalb nicht nur ein großer regulierter Markt sein. Es muss auch ein großer Markt für Wachstum werden. Es muss seine Größe auch als wirtschaftlichen Vorteil nutzen. Dafür müssen nationale Sonderwege abgebaut und Bedingungen geschaffen werden, unter denen aus erfolgreichen Gründungen globale Unternehmen werden können. Sonst riskieren wir, dass Ideen hier entstehen, die daraus resultierende Wertschöpfung aber anderswo wächst.

Widerstandskraft allein reicht nicht

Zwei Jahre DATEV Mittelstandsindex zeigen, wie lange Unternehmen Belastungen auffangen können. Aber eine Volkswirtschaft kann nicht davon leben, dass ihre Unternehmen immer nur widerstandsfähiger werden. Sie braucht neben starken Betrieben auch neue Unternehmen, aus denen die Mittelständler und Weltmarktführer von morgen wachsen können.

Der Mittelstand hat Arbeitsplätze lange gehalten, obwohl die Umsatzentwicklung schwach blieb und die Löhne weiter stiegen. Erst mit Verzögerung ist auch die Beschäftigung unter Druck geraten. Auch viele Unternehmerinnen und Unternehmer absorbieren Belastungen zunächst selbst.

Denn wirtschaftliche Dynamik entsteht in Unternehmen. Geben wir ihnen dafür wieder den nötigen Spielraum.

Gleichzeitig ziehen sich Betriebe aus dem Markt zurück, weil Nachfolge fehlt, Rentabilität sinkt oder die Perspektive nicht mehr ausreicht. Umso wichtiger ist ein Umfeld, in dem Menschen bereit sind, Verantwortung und unternehmerisches Risiko zu übernehmen.

Deutschland 2030 braucht einen Kurswechsel

Bis 2030 werden Digitalisierung, künstliche Intelligenz, demografischer Wandel und geopolitische Veränderungen unsere Wirtschaft tiefgreifend verändern. Die Antwort darauf kann nicht sein, Unternehmen immer neue Belastungen aufzubürden.

Deutschland braucht einen Kurswechsel: weniger Bürokratie und steuerliche Belastung, einen schlankeren und leistungsfähigeren Staat und ein Europa, das seine Stärke als gemeinsamer Markt ausspielt. Der Mittelstand hat in den vergangenen Jahren gezeigt, wie viel Belastung er tragen kann. Das sollte die Politik nicht als Einladung verstehen, ihm noch mehr zuzumuten. Denn wirtschaftliche Dynamik entsteht in Unternehmen. Geben wir ihnen dafür wieder den nötigen Spielraum.

Hinweis

Diese Werbung steht im Zusammenhang mit der wirtschaftspolitischen Debatte über Bürokratieabbau, steuerliche Belastungen, die Rolle des Staates und die Rahmenbedingungen für Unternehmen in Deutschland und Europa.
