World.title: 5 fights that will shape NATO’s next Russia war plans
World.content:
At the same time, the Trump administration is weighing a sharp reduction in U.S. forces in Europe, which could leave the alliance short of troops and critical capabilities with fewer like refueling aircraft, long-range missiles and intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance assets.

The negotiations will test how much each country is willing to spend, how much Europe can do without the U.S. and whether NATO’s military plans should make greater use of technologies such as robotics and artificial intelligence.

“It’s going to be tough,” said one senior NATO diplomat, who, like others, was granted anonymity to speak freely on the sensitive issue. “Burden sharing, the U.S., how to combine the level of ambition with political priorities … it’s huge.”

NATO allies will begin discussing the broad mandate for the new targets — known as Political Guidance — in the coming days. It’s the first step in a five-part effort called the NATO Defence Planning Process.

“The ambition … is for this to be a transformation cycle and not one that’s just off the shelf,” said French Adm. Pierre Vandier, NATO’s Supreme Allied Commander Transformation and the alliance’s chief for future warfare.

POLITICO spoke to 15 current and former NATO officials and diplomats to get a sense of the five key debates likely to define the negotiations.

World.title: Cyberattack on French supermarkets tells us more about food security than AI safety
World.content:
While most good and bad actors on the internet are increasingly using AI models to increase speed and capacity, cyber experts say the hackers in question in the French case most likely used traditional methods to take advantage of devices needlessly exposed to the internet.

Connecting devices to the internet in this way is “an old-fashioned bad practice,” said Amir Preminger, chief technology officer at Claroty, a cybersecurity company that identified a software flaw in a product made by Danfoss, one of the refrigeration companies targeted by the French hacks. Danfoss fixed that flaw in 2025.

Food systems

The attacks come at a time when Europe’s food security is already under considerable pressure due to geopolitical insecurity and climate change. The continuing disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz are pushing up fuel and fertilizer prices at a time where farmers struggle with the fallout of extreme drought that caused lower yields in many parts of Europe. These problems are compounded by the blockade of the Black Sea which is fueling the rise of global food prices.

“It is very serious that cyber criminals attack our food systems,” said Else Groen, director general of trade body Independent Retail Europe. She nonetheless stressed that food supply chains are resilient, which reduces the chances that consumer food supply would be endangered — even if such attacks are already a “major blow” for retailers operating on razor-thin margins.

The incidents bring to the fore a long-running problem with so-called operational technology, meaning industrial devices with physical outputs, like refrigeration systems. Critical sectors are packed with these kinds of devices, many of which are old, poorly protected, unnecessarily connected to the Internet, or some combination of the three. They’re also obscure and sometimes forgotten, despite the ramifications if they’re tampered with.

And last week's problems are far from solved. French and German cyber authorities warned that attacks were probably still ongoing, and the Greek cyber agency and an industry tracker said after the attack that there were hundreds of devices still connected to the internet.

World.title: The EU heads into a perfect political storm
World.content:
The EU is facing an unprecedented dilemma: Its four biggest economies are all heading into elections or political upheaval, potentially hamstringing the bloc’s ability to get anything done.

Spain will go to the polls next month, with the center right and far right on track to take power. France is changing presidents in April, with polls favoring far-right figurehead Marine Le Pen. The Alternative for Germany is ascendant, putting Friedrich Merz’s chancellorship in doubt. And Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni’s unusually long-serving government is also heading to an election in 2027.

The consequences are already becoming clear.

António Costa, Volodymyr Zelenskyy and Ursula von der Leyen arrive to attend an EU summit in Brussels on Oct. 16, 2026. | Nicolas Tucat/AFP via Getty Images

The bloc’s latest summit offered an early taste of what lies ahead: After two days of talks, leaders failed to make headway on the €2 trillion budget and instead became embroiled in an unexpectedly bitter row on energy policy. The summit’s conclusions notably omitted any mention of finding consensus on the budget before the end of the year, with member countries resisting a push by European Council President Antonio Costa for an end-2026 deadline, although there are summits scheduled for November and December.

If those meetings fail to produce a deal, then the already fractious talks will spill over into 2027, when electoral battles are likely to loom even larger over negotiations — and governments may be increasingly reluctant to make the compromises needed to reach agreement.

Triple assault

The paralysis Brussels fears as Europe’s election cycle gathers pace is already beginning to take hold, with last week’s summit exposing how difficult it is becoming to forge the compromises the bloc needs.

World.title: EU liberal chief urges conservatives to shun far right ahead of big election year
World.content:
Speaking by phone after a gathering of EU liberals ahead of a leaders’ summit on Thursday, Hayer said “we need a strong European platform from the center to deliver for Europeans” on issues such as competitiveness, defense, climate change and decarbonization, especially with major EU countries facing national elections, including Spain in November and Italy, France and Poland in 2027. “We should be prepared for this new cycle of elections.”

To lock in the centrist majority, Hayer wants the three groups to strike a detailed coalition agreement. The EPP has largely voted with its centrist allies during the first half of the current term, but has occasionally turned to the right to pass legislation when disagreements with its traditional partners proved too difficult to bridge.

Hayer said Renew would not back any candidate for Parliament president without first agreeing on a detailed coalition deal. “A majority needs a program before it needs a president, so we need a coalition agreement before any leadership agreement, and no coalition agreement would mean no leadership deal.”

That could force the EPP to the negotiating table, as the conservatives want to get Roberta Metsola reelected for a third term in January. However, the EPP has in the past been reluctant to sign a detailed coalition agreement.

Hayer and the leaders of the EPP (Manfred Weber) and Socialists and Democrats (Iratxe García) already signed a two-page agreement to work with each other after the 2024 EU election, but the EPP has nonetheless voted on laws with far-right groups.

To prevent this, Hayer wants not only leaders but all “key members” of the groups, including vice-chairs, whips and coordinators, to negotiate and endorse the agreement.

World.title: Macron vows ‘full transparency’ in France after protests turn to widespread unrest
World.content:
The French government has been accused of mismanaging and underestimating the protests, with calls for Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez to resign emerging both on the left and the far right.

According to the latest figures from the French interior ministry, some 2,000 people were arrested during the turmoil. Police, firefighters and demonstrators suffered injuries as the situation unraveled.

Serge Papin, France’s minister for small business, will meet with company reps at the Ministry of Economy tomorrow to assess the damage and suggest assistance for businesses that were affected.

Macron said he was awaiting “clear answers” on why the protests turned violent. The French president accused “troublemakers from far-left splinter groups, joined by numerous delinquents” of engaging in “unbridled violence.”

With six months to go before next year’s presidential election in France, the events of Saturday quickly took on a political dimension.

Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu also accused the “ultra-left” of fomenting the violence, alleging that the France Unbowed movement and its presidential candidate Jean-Luc Mélenchon had played an “important role” within a “far-left network” driving the unrest.

World.title: 'I hold children who will probably not survive because of the cuts I'm forced to make', says UN aid chief UN
World.content:
UN humanitarian chief Tom Fletcher has warned of worsening conditions in conflict zones, describing places such as Sudan and Gaza as an “atrocities lab”, where new weapons are being developed and tested amid devastating human suffering.

 

Fletcher also condemned the killing of around 1,000 aid workers over the past three years, lamenting what he described as a near-total lack of accountability: “No accountability, never investigations.” He called the situation “terrifying”.

World.title: Body horror and 'Becoming America': The best things to do, hear, see or watch in Europe this week
World.content:
It's a big week for DC Universe fans as Clayface hits cinemas — but an even bigger week for those needing an extra hour of sleep.

 

The clocks fall back this Sunday, so it's officially time to pull out your chunkiest knitwear, pour something pumpkin spiced, and embrace the darker days by burrowing under the covers with an 8-part crime thriller on Prime.

Of course, if you're not ready to go full hibernation mode yet, this week also sees plenty of new exhibitions opening across the continent. Notable highlights include an exploration of North America's early history at London's Science Museum, and German painter Conny Maier's imaginary paradise at Munich's Pinakothek der Moderne.

As an added bonus, don't forget to check out our Lumière Film Festival content. Although the event has now ended in Lyon, our resident film critic David Mouriquand has been busy publishing highlights and interviews with acclaimed filmmakers like Todd Haynes and Tsui Hark — so even if you missed out, you can at least feel like you were there!

Until next time — here's what's coming up.

Exhibitions and events

Becoming America: How Science Shaped a Nation

A map of the British and French dominions in North America, John Mitchell, 1755. Courtesy of the Library of Congress.

When: 23 October 2026 — 25 April 2027

Where: Science Museum (London, United Kingdom)

The Declaration of Independence was signed 250 years ago, marking the birth of a country that would go on to become one of the world's most powerful, influential — and divisive. The Science Museum marks this through a fascinating look at how science and technology shaped North America's early developments, spanning four decades of its history up to the 1790s, when George Washington was elected as the first US president. There are more than a hundred rare objects on display, including a first print of the Declaration of Independence and a map by Benjamin Franklin that charted the Atlantic Gulf Stream. Find out more here.

Conny Maier: Searching for Paradise

Conny Maier Gebrüder Q., 2026. Courtesy the artist, Société, Berlin und Hauser & Wirth Foto: Staatliche Graphische Sammlung München.

When: 21 October 2026 — 17 January 2027

Where: Pinakothek der Moderne (Munich, Germany)

German painter Conny Maier, who previously won the Deutsche Bank Artist of the Year award in 2021, has transformed the Pinakothek der Moderne museum into an eery and enchanting purgatory. From pastel pink florals to flaming woodland, her bold and evocative canvasses create an immersive atmosphere that carries visitors between paradise and apocalypse; drawing on medieval art, Expressionism and more to expose non-human worlds — and our collective fragility. Find out more here.

Bonus highlight: The fifth edition of Art Basel Paris, a vast and vibrant annual contemporary art fair, takes place from 23 - 25 October 2026 at the Grand Palais.

Movies

Clayface

Tom Rhys Harries in 'Clayface'. DC Studios/Warner Bros. Pictures.

Where: Cinemas

When: 23 October

The DC Universe's new 'Gods and Monsters' chapter continues with an origin story for one of Batman's most famous foes: Clayface. Tom Rhys Harries stars as Matt Hagen, an actor who undergoes experimental facial reconstruction surgery after being left disfigured by a mob boss. Written by Mike Flanagan (best known for his Stephen King adaptations), the movie leans heavily into its body horror elements as Hagen finds himself mutating into a clay-like form while his grip on reality also begins to crumble.

Bonus highlight: A poorly young girl is gifted a companion robot (Jenna Ortega) in Taika Waititi's adaptation of Kazuo Ishiguro's best-selling book, Klara and the Sun. Out from 23 October in most parts of Europe.

TV series

The Terminal List

Chris Pratt in 'The Terminal List'. Photo by Justin Lubin/Justin Lubin/Prime - © Amazon Content Services LLC.

Where: Prime Video

When: 21 October

For those stuck in a post-Reacher streaming slump, Prime's got another gritty action show to fill the void. Based on Jack Carr's popular series of novels, The Terminal List follows US Navy SEAL James Reece (Chris Pratt) as he sets out to avenge the deaths of his platoon — uncovering dark governmental secrets along the way. In this second series, Reece's grief, anger, and desire for redemption has grown even stronger after the murder of his family, leading him across the world on a violent mission for answers and justice.

Bonus highlight: The third season of Netflix comedy Nobody Wants This, starring Kristen Bell and Adam Brody as a couple facing complicated cultural challenges, streams from 22 October.

Music

John Legend: Muse

When: 23 October

American singer and pianist John Legend is back with a new blend of soul-soothing gospel, hip-hop and Afrobeats — this time in collaboration with Pharrell Williams. Recorded at Pharrell's studio within the Louis Vuitton HQ in Paris, 'Muse' features 16 tracks that explore faith, devotion and intimacy through experimental new sounds; the album acting like a form of reconnection and rebirth for two longterm friends.

Bonus highlights: The fifth album from British singer-songwriter Michael Kiwanuka, FUDGE is a passion-fuelled swell of psychedelic soul — released on 23 October 2026.

World.title: Greek authorities say 12 migrants die in two incidents in Aegean Sea
World.content:
Greek authorities said on Monday that 12 migrants had died attempting to cross the Aegean Sea including six whose bodies were found after their boat collided with a police vessel.

 

A baby and four women were among six people who died off the island of Lesbos on Monday following the collision, the coast guard said.

The other six dead were on a small boat that capsized off the island of Samos, the coast guard added.

At least 1,209 migrants have died or gone missing in the Mediterranean since the beginning of the year, according to the International Organisation for Migration.

This is a developing story and our journalists are working on further updates.

World.title: How much does inflation cost you? Ask the Euronews AI chatbot
World.content:
Inflation in the Euro area reached 3.8% in September 2026, up from 3.2% in August, according to European Central Bank (ECB) estimates. Values vary, with Lithuania leading at 6.1%, followed by Bulgaria (5.6%) and Luxembourg and Cyprus at 5.2%. Malta recorded the lowest increase at 2.4%.

 

Energy is the main driver, with prices rising 18.8% in September as the war in the Middle East halted liquefied natural gas production, fuelled gas-price volatility and sent the global energy market into shock.

In response, the EU proposed several measures, including AccelerateEU, to strengthen energy resilience. Member states have introduced targeted relief measures, such as electricity price caps and energy vouchers, and lower fuel excise duties.

But higher energy bills affect the entire economy. Energy-intensive sectors, including manufacturing, chemicals, and agriculture, face rising production costs. Other sectors, such as food processing and pharmaceuticals, are indirectly hit by higher operational and supply-chain costs.

Companies pass these increases on to consumers, driving up the overall cost of goods and deepening Europe’s cost-of-living crisis.

Daily essentials, including food, alcohol, and tobacco, recorded 1.4% inflation in September. Service inflation in healthcare, education, and transport rose to 3.2%, while industrial goods inflation reached 1.1%, according to the ECB.

Inflation also hit the housing market. Eurostat reports that house prices rose by 5.1% and rents by 3% in the first quarter of 2026, compared with the first quarter of 2025, sparking protests across Europe.

Member states, including Italy and Greece, have asked for more fiscal flexibility to help families and businesses cope with surging prices, but Brussels has denied it.

Do you want to know more about the EU’s inflation crisis? Ask the Euronews AI chatbot!

World.title: Marco Rubio denies there was any pause in US intelligence sharing with Ukraine
World.content:
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio denied on Monday that there had been any suspension of intelligence sharing with Ukraine and called on President Volodymyr Zelenskyy to "focus" on ending the war with Russia.

 

"There has been no pause," Rubio told reporters when asked about Ukraine's claims that the United States had briefly halted the sending of intelligence to help counter Russia's missile attacks.

The Ukrainian leader told US media on Sunday that the move had been "deblocked by the American side" after a three-day suspension.

Rubio, who is in Uzbekistan for talks with Central Asian officials, said that President Donald Trump wanted Zelenskyy and Russia's President Vladimir Putin to concentrate on ending the Russian invasion, now into its fifth year.

"What he (Zelenskyy) should be focused on and what we want to be focused on is bringing an end to this war," Rubio said.

"That's what we want everybody to be focused on. That's what we want the Russians to be focused on. That's what we should be focused on. That's what the president has made a priority: is trying to bring a war and an end to this war," the top US diplomat said.

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio attends a meeting in Samarkand, 19 October, 2026 AP Photo

Trump, who says he has made a deal with Russia to secure fuel exports in exchange for the easing of sanctions, has made renewed attacks on Zelenskyy in recent days over the war.

The US leader wrote on his Truth Social platform on Sunday that he was making "great progress" in negotiating peace between Russia and Ukraine, but claimed: "Zelenskyyy doesn't care, and frankly, with all of the money that Europe is famously giving him...he doesn't want to end this war and probably never did."

"Zelenskyyy is using Diesel Refineries in Russia as a target, knowing that these attacks are seriously hurting the world diesel markets, including those in the United States," Trump said.

Resumed intelligence sharing

But Zelenskyy said he was "thankful" that the United States has resumed intelligence sharing after a pause had left his country more vulnerable to Russian missile strikes.

"It was blocked for some period of time. And then it was deblocked by the American side. We are very thankful for this. Now it works," he told NBC's "Meet the Press" in an interview published on Sunday.

"Only (the) United States has this unique intelligence to tell our side when Russia uses ballistic missiles. And we didn't get it during ballistic attacks during three days," Zelensky added.

In the past week, Kyiv also reported restrictions to satellite services operated by Elon Musk's SpaceX, which Ukraine relies on for battlefield communications, shortly after US President Donald Trump criticised Ukraine and urged it to stop targeting Russian oil refineries.

A screenshot of a post on US President Donald Trump's Truth Social account, 19 October, 2026 @realDonaldTrump

Zelenskyy said he believed "it was a message from American government to limit the speed. And technically, SpaceX did it."

The Trump administration has denied it was behind any slowdown and Zelensky's remark drew a quick rebuke from a top US official.

"President (Donald) Trump and Secretary (of State Marco) Rubio have categorically said that no one in the Trump administration did that. And I think it is very reckless for President Zelenskyy to make such a charge," Bessent told NBC in a separate interview aired on the same show Sunday.

Bessent did not provide an alternative explanation.

Musk, who has himself been critical of Zelenskyy and has called on him "to go," said on Wednesday that any disruptions reported by Ukraine in using the Starshield satellite communications system would be the responsibility of the US government.

Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskyy arrives for a media conference at the EU summit in Brussels, 16 October, 2026 AP Photo

European alternatives

Meanwhile, Ukraine is pushing ahead with plans to develop European alternatives to US-made air defence systems and Starlink satellite communications, with discussions under way and Kyiv expecting progress considerably sooner than sceptics anticipate, a senior Ukrainian presidential official told Euronews last week.

In an exclusive interview with Euronews’ Europe Today programme, Ihor Zhovkva, deputy head of President Volodymyr Zelenskyy's office, said Ukraine was seeking to reduce its reliance on American capabilities as uncertainty over Washington's support places growing pressure on Europe to strengthen its own defences.

"We are, of course, relying on the unique capabilities provided by the United States, whether air defence systems or Starlink," Zhovkva said.

"But Ukraine has already begun substantive discussions with European countries about a European air defence system."

World.title: Place de la République flares again as Macron admits intelligence failures
World.content:
Tension rose again on Paris’ Place de la République on Sunday afternoon as groups of young people returned to the square under the close watch of riot police.

 

“Be careful, it’s about to blow up again,” one officer warned as the crowd grew.

Several small police squads were standing among apparently peaceful groups of youths when sudden scuffles set off a new wave of defiance. Chants of “ACAB” (All Cops Are Bastards) rang out as officers isolated a boy who appeared to be in his early teens and led him away, with youths shouting for his release.

A handful of tear gas grenades were fired as the two sides edged warily around each other. Police then withdrew from the square, clearing people from their path as they went.

The skirmishes followed a night of some of the worst urban violence France has seen in years, as demonstrations over the cost of living gave way to clashes with police, mass looting and fires across the country.

Nearly 2,400 people were arrested on Saturday and almost 1,000 police and gendarmes were injured, according to the interior ministry. Late on Saturday, Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu had condemned “violence of extreme intensity”, putting the figures at the time at 1,200 arrests and 150 officers hurt.

Macron refuses minister’s resignation

On Monday, President Emmanuel Macron acknowledged “failures in anticipation and intelligence” but refused the resignation of Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez, the Élysée Palace said.

“The interior minister submitted his resignation to the president on Sunday,” the palace said in a statement. “Given the necessity for continued leadership of law enforcement at this time, the president refused.”

Some opposition politicians had called for Nuñez to be sacked. Macron instead asked him to “take all necessary steps to ensure transparency over the failures in planning and intelligence that led to the violence”, and to “put in place new operational methods for security forces” to handle the crisis.

Back on Place de la République, people trickled in once the police had gone. The square soon filled with curious passers-by who had come to see the damage from the night before, stopping in the surrounding streets to photograph burned cars, heaps of wrecked bicycles and shattered glass.

“It’s like a museum,” one woman said. “Well, now we’ve seen it, we can go home.”

'People are desperate'

Paris mayor Emmanuel Grégoire said whole streets in the capital “have been devastated”. He drew a line between the “fundamental” right to protest and “unacceptable” violence.

On a nearby street, Ilan, 21, was sweeping debris from the front of his small delicatessen. Its window, smashed by looters, had been patched with cardboard, and he had opened for only a few hours.

“I was lucky, but just next door they lost everything,” he said. “How are they going to cope? Some people are really desperate.”

He did not plan to stay open long. “They’re going to come back tonight,” he said. “I’m not staying much longer.”

Cash machines were destroyed in the demonstration against rising living costs and students protests. 18 October, 2026. AP Photo

Across the road stood a restaurant that looters had burned out and ransacked. Shortly afterwards, panic swept the street as rumours of new clashes spread and tear gas grenades could be heard exploding, sending groups running from the square.

Nearby, tear gas fumes drifted past Le Carillon, one of the bars targeted in the November 2015 Paris attacks. Hooded youths ran past its windows with riot police in pursuit, and staff hurried to shut them.

World.title: France grapples with the aftermath of a weekend of violence
World.content:
France reels: France continues to grapple this morning with the fallout of this weekend’s events, when anti-austerity protests spilled over into violent riots across the country. Around 2000 people were arrested and more than 500 police officers, gendarmes and firefighters were injured, amid scenes of chaos, burning buildings, and violent clashes in cities from Marseille to Paris to Lyon.

 

Saturday’s protests started peacefully, with demonstrators calling for more public spending to repair decrepit schools and improve education standards, as well as measures to tackle the rising cost of living. But the marches were hijacked by groups of masked rioters, who started fires, smashed storefronts and built barricades.

Euronews’ France correspondent Estelle Nilsson-Julien was among the journalists targeted by looters on Saturday in central Paris. “The calmer protests earlier in the day descended into complete anarchy,” Estelle told me last night, describing how masked individuals encircled her and attacked her camera operator.

‘Honte et colêre’: In an address to the nation last night, French President Emmanuel Macron said the nation felt shame and anger, as he made a plea for unity.

Picking up the pieces: The wreckage is on the one hand material: trade bodies estimate the damages to be in the hundreds of millions of euros. But this weekend’s events will also likely leave a deep mark on French society and politics, as the country enters what many see as one of its most consequential periods in history ahead of April’s presidential election.

Questions are now being asked about where the political responsibility lies. The government has failed to make sufficient concessions to address the grievances of students, who have been holding demonstrations for weeks. Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez handed in his resignation this morning, but his request has been rejected by President Macron.

On Sunday, Marine Le Pen of the far-right National Rally (RN), the frontrunner to become the next French President, spoke of a “crisis of confidence” and a “threat to democracy”.

Jean-Luc Mélenchon, the leader of the far-left France Unbowed (LFI), has also come under fire from government figures and right-wing leaders, with the centrist presidential candidate Edouard Philippe saying his party carries “considerable responsibility” for the violence of recent days.

Contagion: The scenes seem to have awakened an underlying unease in other parts of Europe, with similar demonstrations over the weekend descending into violence, including in Belgium, Italy and Portugal.

Magyar’s take: Hungarian Prime Minister Péter Magyar has linked the riots to immigration levels, saying the “shocking scenes” vindicated his government’s tough migration policies. More from my colleague Sándor Zsiros in our top story below.

Trump berates Zelenskyy: Meanwhile, US President Donald Trump has said that Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy “doesn’t want to end this war, and probably never did”, after Kyiv launched a major drone attack on an oil terminal in Saint Petersburg over the weekend.

“His (Zelenskyy’s) country is in shambles, a large portion of his land is lost, his oceans and seas are gone, and his male population is low, wounded and/or dead,” Trump also said in a blistering Truth Social post.

Ukraine-US talks continue: The escalation came just after a sign of a possible détente. Zelenskyy said on Sunday that he held talks with US negotiators Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner to discuss the next steps in diplomatic efforts to end Russia’s war.

Zelenskyy also revealed that Washington had restored intelligence-sharing on incoming Russian ballistic missiles after a three-day interruption. "We are very thankful for this," he told NBC News. "Now it works."

But the Ukrainian leader also painted a dire picture of the relationship with the US in a separate interview with Bloomberg, where he said he believed “steps have been taken to convince Ukraine to capitulate" to Russia, and suggested Washington was slowing down Patriot missile deliveries via NATO’s PURL scheme.

Russia continues to pound Ukraine: Russia meanwhile launched successive ballistic missile attacks on Kyiv overnight, damaging a metro station and nearby railway infrastructure. This time, unlike during the previous evening's strikes, residents received advance air-raid warnings.

Moscow’s relentless attacks have turned Kyiv into a "true frontline city", the EU's ambassador to Ukraine, Katarína Mathernová, exclusively told my colleague Sasha Vakulina in an interview, as she described the growing disruption to everyday life in the capital. Watch.

The day after: Meanwhile, Brussels will today begin to reckon with the aftermath of last week’s momentous summit, where EU leaders committed to addressing Ukraine’s request for an additional €70 billion in financial and military support for next year, Jorge Liboreiro, who covered the two-day meeting, writes.

The European Commission has been tasked with presenting options to fund the €70 billion gap, which will come on top of the €90 billion loan that leaders agreed to less than a year ago. It’s painful for leaders to reopen the debate, but Russia’s all-out escalation, aimed at collapsing Ukraine’s economy, has radically changed the equation and ballooned wartime costs.

“At the time when we planned for the €90 billion (loan), we could not foresee what 2027 would look like, but now it is clear that we have a gap of €70 billion that has to be covered,” Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said.

What now? For now, issuing a new round of joint debt looks like the easiest and fastest option, though it will be significantly costlier, both financially and politically. Some countries, like Germany, Spain and the Netherlands, prefer to tap into the €210 billion of immobilised Russian assets. But Belgian Prime Minister Bart De Wever made clear during the summit that his objections still stand.

Other options, such as redeploying EU funds and coordinating bilateral contributions, are much more limited.

Brussels insists the EU won’t be left shouldering the €70 billion alone. But Western allies haven’t stepped up enough, deepening Kyiv’s financial shortfall. It seems that this time, the bloc will have to carry the torch. President Zelenskyy told leaders as much: “This is a realistic amount. And I ask you to find this support.”

Explosive mix: The effort to find the cash will overlap with the bitter negotiations over the next EU budget. The summit laid bare the enormous differences that still exist among capitals, which are sticking to their red lines. The frugals insist larger cuts are needed, but the Friends of Cohesion oppose further reductions. António Costa, the president of the European Council, has taken charge of the process and will present a new compromise text in the coming weeks. Can the funding for Ukraine be agreed in tandem with the budget? Some say it must, others say it shouldn’t.

Magyar links French riots to migration, says ‘shocking scenes’ justify hard line

Hungarian Prime Minister Péter Magyar has linked the weekend riots in France to immigration levels, saying the “shocking scenes” vindicated his government’s tough migration policies.

“Seeing this senseless destruction and unjustified violence, perhaps it is now clear to everyone why Hungary takes the toughest possible stance on migration,” Magyar wrote on social media on Sunday, alongside a video showing buildings on fire.

He also said that the "overwhelming majority of European countries" want a tougher approach to migration and have "finally woken up".

At a European summit held last week, a group of countries, including Denmark, Italy and Hungary, pushed for stronger language on migration in the conclusions. French President Emmanuel Macron warned against “the stigmatisation” of immigrants and Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez praised their positive contribution.

Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk shared a similar message on Sunday, saying Poland would “not repeat the mistakes of other European countries” on immigration.

My colleague Sándor Zsiros has more.

More from our newsrooms

Wages vs prices: The economic pressures behind Europe's protests. From rising food prices and unaffordable housing to stagnant purchasing power and strained public services, demonstrations across Europe highlight growing frustration over living standards. Angela Barnes has the details.

Can Spain afford its pensions? What to know about the funding debate ahead of the election. This year, Spain has set a new record for its monthly pension bill, at almost €14.5 billion. Its Social Security system, which pays pensions and other benefits, reported its smallest deficit since 2011. How could this play into the electoral campaign ahead of the November 29 vote? Cristian Caraballo explains.

Trump endorses Netanyahu nine days before Israeli election, breaking months of silence. US President Donald Trump on Sunday endorsed embattled Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in the final stretch of his reelection campaign, after the two leaders’ strategies on Iran and Gaza have diverged. Jeremiah Fisayo-Bambi has more.

We’re also keeping an eye on

EU employment and social affairs ministers gather in Luxembourg.

The European Parliament’s plenary session kicks off later this evening.

European Commissioner for Migration Magnus Brunner is in London for meetings with government representatives.

That’s it for today. Jorge Liboreiro and Sasha Vakulina contributed to this newsletter.

World.title: Europe Today: France counts cost of violence as Ukraine hits St Petersburg, Leningrad
World.content:
On today's show:

Valerie Gauriat, Euronews correspondent, reports from Paris on the destruction left by the weekend's protests, how it compares with the war zones she usually covers, what the final cost could be, and whether the government has regained control after President Emmanuel Macron vowed in an address to the nation to catch all those responsible.

 

Alberto Alemanno, Professor of EU law at HEC Paris, looks at the cost-of-living and housing protests spreading across Europe, from Albania to Portugal and Italy, and how long they could last.

Sasha Vakulina reports on the Ukrainian drone attack on St Petersburg, which Russian officials say hit an oil terminal and a data centre, with reports of a bridge also being targeted, and what it means for Donald Trump's energy ceasefire. She speaks exclusively to Katarina Mathernova, the EU's Ambassador to Ukraine.

Tom Fletcher, UN aid chief, discusses how bad the plight of aid workers is, after more than 1,000 were killed in three years. He was in Brussels for an EU conference on the protection of humanitarian aid workers, as a fight unfolds over how development, humanitarian aid and geopolitical priorities will be financed in the EU's 2028–2034 budget.

When and where to watch Europe Today?

You can join Euronews’ anchors Méabh Mc Mahon and Stefan Grobe live on TV and Euronews' website, as well as digital platforms (YouTube, Facebook, X, and Instagram), every weekday at 8 am Brussels time.

In just 20 minutes, we bring you the day's key events plus crucial analysis of all the stories shaping the EU and beyond. Also available as a newsletter and podcast.

World.title: Shipping attacks threaten Turkey's resolve to keep warships out of Black Sea
World.content:
A wave of deadly attacks on cargo ships in the waters of NATO members Bulgaria and Romania has jolted the alliance into calling an emergency meeting on Black Sea security. Yet any move to send NATO ships hinges on Turkey reversing its steadfast refusal to allow warships into the Black Sea.

Advertising

Thursday saw two chemical tankers struck by drones close to a Romanian port.

It follows two similar attacks in Bulgarian waters in the past week. More than 20 sailors have been killed or remain missing.

“The war has come in full force to the Black Sea now,” said Yoruk Isik, a maritime analyst who runs the Istanbul-based Bosphorus Observer consultancy. “With the change in technology compared to the beginning of the war, drones really disrupted maritime traffic.”

According to Isik, the latest attacks underscore the growing spread of the conflict between Russia and Ukraine. “Russian ports and Ukrainian ports are heavily targeted, but now even in NATO waters ships are getting hit, in Bulgarian waters, Romanian waters.

“We are at a point where there is no safe place.”

The latest strikes targeted vessels along a key Ukrainian shipping route, casting Russia as NATO’s prime suspect as Moscow intensifies its assault on Ukrainian trade.

After meeting on Thursday with the leaders of Bulgaria and Romania, both NATO members, Secretary-General Mark Rutte said the military alliance would “continue to work closely with our allies in the Black Sea, adjusting our deterrence and defence posture as needed”.

Romanian President Nicușor Dan said NATO would hold a crisis meeting next week to discuss the situation.

Gatekeeper to the Black Sea

NATO could deploy air defence systems against drones to protect Bulgarian and Romanian waters.

But any deployment of naval ships will depend on NATO member Turkey, which controls access to the Black Sea through the Turkish Straits under a long-standing international treaty, the 1936 Montreux Convention.

Since Russia invaded Ukraine in February 2022, Ankara has blocked entry of Russian and Ukrainian warships or military vessels belonging to NATO members without a Black Sea coast, arguing for a diplomatic solution.

In recent weeks the Turkish government has sought to broker a ceasefire on commercial shipping, without success. Isik claims that failure, coupled with the latest escalation in attacks, is increasingly calling into question Ankara’s reliance on diplomacy alone.

“Either they’re going to have a breakthrough and the Kremlin is going to de-escalate, or Ankara is going to accept the reality that there needs to be a more credible force here – bigger vessels have to come,” the analyst said.

He pointed out that the navies of Romania and Bulgaria are not equipped to handle such an operation alone, with Cold War-era ships nearing the end of their lifespan.

“So Turkey's engagement is key to any successful NATO planning in the Black Sea.”

Russian leverage

Despite Turkish-owned cargo ships coming under attack in recent weeks, and Turkey’s deep reliance on Black Sea trade, Ankara has so far kept its powerful navy on the sidelines.

International relations expert Huseyin Bagci, of Ankara’s Middle East Technical University, says Turkey fears an escalation in the conflict and will be wary of allowing NATO ships into the Black Sea.

“I do not think the government would dare,” said Bagci. “Probably the government considers this a provocation to drag Turkey into the war... Turkey is afraid of getting involved in the Black Sea against Russia, this is somehow a trauma in the Turkish mind.”

Moscow also retains powerful leverage over Ankara, he suggested.

Russia’s state nuclear company Rosatom is about to complete a multi-billion-dollar nuclear power station in Akkuyu, southern Turkey. Ankara sees it as vital to the drive to reduce its heavy dependence on imported energy. “It is illogical to oppose Russia now while you let the Russians complete the nuclear plant,” said Bagci.

Erdogan hints at larger nuclear partnership with Russia, unsettling Turkey's allies

Ankara also knows that letting NATO vessels in while barring Russian warships could provoke Moscow into contesting Turkey’s prized status as the gatekeeper to the Black Sea.

However, retired Turkish diplomat Selim Kuneralp, an expert on the Montreux Convention, warns Turkey’s control over Black Sea access is likely already in Russian President Vladimir Putin’s sights.

“This has probably had an impact on Russia’s ability to conduct the war, and I doubt that Putin is very happy with the situation,” said Kuneralp. “So if he were to win the war, there is a very strong risk that he will take the initiative of saying: ‘this is unacceptable and we want to have free passage of warships from now on, regardless of whether there is a war’.”

As a signatory, Moscow has the right to call for a revision of the Montreux Convention every five years.

For centuries, Russia fought repeated wars with the then Ottoman Empire for control of the Turkish Straits. In the early years of the Cold War, even Joseph Stalin tried his hand, but the United States intervened and thwarted him.

Now Ankara walks a tightrope between Moscow and its NATO partners to avoid a resurrection of those historical rivalries.

World.title: Germany news: Berlin conference seeks to drum up investment
World.content:
A two-day conference entitled "Invest in Germany Summit" is to begin on Monday evening in Berlin as the government seeks to shore up public-sector spending with private money.

Chancellor Friedrich Merz will deliver the opening speech at the conference, which will be attended by an expected 200 representatives from large German and international companies.

The CEO of the US chip manufacturer Nvidia, Jensen Huang, is to be one of the key guests at the conference.

The German government is looking to cooperate strongly with the company, whose products are central to the boom in artificial intelligence, in a bid to help Germany catch up in the sector.

Nividia's Jensen Huang, seen here in Davos in 2026, is to be a key guest Image: Mattias Nutt/Avalon/Photoshot/picture alliance

Don't expect too much: Economic institute

The German Economic Institute (IW) has, however, warned against any too high expectations from the summit, saying that high costs for labor, energy and bureaucracy in Germany were a deterrent to investment in the country.

"It would be naive to believe that the summit will change that in the short term. Companies don't choose Germany because of a promotional event. What matters is whether they can make money here," IW director Michael Hüther told the DPA news agency.

He said it would be more effective if the government were to swiftly implement its reform agenda.

A study by Allianz Research has shown that investment in Germany fell by 6.4% between 2019 and 2025, while it grew by 6.7% in the rest of the eurozone and a whole 20.2% in the US.

World.title: India news: CJP alleges 'deliberate' delay in leaders' release
World.content:
10/19/2026 October 19, 2026 CJP leaders remain in custody, magistrate alleges threat to life

The release of Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) leaders Ashutosh Ranka and Saurav Das, who were sent to five days of judicial custody on October 14 for entering Jantar Mantar, has been delayed.

Jantar Mantar has been a prominent protest site in the heart of Delhi for decades. However, Delhi police blocked it amid heavy barricading and deployment.

The duo's judicial custody was supposed to end on Sunday, but their bail hearing was stalled after the special executive magistrate failed to arrive at the scheduled time and later recused himself, citing a threat to his life.

The Delhi Police have registered a case against unknown persons for threatening the magistrate in connection with Ranka and Das's bails.

According to The Times of India, police sources said the magistrate is being pressured to release Ranka and Das without delay.

CJP's legal affairs chief, Ratna Singh, has alleged a "deliberate use of delaying tactics" to keep Das and Ranka "behind bars."

On Sunday, Singh said they had completed every required procedure and were "merely waiting for formal approval."

The CJP were detained amid calls for protests demanding the removal of top election official Gyanesh Kumar over his alleged involvement in electroal irregularities and mass deletions from voter rolls.

World.title: Brazil: Lula, Bolsonaro clash in heated presidential debate
World.content:
The candidates traded barbs, including over Bolsonaro's ties to US President Donald Trump in their first debate, days before the October 25 election runoff.

Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva and populist Senator Flavio Bolsonaro on Sunday had a heated exchange during their first face-to-face presidential debate.

The televised debate, which saw the candidates trade insults and accusations, came a week before the October 25 presidential runoff.

Bolsonaro finished nearly two points ahead of Lula in the election's first round earlier this month.

How did the presidential debate turn heated?

The contentious debate focused on the economy, public security, corruption and Brazil's relations with the United States, before it devolved into personal attacks.

Bolsonaro criticized Lula over the cost of living, public security and social spending, accusing him of spending recklessly to secure re-election.

Lula called Bolsonaro "a habitual liar, a thug," alluding to his alleged ties to Rio de Janeiro's paramilitary groups.

"Lying is ​the Bolsonaro family's strong suit," Lula said.

Bolsonaro retaliated by accusing Lula of being tainted by corruption, saying during the debate that it was better he maintains a distance "because my wallet could be stolen."

"Brazil is going to retire you," Bolsonaro told Lula.

Meanwhile, Lula also brought up the populist Senator's ties to US President Donald Trump.

"It is striking how the Bolsonaro family is subservient to American interests," said Lula, accusing Bolsonaro of conspiring to "hand over" Brazil's rare earth minerals to the US.

Flavio's father also came up during the discussion. Former President Jair Bolsonaro is currently serving a 27-year sentence under house arrest over a coup attempt after his failed 2022 re-election bid.

The next presidential debate is scheduled for Friday, October 23.

Brazilian politics have been increasingly polarized for nearly a decade Image: Miguel Schincariol/AFP

Thousands rally in support

Meanwhile, tens of thousands of supporters of both candidates rallied in cities across Brazil ahead of the debate, flooding the streets of Sao Paulo, Rio de Janeiro and other cities.

In Sao Paulo, Bolsonaro's supporters called for the release of Jair Bolsonaro.

On the other hand, at Rio's Copacabana Beach, Lula supporters led a "rally for democracy." There were similar events in Brasilia and 16 other state capitals.

World.title: Emmanuel Macron slams 'failures' over protest unrest in France but refuses his interior minister's resignation
World.content:
But France's president has refused his interior minister Laurent Nunez's resignation after nationwide protests turned violent over the weekend.

France's President Emmanuel Macron has condemned the "failures in anticipation and intelligence" by French authorities, the Elysee Palace said Monday, after nationwide cost-of-living protests were marred by violence.

Despite the failures, Macron has refused the resignation of Interior Minister Laurent Nunez, the presidential palace added.

Macron and his government are under pressure from opposition politicians, who have called for Nunez to be removed, after mass rallies on Saturday over the rising cost of living and high fuel costs turned violent.

In some of the worst urban violence France has seen in years, nearly 2,400 people were arrested, while almost 1,000 police and gendarmes (French armed police) were injured, the Interior Ministry said Sunday.

This is a developing story, more to follow...

World.title: What Earth's sixth mass extinction event means for humans
World.content:
Human activity is driving plants and animals to extinction at an unprecedented rate. As countries meet in Armenia to discuss ways to reverse nature loss, DW reveals how declining biodiversity is already harming people.

From the tiniest microbes in the human gut to giant whales in the ocean, biodiversity is the sum of all life on the planet. It's another word for nature. And because nature is like a team, every player has a job.

When various species from trees to animals work together, they regulate weather, maintain soil health, purify water and support food production. These benefits are known as ecosystem services and they underpin human wellbeing.

"It is really an abstract concept, but we experience it absolutely every day," said Rebecca Shaw, chief scientist at conservation group WWF "And we almost never think about it when nature is functioning."

Without biodiversity, the variety of food humans eat would not be available. Declining biodiversity is endangering crop production Image: Burak Kara/Getty Images

But as it declines, she and other scientists are calling on the world to really think about it. Because biodiversity is struggling as humans push ecosystems to the brink through intensive farming, burning fossil fuels,and pollution from sources like plastic and chemicals.

Over the past 52 years, monitored vertebrate populations have collapsed by an average of 73%, while freshwater ecosystems are faring worst with a drop of 85%, according to WWF's recent Living Planet report.

It tallies with other studies that show a million animal and plant species face extinction unless humanity reduces its pressure on nature.

"It is a really steep decline," said Shaw. "What it's telling us is that nature is in trouble, and it's an early warning indicator of the fabric of life that we depend on for freshwater and food and for clean air is unravelling."

Deforestation directly drives biodiversity decline because forests are home to more than 80% of all land-based species Image: Juancho Torres/AA/picture alliance

Thousands of policymakers, business leaders and civil society groups are meeting in Yerevan, Armenia over the next two weeks for COP17, the latest UN biodiversity summit, to advance commitments to reverse nature loss by 2030. But progress towards those targets remains insufficient, with funding and implementation among the biggest challenges.

What happens when ecosystem services decline or disappear?

Take wetlands as an example. Some 85% of these vital ecosystems disappeared between 1700 and 2000. One study from Canada's University of Waterloo found that habitats like marshes and swamps in Southern Ontario provide C$4.2 billion (€2.63 billion) worth of water filtration services each year, removing nutrients like phosphorus and keeping drinking water sources clean.

The study found that as they disappear, water quality worsens, which massively increases the cost of treating it.

Another example is the decline in pollinators like bees and bats. More than 75% of global food crop types rely in part on animal pollination.

Why climate change is driving species loss To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

At the same time, soil and ecosystem degradation coupled with storms and heat waves linked to climate change are already damaging harvests. A recent UK government report stated that every critical ecosystem is on a "pathway to collapse," warning that nature's decline posed a grave threat to global food supply and geopolitical stability.

"The UK, like many other countries, relies on imports for much of the food and so is reliant on ecosystems around the world," said Louise McRae, a research fellow at the Zoological Society of London, who also contributed to WWF's Living Planet report. "This is why we need to care about global biodiversity."

It also provides the basis for many modern human medicines, with some 50% coming from natural compounds.

Poisonous frogs could be a source for new medications but as species disappear we could be missing out on novel drugs Image: Al Carrera/Zoonar/picture alliance

Penicillin, the first antibiotic, is produced by a mold and is estimated to have saved over 500 million lives. Before its discovery, a person could die from a simple cut. Around 70% of cancer drugs come from natural products or synthetic compounds "inspired by nature," according to the World Health Organisation (WHO).

As biodiversity disappears, humans risk losing access to undiscovered treatments.

Does it really matter if one species disappears?

To return to the "nature as a team" metaphor, if a player disappears, sometimes a species with similar functions in the ecosystem can jump in as a substitute. But not always, particularly if it's a "keystone species." They play a disproportionately large role in their environments, and their disappearance has significant knock-on effects.

The oyster is one such species. Wild oyster populations are facing massive declines, while 85% of their reefs have been lost worldwide. An adult oyster filters up to 50 gallons of water a day.

"No one would ever think, they did anything but sit in a shell and be slimy," said Shaw. "But you lose oysters, you can lose water filtration and clean water, you can lose the habitat for many other species that we interact with or sometimes consume."

People around the world rely on oysters and other marine life for their livelihoods and as a food source. Oysters are also a keystone species Image: Misper Apawu/AP Photo/picture alliance

And, said Shaw, the humble oyster protects coastal communities from storm surges. If you lose it "you lose the coastal protection."

The loss of a single species can also lead to more disease. One study suggests a decline in red foxes in North America is linked to the spread of Lyme disease, a tick-borne illness that also impacts humans.

Is humanity living through a sixth mass extinction and is it too late to prevent it?

The planet has experienced five mass extinctions when a large proportion of species globally disappeared over a short geological period. Extinction is a natural process. But the rate at which species are disappearing today, suggests Earth is experiencing a sixth event, driven largely by human activity, according to scientists.

Both McRae and Shaw called the declines extremely worrying, but said they shouldn't provoke despair.

Though she acknowledges that the underlying global trend is moving in the wrong direction and cannot be ignored, McRae says "the statistics are there to just motivate us to action rather than to cause alarm."

And the Living Planet report also highlights conservation successes, showing that nature can recover.

The number of green sea turtles, for example, had fallen significantly, but has now bounced back. This is thanks to a massive worldwide effort to protect nesting beaches and changes to fishing practices that reduce accidental capture.

Since sea otters on the North American Pacific Coast have rebounded, so too have kelp forests Image: Malcolm Schuyl/FLPA/imageBROKER/picture alliance

Sea otters are another example. Prized for their fur, in the 1800s they were hunted to near extinction on the US Pacific Coast. When they disappeared, it meant sea urchins had no predators, leaving them free to decimate kelp forests.

That matters because as well as providing habitat for other species, these giant underwater groves protect coastlines from storm surges and absorb carbon, making them important for climate protection.

Following a ban on commercial hunting, sea otters have also rebounded, helping kelp forests recover.

"You can see that ripple effect that really had an obvious and a measurable impact. But critically, it can be reversed," said McRae, adding that biodiversity loss and climate change are intertwined and exacerbate each other but have joint solutions.

"We're learning how to turn things around at very small scales," said Shaw. "Now the real challenge is to turn things around at very big scale so we can see it in the global indicators."

World.title: Austrian Airlines flight from Tel Aviv makes emergency landing after bomb threat
World.content:
An Austrian Airlines flight from Tel Aviv to Vienna made an emergency landing in Bulgaria after a bomb threat was reported near the Bulgarian-Romanian border. A MiG-29 fighter jet escorted the plane.

An Austrian Airlines flight from Tel Aviv to Vienna made an emergency landing in Sofia on Sunday after a bomb threat, Bulgarian authorities said.

The Airbus A320 landed safely with 51 passengers and six crew members aboard after reportedly receiving a bomb threat near the Bulgarian-Romanian border.

"During the flight, ​on the border with Romania, the crew reported a ​bomb threat signal and decided to land in Sofia extraordinarily," the Bulgarian Transport ​Ministry said ​in a ⁠statement.

Austrian Airlines gave the all-clear on Monday morning, confirming in a statement that "no danger was identified" after a search of the aircraft, passengers and crew.

It added that the flight continued to Vienna with all the affected passengers.

Fighter jet escorts plane

The Airbus A320 plane was flying from Tel Aviv for Vienna but was diverted to Sofia in Bulgaria at 9:25 p.m., air tracker Flightradar24 data showed.

Data from another flight-tracking platform, ADS-B Exchange, showed that the flight transmitted a squawk code 7700, a signal for a general emergency, around the time it was diverted.

A Bulgarian MiG-29 fighter jet was scrambled to escort the aircraft.

Following the evacuation of passengers after landing, a security search of the plane was launched, Austrian Airlines said in a statement quoted by Austrian news agency APA.

Last month, the co-pilot of Flydubai flight was suspected of attacking his pilot in the cockpit, and attempting to hijack the plane and crash it intentionally in Israel.

Meanwhile, last week, an accidental hijacking alert from a commercial flight from the Corfu in Greece to the German city of Nuremberg caused both Croatia and Germany both to scrambled fighter jets.

World.title: Trump defends Russia sanctions waivers, accuses Zelenskyy of 'prolonging war'
World.content:
The US president again accused his Ukrainian counterpart Volodymyr Zelenskyy of not wanting to end the war. The remarks come amid renewed tensions over US policy toward Moscow, including waiving some sanctions.

US President Donald Trump on Sunday defended his decision to waive some sanctions on Russia, accusing Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy of not wanting to end the war.

"My decision on Russia is a very simple one. I am in the process of negotiating Peace in the war between Russia and Ukraine, and don't want to do anything that will drive, foolishly, Russia away from the bargaining table," Trump wrote on Truth Social.

"Zelenskyy doesn't care, and frankly, with all of the money that Europe is famously giving him, and that Crooked Joe Biden gave him in the past, he doesn't want to end this war, and probably never did," he added.

Trump signed an executive order late Friday waiving broad new sanctions mandated by legislation named for the late US Senator Lindsey Graham, a staunch supporter of Ukraine's defense.

He has also temporarily waived sanctions on Russian diesel, allowing supplies to flow into global markets in a bid to lower fuel prices ahead of US midterm elections on November 3.

Trump links Russia sanctions waiver to fuel prices ahead of midterms

Opinion polls suggest that Republicans could face significant losses in the election, as voters voice growing frustration over fuel prices that have surged since the Iran war began in late February.

Most economists believe the suspension of congressionally approved sanctions on Russia and the diesel deal with the Kremlin will do little to lower US fuel prices.

Trump also repeated his claim that Ukraine was targeting Russian refineries to hurt Republicans ahead of the midterm election.

How Trump is helping Putin To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The move drew a sharp response from Kyiv and its allies, further straining relations between Trump and Zelenskyy.

Meanwhile, on Sunday, the Wall Street Journal reported that Russian President Vladimir Putin had proposed a meeting with Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping the following month to discuss ending the war in Ukraine.

According to the report, which cited people familiar with the discussions, Zelenskyy would not be included in the proposed talks, which would seek to end the war on terms favorable to Moscow.

Zelenskyy warns Ukraine cannot prevail if US backs Russia

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy warned Sunday that Ukraine would lose its defensive battle against Russia if the United States switched sides and supported Moscow.

"If the United States will take the side of Russia, of course we will not prevail," Zelenskyy told NBC's 'Meet the Press' calling a withdrawal of US support "a historic mistake and big tragedy."

He said Washington had resumed sharing intelligence after it was "blocked for some period of time," adding that Ukraine had missed critical intelligence on ballistic missile attacks for three days.

Zelenskyy also criticized US restrictions affecting Ukraine's war effort, saying, "we are strategic partners," but "we cannot applaud when someone turns against Ukraine."

Meanwhile, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio defended Trump's suspension of new sanctions on Russia, saying Trump wanted to assess their impact on the global and US economies.

Zelenskyy speaks to US envoys as Trump renews criticism

Volodymyr Zelenskyy spoke to US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner as Russia and Ukraine attacked each other's energy infrastructure, leaving thousands without power in Ukraine and setting an oil refinery ablaze near Saint Petersburg.

After the talks, Zelenskyy said "a lot depends" on the US position, adding that "this war must be brought to an end." Ukraine was ready to work "constructively" and "honestly," he said, calling for the same approach from its European and US partners.

Zelenskyy said he also discussed deliveries of US Patriot air defense systems as Kyiv struggles to counter Russian missiles.

A US-led push to end the war has yet to yield a breakthrough, with Trump expressing frustration at both Zelenskyy and Russian President Vladimir Putin.

Kyiv hit by Russian air strike after Ukraine targets Saint Petersburg

Zelenskyy accused Moscow of violating Trump's "energy ceasefire" 76 times and warned Russia planned to deprive Ukrainians of heat and electricity before winter. Russian strikes left "tens of thousands" without power, he said, while Ukrainian officials reported three deaths.

An overnight Russian air strike damaged a subway station on the left bank of Kyiv, killing a 21-year-old woman and injuring three others, Mayor Vitali Klitschko said on Telegram on Monday. A medical facility and a non-residential building were also damaged.

On Sunday, Ukraine launched drones at Putin's hometown of Saint Petersburg, setting an oil refinery ablaze and killing one person, Moscow said.

World.title: Canada: Fire at Alberta military Base kills four, leaves 19 in critical condition
World.content:
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney says a "serious incident" sparked a major fire at on Alberta military base. Four people have died, 39 are in hospital and at least 19 are in critical condition.

Alberta Premier Danielle Smith said on Sunday that 39 people were in the hospital after a fire at a Canadian military base killed four people. At least 19 were in critical condition.

The fire broke out at Canadian Forces Base Wainwright, one of Canada's busiest military training bases, at about 4 p.m. local time (2200 GMT) Saturday.

Maj. Gen. Wade Rutland, commander of the 1st Canadian Division, said the army responded to a "serious fire incident" during a training exercise conducted by the Third Battalion, Princess Patricia's Canadian Light Infantry.

A grass fire ignited in the training area during the exercise, Rutland said at a news conference Sunday, adding that the cause was under investigation.

"What I would say is there was multiple training activities happening throughout the training area at the time," he said, adding that "uncommonly strong winds caused the fire to spread rapidly and shift direction towards the range administrative area."

Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney on Saturday called the incident one of the worst tragedies the army has suffered in peace time.

"It is with deep sadness that I can confirm, at this time, that four service members have lost their lives and that their loved ones have been notified," Carney said in the capital Ottawa, adding that "dozens of others have been seriously injured."

"We will care for the injured through every step of their recovery," Carney said.

"And we will stand by the women and men of our armed forces as they bear the weight of this loss, they will not carry it alone because in Canada we take care of one another."

Medical facilities around base 'overwhelmed'

A doctor at a hospital in the city of Edmonton, which is located some 180 kilometers (120 miles) northwest of the base, told national broadcaster CBC that people were being brought to hospitals across the city.

Dr. Warren Thirsk, an emergency department physician at the Royal Alexandra Hospital, said health-care facilities around the base itself had been "completely overwhelmed" by the number of people requiring medical aid.

"This number of patients would overwhelm the city of Edmonton," he said. "It is more patients than any of us want to count right now. It’s a disaster. It’s a one in every 15 to 25-year disaster."

The injured were brought to Wainwright Health Center Image: John Ulan/The Canadian Press/AP Photo/picture alliance

What else do we know about the major fire in Alberta?

The Municipal District of Wainwright said the fire was spreading rapidly due to high winds.

"The fire south of Wainwright crossed the base fence earlier today and is being actively managed ... Emergency crews remain focused on protecting life safety, homes, and other structures," it said.

The incident occurred just days before people in Alberta, home to the world's fourth-largest proven oil reserves, will vote in the October 19 referendum on whether the province wants to begin the process of separating from the rest of Canada.

Edited by: Sean Sinico
