World.title: Croatian Football Fans’ Pro-Nazi Chants Prompt Arrests
World.content:
Torcida fan group march before match on Thursday. Photo: Torcida Split/Facebook

Police in Split have arrested several people after members of Torcida, a group of hardcore supporters of Hajduk Split football club, marched through the city chanting antisemitic slogans, including “Trample, trample the Jews,” “Auschwitz, Auschwitz,” and “Rise, Adolf”, referencing Adolf Hitler.

The incidents are being investigated for hate speech. Further arrests are expected on Friday. All those detained are members of Torcida and already known to the police. An investigating judge will decide whether to order pre-trial detention.

The chants occurred a few hours before Hajduk’s match against Dutch club Ajax – a club seen as having a longstanding Jewish connection.

The incident has been condemned by the Croatian government, the mayor of Split, political parties and members of the public.

“We strongly condemn the unacceptable chants glorifying the Nazi regime,” the government stated on its X profile. “Such shameful behaviour represents a negation of sport and the democratic values ​​that modern Croatia upholds,” the post added.

Torcida fans are known for expressing extremist views.

A series of incidents occurred before the Conference League match, when Hajduk chanted fans marched in a column led by a VW Golf Mk1 with a coffin on its roof, on which the word “Ajax” was written.

The Israeli embassy in Zagreb also condemned the incidents.

The embassy was “deeply shocked by the grave antisemitic incident that occurred yesterday in Split and condemns it in the strongest possible terms,” ​​a statement provided to the news agency Hina said.

“We are deeply grateful to the Government of the Republic of Croatia and to Sara Lustig, Special Advisor to the Prime Minister on Holocaust Issues, for their swift response and clear condemnation of this event,” it added, expressing confidence that “authorities will act quickly and decisively regarding this matter”.

“Such incidents should be unequivocally and decisively condemned by all competent authorities at every level,” it continued.

Croatian President Zoran Milanovic said verbal condemnation was not enough.

“Words of condemnation, such as those we hear from the government, are no longer sufficient; measures and sanctions are necessary to demonstrate that there is no place in Croatia for the glorification of Nazism and Ustasha ideology,” Milanovic said in a press release, referencing Croatia’s World War II fascist movement.

The game itself was halted for 12 minutes during the second half after Hajduk fans let off various pyrotechnic devices, including flares and powerful firecrackers.

Hajduk could face a heavy fine from UEFA. Following the match, Hajduk issued an official apology.

“When situations like today’s occur, we are obligated to apologise,” it stated. The club also apologised to the management and players of Ajax, who witnessed scenes “by which we do not wish to be remembered in Europe”. It did not mention the specific events before the match or the Nazi chants.

The match ended with a 2-1 victory for Hajduk.

World.title: Eesti 200 and Greens will not merge
World.content:
Eesti 200 decided at its council meeting Sunday not to merge with the non-parliamentary Estonian Greens ahead of the 2027 general elections.

While consultations had previously been held on a possible merger, Eesti 200 has now decided not to enter into merger negotiations with the Greens.

Party leader Kristina Kallas said the meeting heard the views of parliamentary group members and regional representatives and that the discussion was lengthy and heated.

"Ultimately, the party council decided that we would not enter into merger negotiations with the Greens and that Eesti 200 would continue as an independent party and begin preparing for the elections," she said.

The coalition party's head of communications, Johannes Merilai, said the Greens' policies differ from those of Eesti 200 and that a merger would add nothing to the party's core identity, which is based on progressive and liberal views.

Kristina Kallas. Source: Priit Mürk/ERR

"They have strong positions on certain issues, but if we were to bring the two parties together, it's not clear whether that would add anything," Merilai said.

He noted that Sunday's meeting did not address whether Eesti 200 would participate in next spring's Riigikogu elections. "There is still time to make that decision. There's no need to rush," Merilai said. He added that the party is currently preparing for the elections and aims to field a full slate of candidates. However, no final decision was made on Sunday.

Greens: Eesti 200 made a poor decision

The Greens met Sunday evening to discuss next steps. Party council chair Marti Soosaar said that while the party will likely still take part in the 2027 elections, the final decision is up to the party's new board and council.

According to Soosaar, the discussion focused primarily on why Eesti 200 had voted overwhelmingly against the merger. "They said the main reason was that they considered it the responsible thing to do — otherwise, a government crisis could arise, some important things might be left undone and that would be irresponsible," he explained.

"Whether everyone who used that as their justification genuinely believed it or whether some simply wanted to serve out the remainder of their term in government or as substitute members of the Riigikogu, is a matter for their own conscience," Soosaar continued. He said Eesti 200's overall reasoning was that a government crisis could arise and that the party wanted to avoid it.

Marti Soosaar. Source: Ken Mürk/ERR

Soosaar believes Eesti 200 made a poor decision. "In my view, what they decided as a party was whether to continue operating at all or cease their activities," he said.

He explained that taxpayers expect political parties to run in elections and seek a new mandate. Soosaar noted that, with the Greens' help, Eesti 200 could have built a stronger team with more people and a broader range of ideas.

Toomas Uibo, chairman of Eesti 200's Riigikogu parliamentary group, announced in a social media comment on Thursday that he does not intend to run in the next Riigikogu elections. Fellow party member Irja Lutsar announced similar plans in July, although just three and a half months ago, party leader Kristina Kallas said that, to her knowledge, all Eesti 200 MPs were prepared to run for reelection.

The latest weekly poll conducted by the Institute for Societal Studies (MTÜ Ühiskonnauuringute Instituut) and polling firm Norstat Eesti AS showed support for Eesti 200 at 1.2 percent.

The article was updated to add comments from Eesti 200 and Estonian Greens members.

World.title: Estonian municipality hosting refugee center mulls court action as migration pressure mounts
World.content:
Effective measures and border controls in Poland and Lithuania have led to a significant increase in migration flows toward Estonia. Police predict that migration pressure will only grow.

So far this year, 542 people from 48 countries have been detained both within Estonia and at its borders.

The largest group, 111 people, came from Somalia, followed by 45 from Sudan, 43 from Ethiopia, 43 from Eritrea and 33 from Bangladesh. Another 32 people have attempted to enter from Ukraine, while significant numbers have also come from Turkey and Moldova.

Migrants often begin their journeys in Russia and Belarus where they are directed toward the Latvian, Lithuanian or Polish borders and forced to cross. Those apprehended at land borders are sent back to Russia. Those detained at airports are placed in detention centers until return flights can be arranged.

As of Sunday, Estonia had returned 120 people to Latvia this year. Another three people have been returned to their countries of origin: two to Bangladesh and one to India.

Local governments feel abandoned

According to the Police and Border Guard Board (PPA), Estonia is experiencing its highest level of illegal migration pressure in recent years, testing the capacity of both local governments and the country as a whole. The Social Insurance Board acknowledges that the state was unprepared for the situation and is trying to provide assistance in dealing with underage migrants. Local governments say they have not received the support they need and Rae Municipality near Tallinn is planning to take legal action.

The closest historical parallel to the current migration pressure is the 2021 Belarus border crisis. Estonia was not the migrants' primary destination at that time either and the pressure on Estonian authorities and public services was less severe than it is today.

Indrek Aru, head of the border guard bureau at the PPA's Northern Prefecture, cannot recall Estonia ever experiencing a period like the current one.

"This requires an enormous amount of resources, both from the police and from all our partners involved in handling the situation," Aru said.

He added that several partner organizations have reported raising their readiness levels and allocating additional resources to their operations.

"From the police perspective, of course, we are only human, too, and this is difficult for us as well," Aru said.

Detentions centers full to bursting

Migrants are not immediately deported after being detained. Authorities must first establish their identities and countries of origin and determine whether they qualify for international protection. Some are placed in detention centers while these procedures are carried out.

"The facility is pretty full. There are a lot of people there," Aru said. He explained that the regular detention cells are operating beyond their standard capacity, prompting authorities to open additional temporary spaces. "We've ordered extra beds for those areas," Aru said.

He noted that detainees are being provided with basic living conditions, including food, washing facilities and a safe environment. "Of course, we're also working to establish alternative detention facilities," Aru said.

Interior Minister Igor Taro (Eesti 200) said Estonia has not yet exhausted its capacity to handle migrants, meaning the situation can only be described as a crisis once existing resources are no longer sufficient.

A detention center in Rae Municipality, just outside of Tallinn. Source: ERR

"We don't have additional centers, but we do have police detention facilities," Taro said. He explained that detention facilities for illegal immigrants are available across Estonia, with several hundred spaces still vacant.

"Of course, we don't see filling those hundreds of spaces as a positive development or something we would want," Taro added.

He acknowledged that Rae Municipality has come under pressure because the country's main detention center is located within its boundaries.

Migrants claiming they're minors

Under the law, the local government in whose jurisdiction a detention center is located assumes the responsibilities of a parent, so to speak. Because migrants want greater rights and additional protection, they falsely claim to be minors.

Rae Deputy Mayor Alina Ader said that if an illegal immigrant is classified as a child, they cannot be immediately sent back.

"We still have to treat them differently, explain their rights to them and provide them with greater care, which is entirely understandable. If they really were unaccompanied children, they would be in a very difficult situation," she explained.

As a result, the municipality's child protection service has come under particularly heavy pressure.

Ader explained that the recommended ratio is 1,000 children living in a municipality per child protection worker. In Rae Municipality, that figure had already reached 1,300 before the arrival of unaccompanied minors.

A PPA swoop on suspected illegal migrants in the Nõmme district of Tallinn in July. Source: ERR

"The workload was already too high before," Ader acknowledged.

She said the additional workload is now equivalent to that of two full-time employees.

"We currently have six child protection specialists. One is off work for health reasons, another hasn't been able to take any vacation since the summer and although nobody has said it outright, we're genuinely worried that someone might decide to leave," Ader explained.

Meanwhile, the state is advising the municipality to hire more staff. Ader noted that a job vacancy has been advertised for an entire month, but not a single qualified specialist has applied.

Tallinn deputy mayor: The state must take greater responsibility

Tallinn Deputy Mayor Riina Solman said the capital stepped in to help the state using its own resources after police requested assistance. She said it is unfair to place so much responsibility on local governments and that the state must shoulder a greater share of the burden.

"One state official said that the food bill alone rose from €30,000 to €100,000 in a single month," Solman said. She added that accommodation costs, medication, hygiene supplies and officials' working hours come on top of food expenses, none of which had been budgeted for.

"In fact, the Social Insurance Board and the Ministry of Social Affairs should be the ones resolving this problem and dealing with the unexpected pressure," Solman said. She added that their role cannot be limited to issuing instructions to local governments and telling them how to respond.

The Social Insurance Board acknowledges that real problems have emerged in implementing legislation that took effect this summer and that local governments' criticism is justified. The agency is prepared to take over all cases involving the representation of minors.

Kaja Rattas, head of the Social Insurance Board's substitute care unit, said the agency had not been prepared for the increase in migration or the volume of administrative procedures involved.

"The Social Insurance Board will, in any case, represent all minors in cases where the Police and Border Guard Board is conducting proceedings," she said.

Rae Municipality has submitted a request for assistance to the Social Insurance Board and Rattas confirmed that the agency is prepared to take over all cases.

"The same applies to the City of Tallinn. We do not expect the city to represent, for example, minors held at the detention center in Rae Municipality during proceedings conducted by the Police and Border Guard Board," Rattas said.

Nevertheless, Rae Municipality is considering taking legal action. Ader said the state had imposed an obligation on the municipality without consulting it beforehand or providing additional resources to fulfill it.

World.title: Expert: Trump parroting Putin's narratives and harming Ukraine's interests
World.content:
Donald Trump has taken steps in recent days that are clearly harmful to Ukraine and are helping Russia conduct information operations, at the very least. There are also fears that these moves could help Russia emerge from isolation to some extent. Do you have an explanation for why Trump is doing this?

We have to look directly at U.S. domestic politics and the upcoming midterm elections. Of course, we can debate whether these moves have been the right ones or whether they will have any impact on the midterms at all. All the experts have said that the impact of Trump's diesel deal on global oil prices, for example, is practically nonexistent.

Second, American voters are generally not supporters of Putin and roughly two-thirds of them still back Ukraine. So it is highly questionable whether Trump's moves will actually have any effect on the midterm elections. But perhaps what they demonstrate more than anything is that Trump is far more willing to support Putin than Ukraine.

President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, for his part, raised the stakes by saying in a remarkable interview with Piers Morgan that he feels betrayed by Trump. We all understand that sometimes you desperately want to say certain things, but did Zelenskyy go too far this time?

In my assessment, he did not. What would the alternative have been? To remain silent?

Trump takes offense, holds grudges and retaliates.

Yes, but I think allies can have disagreements and differences of opinion. What Zelenskyy is doing now is drawing attention to the reality of the situation. As president of his country, Zelenskyy's primary responsibility is to protect his country and its people.

You cannot keep playing this game of flattery indefinitely when it has not actually produced results. After senior U.S. administration officials ganged up on Zelenskyy at the White House, he tried to continue with that approach.

And for a while, it seemed that everything was going smoothly.

Exactly, for almost a year. But ultimately, we still see Trump making decisions based on other considerations — what those considerations are, we do not know. It seems that decisions that are extremely damaging to Ukraine and Europe always come after Trump has had a constructive phone call with Putin.

When it comes to diesel prices, Donald Trump should look in the mirror and think about the Strait of Hormuz and the war with Iran. Was it really necessary to go about it in this way?

Absolutely. What Trump is apparently trying to do is shift the blame onto someone else — rather than acknowledge that his intervention in Iran was the cause, he wants to place the blame squarely on Ukraine. In doing so, he hopes to divert the attention of his domestic audience away from the war with Iran.

Marek Kohv and Andres Kuusk. Source: Siim Lõvi / ERR

And there is another very important point here: I cannot think of a single instance in history when making concessions to Russia has motivated it to change its policies and come to the negotiating table.

Absolutely. Just take this example: When Trump unilaterally announced a ceasefire, supposedly with the agreement of both sides, Russia's response was to launch another strike against Ukraine's energy sector just minutes later.

Ukraine once again tried to act as a responsible partner and refrained from attacking Russian oil refineries for three days. Russia, meanwhile, continued its brutal attacks throughout that period, so Ukraine eventually abandoned its restraint as well.

What is your assessment of the restrictions on satellite communications, considering that, according to Reuters, the order came directly from the White House?

It has long been known that Musk owns the company and that he has the ability to implement such measures. But considering the geopolitical implications, an order like this really could only have come from the White House.

The fact that both Trump and Musk are now refusing to acknowledge which of them gave the order or where the initiative originated suggests that they probably understand just how politically toxic such a decision would be domestically as well. Americans would be quite angry if they realized that the United States had acted in a way that resulted in an extraordinarily large number of Ukrainian deaths.

Trump also lost his political nerve on another issue, declaring that Ukraine needs a new president. What business is it of Trump's to say who should be president of Ukraine?

Trump has no say in the matter, but Putin has had a great deal to say about it and Trump is repeating Putin's narratives here. As I said earlier, all of Trump's anti-Ukrainian initiatives seem to emerge after phone calls with Putin. During those calls, Putin can calmly go through all his fundamental positions without anyone interrupting him and Trump seems to absorb them almost word for word.

Ukraine carried out one of its largest attacks of the war, if not the largest, against St. Petersburg. Oil infrastructure is burning there and data centers have been hit. In other words, Ukraine has now responded in kind.

Absolutely. One important point here is that regardless of what happens with other forms of U.S. intelligence support, the Ukrainians are now capable of carrying out these deep strikes entirely on their own. That does not affect the overall process in any way.

Another important point is that Russia's urgency in pushing Trump to hold back on sanctions and apply other forms of pressure stems precisely from the attacks on oil refineries and major data centers.

The Ukrainian president also attended yesterday's European Council summit. He came away with a suitcase full of kind words, but when it came to practical measures, was his backpack empty?

Yes, and it is very sad to see because it is clear that Ukraine cannot expect much assistance from the United States at present. In the coming months, even NATO's PURL initiative could be called into question, along with whether Europe will be able to purchase anything through it.

European countries themselves could certainly do more and provide additional military assistance. If we consider the situation to be critical, building new defense industry factories is a longer-term undertaking. What could be done right now is to provide additional funding for Ukraine's own production capabilities.

Marek Kohv. Source: Siim Lõvi / ERR

Marek Kohv is the head of the Security & Resilience Program at the International Center for Defense and Security (ICDS).

World.title: Experts: Everyday household appliances can be targeted in cyberattacks
World.content:
Experts are warning that in the internet age, every connected device is a potential threat, following a cyberattack on a grocery store's refrigerators in France last week.

Hundreds of grocery stores in France were hit by a cyberattack on October 11 when hackers raised the temperature of refrigerators to as high as 50 degrees Celsius. As a result, large quantities of food were spoiled.

Technology expert Glen Pilvre said the damage was huge, running into millions of euros. He said the incident is a reminder that everything is connected, and if the locks on those connections are a little loose, someone can sneak in.

Security vulnerabilities

Pilvre said all kinds of devices are connected to the internet, such as washing machines, vacuum cleaners or refrigerators. Software may not be updated, and passwords could be easy to guess.

"There was one interesting case where the control system of an aquarium in a casino was similarly vulnerable to outside attacks. They gained access through it, and because it was on the internal network, they were able to get their hands on casino customers' data through the aquarium's control system," he told ERR.

The Information System Authority (RIA) is responsible for ensuring that these kinds of security vulnerabilities do not exist in Estonia. Compared with France, the situation here is relatively good, the agency believes. Vital service providers must follow strict requirements and are constantly monitored.

Companies informed

RIA incident response department head Taavi Kupper said few devices are connected to the internet. Those affected have already been contacted and issued instructions about how to hide or close off access points, or informed about countermeasures.

The agency would not disclose to ERR which companies are involved. However, major developments have recently taken place in the cyber sphere, also affecting criminal activity.

University of Tartu professor of space and defense technology Mart Noorma told ERR that AI also plays a role and, in the hands of malicious actors, it is possible to do more harm even faster.

"In the same way, artificial intelligence helps defenders protect themselves better," he added.

Kupper said AI has made the entire attack process very fast and short. "In the past, after discovering a vulnerability, we could hope for a 30-day update cycle before something might be compromised," he said. Now, a vulnerability is exploited within two and 24 hours.

Get rich quick

Nevertheless, experts say that today's hackers do not dream of attacking household appliances, but rather look for ways to get rich quickly. But could a small security vulnerability compromise an entire country's security?

The Estonian Defense Forces told ERR that military infrastructure is subject to much stricter oversight, and an attack would be a waste of time. However, malicious actors constantly test their systems.

Cyber Command chief René Innos explained that there are around 100,000 incidents per day, on average. "We do not see this as a particular threat," he added. There are around 20-30 serious incidents a year, Innos said.

World.title: Police will be able to confiscate illegal scooters under new law
World.content:
Police officers will gain additional powers to confiscate electric scooters without going to court under new legislation aiming to increase safety for both drivers and pedestrians.

Under the existing rules, the police can only remove a scooter from the road by going to court. However, so far, the court has not granted a single request to do so.

A new amendment to the Traffic Act currently under discussion will allow police to confiscate scooters breaking the law from the road independently.

Taavi Kirss, head of traffic supervision at the Police and Border Guard Board, told ERR that, currently, if officers see a vehicle breaking the rules, they can remove it from the street for safety, but not completely confiscate it from the owner.

The offending scooter can be kept at a police station until a procedural decision has been made to return the vehicle or go to court, he said.

The new rules are awaiting the second reading in the Riigikogu.

Margus Tähepõld, head of transport and traffic at the Ministry of Climate, said the police will be able to confiscate a scooter that can travel over 25 km/h or has an engine power of more than 1 kW.

Under the new rules, owners will lose the right to get their vehicles back.

"This should prevent the violation from continuing in the future, where you pay the fine, and soon the vehicle is back on the road," Tähepõld said.

If the new legislation is passed by MPs, it will come into effect in March 2027.

The same bill will make it mandatory for people aged 10–15 to have at least a bicycle license to ride an electric scooter on any road.

World.title: Janno Jakobson: Speaking Estonian not the same as teaching Estonian
World.content:
Students do not choose their parents, the language spoken at home or their socioeconomic background, but teachers can choose how they support students and what learning opportunities they provide, writes Janno Jakobson.

The transition to Estonian-language education is one of the most significant changes in Estonia's education system. No one questions its necessity anymore, but are we, as adults, prepared to make enough of an effort to ensure its success? We are demanding increasingly better Estonian-language skills from students learning Estonian as a second language, but are we also creating the conditions they need to achieve this?

In discussions with colleagues from different schools, one point keeps coming up: The problem is not always a lack of skills among teachers, but rather how existing knowledge and skills are applied in everyday teaching.

Imagine a student who spends an entire school day in Estonian-language classes. The teacher speaks Estonian, the textbooks are in Estonian and the student completes exercises in a workbook. By the end of the day, however, the student has spoken only a handful of sentences in Estonian. Does such a school day do enough to support the student's language development?

To acquire a language, students must have opportunities to speak, ask questions, describe, explain their reasoning and make mistakes. Teaching subjects in Estonian requires teachers to set language-learning objectives alongside subject-specific goals and create opportunities to achieve them. Many teachers already have the methodological knowledge needed to do this. Yet when explaining more complex concepts, it may seem easier to switch to Russian. Students understand the material more quickly and the lesson can move forward.

But what happens when a teacher explains an entire topic in the students' native language, while the quiz or test must be completed in Estonian? Can we expect students to achieve a passing grade if they have not been taught the relevant Estonian vocabulary or given opportunities to use it?

In such cases, students may understand the subject matter perfectly well but struggle to understand the questions or formulate their answers. A poor result may therefore indicate a mismatch between the language of instruction and the language of assessment.

Are we grading knowledge of language proficiency?

Recent fourth-grade national assessments highlighted a contradiction in our education system. While the assessment of Estonian as a second language takes students' expected language proficiency into account, the same students faced significantly more complex vocabulary, lengthy texts and multipart questions in the natural science assessment.

Commenting on the linguistic complexity of the assessments, the Education and Youth Board (Harno) explained that the tasks are aligned with the curriculum and use the same terminology. If students' Estonian-language skills are insufficient, the agency recommends choosing the Russian-language assessment.

However, the Harno representative fails to consider that the students who took the natural science assessment have been studying subjects, including natural science, in Estonian for three years and may not even be familiar with the relevant terminology in Russian. I must admit that such a response is frustrating for teachers. Is recommending a Russian-language assessment really the solution to the challenges of transitioning to Estonian-language education?

Of course, students must also acquire subject-specific terminology in Estonian, but fair assessment means giving them an opportunity to demonstrate their actual knowledge and skills. That is precisely why, rather than simply recommending a switch of languages, we should also seek ways to make assessments in Estonian linguistically accessible to students.

Students cannot be responsible for adults' choices

A range of support measures have been established to facilitate the transition to Estonian-language education. Content and Language Integrated Learning (CLIL) methodology centers operate at educational institutions, the Institute of the Estonian Language provides support through initiatives including the "Keelesamm" program and teachers in Tallinn can turn to the Tallinn Teachers' House and its methodology and competence center, MEKK. Teachers can attend training courses, receive guidance, explore teaching materials and learn from their colleagues' experiences. However, no trainer or methodology center can put what teachers have learned into practice in the classroom for them.

School leadership also has an important role to play. Schools must have a shared understanding of what Estonian-language education means and what principles should guide it. It is not enough for some teachers to consciously create an Estonian-language learning environment if others consistently switch to Russian during their lessons. Nor can the state's responsibility be limited to setting requirements. We need meaningful oversight that assesses whether Estonian-language education is actually working in practice.

Discussions about the transition to Estonian-language education often focus on students' lack of motivation, the language environment at home and parents' attitudes. These factors affect learning, but they cannot justify prejudging students' abilities.

Students do not choose their parents, the language spoken at home or their socioeconomic background. Teachers, however, can choose how they support students and what learning opportunities they provide. Students learning Estonian as a second language do not need lower expectations. They need high-quality teaching, consistent language support and teachers who believe in their abilities.

The transition to Estonian-language education is not simply about changing the language of instruction. Its goal must be to equip students with sufficient Estonian-language proficiency to continue their education, pursue their chosen field of study and compete on an equal footing with others in the future.

Achieving this requires effort from everyone involved. Students have a duty to learn, teachers have a responsibility to teach with clear intent, school leaders must establish shared principles and the state must ensure realistic expectations and meaningful oversight.

World.title: Gallery: Eesti 200 council meets to discuss party's future
World.content:
The council of the Eesti 200 party is meeting Sunday, with discussions focusing on the future of the party whose support is well below the electoral threshold ahead of the March 7 Riigikogu elections.

The agenda for the council meeting includes Eesti 200's future, preparations for the Riigikogu elections and a possible merger with the Estonian Greens, a party spokesperson said.

The meeting, held at the Õuetorn venue at the Telliskivi Creative Hub in Tallinn, began at 11 a.m. and is scheduled to end at 3 p.m.

Support for Eesti 200 has hovered around 2 percent in polls conducted by various polling firms for months. The party, which is currently in the governing coalition with the Reform Party, is divided over whether to take part in the March elections at all, run in alliance with the Greens or sit out this election cycle.

Fourteen MPs were elected to the Riigikogu on Eesti 200's list in the 2023 elections. Following the expulsion of Züleyxa Izmailova and the departure of Kalev Stoicescu, the party's parliamentary group now has 12 members.

According to the Business Register, the party had 548 members as of Sunday.

World.title: Expert: Trump's recent decisions have nothing to do with midterms
World.content:
Analyzing U.S. President Donald Trump's latest moves that have harmed Ukraine and favored Russia, U.S. politics expert Andreas Kaju admitted he could not explain why the president was making such decisions.

Fuel retailer Alexela's head of energy sales, Tarmo Kärsna, does not believe Russian diesel will help U.S. President Donald Trump achieve his goals of lowering fuel prices and saving American farmers.

"If Russian diesel were brought to the U.S. market, we would be talking about less than a day's consumption. It's a drop in the ocean. Markets are also skeptical today, questioning whether Russia even has the capacity to increase its diesel exports from their current level. After all, exports have fallen sevenfold since January of this year," Kärsna said.

The curtailment of Ukraine's satellite capabilities for striking Russia and defending itself, followed by the decision to abandon planned sanctions, are the latest surprises.

"It is clear that President Trump has taken Russia's side in the war and is clearly acting against Ukraine's interests. This is a very bad development," said European Parliament member Riho Terras (Isamaa).

Why? U.S. politics expert Andreas Kaju said he did not know. The midterm elections have nothing to do with it.

"If he wanted to win elections, he would have acted very differently long ago. What he has been doing consistently over the past year is endorsing extremely unpopular candidates within the Republican Party in various states. As a result, it is entirely possible that Republicans will lose states in the midterm elections that previously would have been unthinkable," Kaju said.

Kaju pointed to an article in the U.S. conservative publication National Review.

"The article argued that it is time for Republicans and Democrats to jointly launch a major congressional investigation into the reasons behind President Trump's Russia policy," Kaju said.

Kaju speculated that such investigations might indeed begin in Congress, including the Senate, after the midterm elections.

World.title: Asian stocks start week on back foot, tracking tech-led Wall St losses
World.content:
Hong Kong – Asian stocks mostly fell Monday as traders tracked a tech-heavy selloff on Wall Street that was fuelled by growing worries over the AI investment boom.

Chipmakers and other firms linked to artificial intelligence were once again under pressure owing to concerns about surging inflation, rising costs and questions about when the vast sums pumped into the sector in recent years would see a return.

Last week saw wild swings that ended on a largely positive note on Friday, though investors remain on edge heading into a crucial earnings season that sees tech titans Tesla and Meta report this week.

Markets have also been spooked by concerns about “neocloud” firm CoreWeave’s huge debt pile.

The company’s stock price has tanked around 30 percent this month as yields on some of its bonds soared, reflecting heightened angst over its future.

Reassuring comments from Nvidia chief Jensen Huang on CoreWeave’s financial health provided some support to Asia on Friday but that optimism faded as the new week started.

Investors are also looking to next week’s Federal Reserve interest rate decision, with bets on a second successive hike jumping after forecast-topping US inflation data. Higher rates hurt tech firms as many rely on borrowing to fund their huge investments.

All three main indexes on Wall Street ended sharply lower, with the Nasdaq more than two percent down, dragged by giants including Microsoft, Nvidia, AMD and Amazon.

“The US equity sell-off reflected a reassessment of the economics underpinning the AI investment boom rather than a simple downgrade to end-demand,” said National Australia Bank’s Rodrigo Catril.

“Investors are increasingly questioning whether future revenue can justify the capital and financing required for data centers, chips and power infrastructure.”

And the selling rolled over into Asia, where Tokyo was pulled down by tech investment titan SoftBank as well as Advantest and Tokyo Electron.

Seoul followed suit owing to more losses for chipmakers SK hynix and Samsung.

There were also losses in Taipei, Shanghai, Sydney, Singapore and Wellington. Hong Kong was closed for a holiday.

There was little immediate reaction to data showing China’s economy grew 4.5 percent in the third quarter, slightly better than forecast in an AFP survey.

Oil prices slipped but both main contracts held above $100 after soaring more than three percent Friday following a big drop in US commercial inventories.

The latest dip came on the back of signs that supplies continue to leave the Middle East despite Iran’s chokehold on the Strait of Hormuz and ongoing attacks by Yemen’s Houthis on key Saudi Arabian crude sites.

On currency markets the euro fell on concerns about the French economy as the country is hit by widespread protests, with President Emmanuel Macron slamming the “unbridled” violence that erupted in cost-of-living demonstrations.

World.title: Gaza teen amputees recount hopes, lost dreams in Jordan centre
World.content:
Amman – At 15 years old, Mahmoud Abou Nusair recalls the love he had for football, before Israeli fire in Gaza took his leg and his dreams away.

He is one of more than 450 Palestinian amputees receiving care and prosthetic limbs at a centre in Amman and in Gaza, part of an initiative run by Jordan’s Restoring Hope Society.

– Mahmoud, 15 –

On October 31, 2025, during the ongoing Gaza ceasefire agreed that month, Mahmoud Abou Nusair was looking for firewood in Deir al-Balah, in the central Gaza Strip, when a bullet struck his right leg.

With Gaza’s healthcare system decimated after three years of war, he had to undergo an amputation below the knee after his injury worsened.

“The doctor came to see me and told me, ‘We have to amputate your foot’,” he told AFP.

“My mother said, ‘No, doctor, that’s his soul. What will he do if he wants to go out, play football, skate or go to the beach? It’s a sin to cut off his foot’.”

“My first reaction was to scream,” he said. “Then I took a look at the injured people around me in the hospital. They all had amputated arms and legs, so I told myself: my injury is better.

“Then I said, ‘Amputate it, doctor’.”

After his injury, he recalls having to wait half an hour until a horse-drawn cart picked him up and took him to Al-Aqsa hospital.

He was taken to Nasser hospital in Khan Younis in southern Gaza, where he spent two weeks.

He still mourns the loss of his sports equipment and his five balls, all of which he lost when his home was destroyed.

– Zuhdi, 17 –

At the facility in Amman, Zuhdi Abou Shanab, 17, says he lost his entire right leg in a strike that killed nine people and injured 28 others on September 8, 2025.

“I was on my way to buy groceries for my mother and I ran into a friend so we stopped to talk,” he told AFP.

“When they struck the building we were standing next to, I lost consciousness and when I woke up, I found myself wounded and bleeding.

“A week later, the doctors told me that I was suffering from an infection in the artery in my leg and that three veins and three arteries in my leg had been severed,” he continued.

“I underwent an operation to reattach the arteries and veins, but it failed, so they decided to amputate my leg.”

“The war has devastated us and torn us away from our friends… there is nothing left,” he added.

But he still holds on to hope that his condition will improve, dreaming of “returning to Gaza”.

“I miss my mother, my brothers and my sisters.”

– Abdulrahman, 16 –

Abdulrahman Rihan lost the use of his legs when his family home in Jabalia, northern Gaza was bombed, the morning of January 12, 2025.

Both he and his father suffered severe wounds. They were taken to multiple hospitals in Gaza, where they “underwent difficult and painful surgeries”, Abdulrahman recounted.

Three of his brothers were also wounded. Their father, Imad Rihan, 42, said he had to “undergo some surgeries without anaesthetic in Gaza”.

“This war was very hard on us,” said the father, who lost his left leg.

“No matter how much we talk about the war, or how much you have seen of it, all of this remains but a drop in the ocean compared to the reality that we witnessed with our own eyes.”

World.title: Wembanyama targets title breakthrough as NBA season tips off
World.content:
Los Angeles – French phenomenon Victor Wembanyama, knocking on the door almost since his arrival in the NBA three years ago, is poised for the ultimate breakout season with the San Antonio Spurs.

“He just changes everything,” superstar LeBron James said of the towering 22-year-old, who will be aiming to further break the mold with his ferocious defense and an extraordinarily versatile playing style for a player who stands 7-foot-4 (2.24m).

Wembanyama was unanimously voted Defensive Player of the Year last season. With spectacular averages of 25 points, 11.5 rebounds and 3.1 blocks he finished third in Most Valuable Player voting.

With another year under his belt Wembanyama is widely tipped to contend for both awards — and lead the young, ultra-talented Spurs back to the Finals a year after they were agonizingly denied by the New York Knicks.

“We’re very hopeful, very ambitious and ready,” Wembanyama said as training camp began.

Rejoining Wembanyama for another title tilt are 21-year-old Stephon Castle and 20-year-old Dylan Harper.

In the offseason they added another piece to the puzzle in 34-year-old veteran Tobias Harris, who along with experience adds size and strength in the paint.

Harris was tabbed as the most underrated signing of the offseason in a survey of the league’s general managers.

But the Spurs fortunes will ultimately rest with Wemby.

“I think he has a ton of room to improve in all aspects,” says Spurs coach Mitch Johnson, who took the helm in May 2025 as the Spurs said goodbye to the iconic Gregg Popovich, who led the team to five titles.

“One thing for him will just be continue to manipulate the game and dictate the game, not just by scoring but by making plays for his teammates forcing the defense to make a decision, and taking advantage of opportunities in front of him,” said Johnson, who wants to see his star “almost puppeteering the game as we see the best players in our game do and we’ve seen him do.

“I think that’s an area for him to continue growing.”

Steve Nash, the former two-time Most Valuable Player, says Wembanyama has the tools to earn MVP honors.

“In my eyes, Wemby had a case for MVP last year because of the totality of how he affects the game,” Nash said as he discussed Wembanyama’s MVP prospects with James on the “Mind the Game” podcast.

– MVP? 1000% –

“I think the difference is that traditionally you look at who closed the game for your team and Wemby can close games, but he doesn’t, he’s not necessarily a closer,” Nash said. “Some nights, it’s not his thing.”

Nevertheless, Warriors veteran Draymond Green didn’t hesitate to tip Wembanyama for MVP — and Defensive Player of the Year again.

“With his impact defensively and offensively, the only thing that can stop him from MVP this year is injury … 1000% I think he takes home both of them this year,” Green said on his podcast.

Having enjoyed a spectacular ascent in his first three seasons, Wembanyama seems more than happy to embrace the expectations.

“We’re fighting for the top spot of the mountain,” he said. “We’re goig to have to move people in our way.”

World.title: Nations seek reset at UN talks as nature goals off track
World.content:
Yerevan – Nearly 200 nations are gathering in Armenia on Monday for critical negotiations as governments come under pressure to salvage a landmark nature pact whose goals are slipping out of reach.

Most countries joined a historic call four years ago to halt and reverse the destruction of nature by 2030 but governments have been slow to act on these pledges.

Many goals of the so-called “Paris Agreement for Nature” are falling behind, including a centrepiece commitment to protect 30 percent of Earth’s land and oceans.

Some of the toughest objectives of the pact, such as cutting subsidies for fossil fuels and other powerful industries, have made little progress.

“We must honestly admit that collectively, we are not yet on track as needed,” Armenia’s Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan said Friday ahead of the formal UN negotiations known as COP17.

The summit comes at a difficult time, with public finances under strain and political attention fixed on conflicts, geopolitical tensions and a global energy crisis.

Only a handful of world leaders, including UN chief Antonio Guterres but mostly heads of state from nearby Central Asian nations, turned up for a high-level session ahead of the formal negotiations.

But the stakes could not be higher, Guterres said at the event on Friday, describing an unrelenting “war on nature” that threatened the very livability of the planet for future generations.

“We need more action, more speed and more will,” he said.

“Halfway to 2030, Yerevan is our moment of accountability. It is time to ask ourselves — are we doing enough?”

– Falling short –

A United Nations scorecard issued ahead of COP17 reported that progress toward the 23 biodiversity targets was being made — but unevenly, and not at pace to meet the 2030 deadline.

A major tension at the summit will be money, with the report finding that the effort to close a yawning gap in necessary finance “falls far short” of what is needed.

European and other wealthy nations obligated to provide biodiversity finance have been pushing for large emerging economies like China to also contribute.

But attention is likely to focus more on how private capital, not public finances, might help plug the shortfall.

A key priority will be encouraging corporations to donate a share of profits to a near-empty UN fund to support conservation in developing countries.

Guterres also fixed the spotlight on state incentives for extractive industries, scolding governments for “spending money on the wrong things” despite pledging to reform harmful subsidies.

“Subsidising fossil fuels is subsidising suicide,” said Guterres of the coal, oil and gas that are “boiling our planet and are the scourge of biodiversity”.

For the mountainous Caucasus nation of Armenia, the summit is one of the largest international events it has ever hosted, with thousands of visitors expected over the next two weeks.

The hosts have stressed that action — not new pledges — would define success at COP17.

“The world does not need a new vision. We have one. What it needs is delivery,” Adil Najam, global president of WWF International, said Friday.

World.title: With LeBron on board it’s title or bust for Philly fans
World.content:
Philadelphia – Long-suffering Philadelphia 76ers fans haven’t celebrated an NBA title in 43 years, but with newly arrived LeBron James headlining a star-studded team they are daring to dream.

“We never had a team like this,” enthuses Kairee Harvey, a 32-year-old police officer and die-hard LeBron supporter.

“I still can’t believe it,” the resident of neighboring New Jersey said of the arrival of James in July. “I feel like I’m in a dream a little bit.”

Suddenly, Harvey said, “I think that this will be our year to win a championship.”

On paper, Philadelphia’s starting five looks like a daunting prospect, boasting two former MVPs and a former Finals MVP.

But the City of Brotherly Love has learned the hard way that talent doesn’t always translate into trophies.

Philly has seen NBA icons, from Charles Barkley to Joel Embiid, with Allen Iverson in between, but hasn’t won it all since 1983.

“I think there’s always gonna be some caution with Philly fans,” says Rob Nero, a local artist who has created several works depicting Sixers players, displayed on walls all across the city.

“We’re so used to getting our hopes up and having our hearts broken,” Nero said. “But that’s never gonna stop us from getting excited and believing in our teams.”

The Sixers’ final preseason game at the Xfinity Mobile Arena was sold out, fans sharing a few early moments of euphoria.

“They let me down at times as a team, but I’m there to cheer them on no matter what,” said Laurie Ney, who was accompanied by her two Yorkshire terriers — both, like her, wearing Sixers jerseys.

Historically Philadelphia is an Eagles town and in the streets the NFL team’s green dominates the blue of the Sixers.

Even last year, Matthew Merovitz would have put Major League Baseball’s Philadelphia Phillies in second place in the city’s popularity scale.

“But if you’re looking into this season where the other teams stand, I would say the Sixers are easily at the top of the city,” said the young professional clad in a Sixers jersey.

Philly sports fans could certainly do with a lift from the Sixers.

The Phillies were knocked out of the first round of the MLB playoffs. The Eagles are on a four-game skid with star quarterback Jalen Hurts out indefinitely and the Flyers are languishing in last place in the NHL Eastern Conference.

– Becoming a team –

The question is whether the show on the court will live up to the names on the marquee and whether the collection of stars come together to function as a unit.

“We’ve already seen some exciting things in the preseason, especially from Jaylen Brown and VJ Edgecombe,” Nero said.

With no clear hierarchy yet established, many fans expect Brown, acquired in a blockbuster trade from Boston, to take control.

“This is a lot of good players together,” says Brian Yoder, a septuagenarian who remembers the championship Sixers of Julius Erving and Moses Malone. “They’ve just got to become a team.”

The 1983 squad, which swept Magic Johnson’s Lakers 4-0 in the Finals, had also been shaken up the previous offseason with the arrival of reigning MVP Malone.

“They just gelled together,” Yoder recalled. “That’s what made it fantastic. They were a team.”

Clemon Johnson, one of the heroes of the 1983 triumph, thinks it can happen again.

“I’m looking forward to watching them raise the banner next year,” he told AFP.

Nothing less will do if King James is to reign in Philadelphia sports fans’ hearts. For most, the throne still belongs to electrifying point guard Iverson, who carried the Sixers to the Finals in 2001.

Elijah Davis, a salesman at vintage jersey story Mitchell & Ness, said the two-year deal inked by James defines the window for success.

“If we don’t get anything now or like in the next year … I wouldn’t say the organization is cooked, but it’s definitely going to need some changes for sure.”

World.title: Rubio seeks to strengthen US foothold in Central Asia
World.content:
Samarkand – US Secretary of State Marco Rubio launches into talks on Monday with key Central Asian states before heading to India on a tour to a region with vast natural resources and China as a key competitor.

Rubio arrived in Uzbekistan’s Silk Road city of Samarkand late Sunday to prepare for talks with top officials from Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan, Turkmenistan and the Uzbek hosts.

The leaders of the five former Soviet republics held talks with US President Donald Trump at the White House in November last year.

At the head of a delegation that includes 200 business executives, Rubio will visit the Samarkand’s old city, a historic staging post between China and the West, before starting talks aimed at the modern-day rivalry with China.

With the United States stuck in a war with Iran and unable to halt the Russian invasion of Ukraine, Rubio has stepped up his foreign travel with recent trips to Europe and Latin America while leaving Trump to handle the conflicts and the US mid-term elections.

But Rubio insisted this week’s tour is of strategic importance.

“This is an important relationship,” he said shortly before his departure. “There’s countries you’d like to get to because we want to build our relationships with them.”

A senior State Department official told reporters on Friday that Rubio was demonstrating US goodwill towards the “deepening partnership across Central Asia”, especially in the energy sector.

– India deal ‘very close’ –

After Uzbekistan, Rubio will go to India where the US ambassador is Sergio Gor, who was born in Uzbekistan and is also the US special envoy for Central Asia.

The central Asian states remain linked to Russia by energy pipelines and security and migratory networks, but Russian influence has eroded since the start of its invasion of Ukraine.

And China has reaped the benefits. It is now the main trade partner of all five nations.

Chinese companies have signed a number of energy-related deals, seeking to buy natural gas in Turkmenistan, uranium in Kazakhstan and rare earths in Tajikistan.

On his second visit to India this year, Rubio will have stops in Mumbai and Jamnagar in Gujarat state. Both are major port cities.

“We’re very close” to a trade deal with India, a second senior US official said of negotiations with the Asian giant that have dragged on for months.

The two sides reached a provisional agreement in February aimed at reducing US tariffs on Indian products.

But legal battles in US courts over Trump’s tariffs have fuelled uncertainty about when a bilateral trade deal could take effect.

India-US relations were also rattled when Trump imposed 25 percent tariffs on Indian goods in retaliation for Delhi’s purchases of Russian oil, but those duties have since been lifted.

World.title: LeBron joins 76ers to chase one more NBA title at age 41
World.content:
Philadelphia – LeBron James, yearning to capture a fifth career NBA title, tips off his record 24th campaign on Tuesday at age 41 with his new Philadelphia 76ers teammates chasing a long-sought crown.

The league’s 81st season launches with the Sixers at New York, watching the Knicks hoist their first championship banner since 1973.

James made it clear in July when he announced he was joining the 76ers that his move was all about making one more title run himself.

“I believe I can help make the Philadelphia 76ers a championship team and I am so excited to energize a new fan base and start this incredible journey one last time,” James posted on X on July 24.

“I’m not going for money. I’m not going for family. What am I really playing for at this point? I still want to sacrifice. I still want to work. I still want to grind. I still want to compete, to win and to have a chance at the feeling of winning another championship.”

James, the NBA’s all-time leading scorer, said in June he was leaving the Los Angeles Lakers. On July 24, James revealed he was going to Philadelphia and two days later, the team revealed James had signed a two-year deal worth $8 million.

James, a four-time NBA Most Valuable Player, won two NBA titles with Miami, another with hometown club Cleveland and a fourth with the Lakers and hopes to bring the 76ers their first NBA title since 1983.

He could become the first player to win NBA titles with four or more clubs.

It’s a goal that James, who turns 42 in December, shares with former Boston star Jaylen Brown, Joel Embiid, Tyrese Maxey and V.J. Edgecombe — all seeking a first NBA title.

“Everybody is kind of on the same page,” James said. “We want to put the work in. That’s most important.

“Everyone is highly motivated to get 1% better every single day… Everyone is excited to be here and that’s exciting to be a part of.

“If we’re trying to do something special, which I believe we are, it’s a positive. If you have this championship approach every day, it’ll definitely work in our favor.”

James has career averages of 26.8 points, 7.5 rebounds, 7.4 assists and 1.5 steals over 1,622 games.

James said his teammates are willing to make sacrfices to become a contender, not content with big individual statistics and early playoff exits.

“I don’t think anybody in the locker room wants their career to be like that or we wouldn’t be here,” James said.

James hopes to help 2024 US Olympic gold medal teammate Embiid grab his first NBA crown.

“Hopefully I can give him resources and whatever he needs on a day-to-day basis to make him feel even more comfortable about where he is, about where we are as a team,” James said.

James had 10 points, five assists and four rebounds in his pre-season debut for the 76ers in a 114-108 loss at Brooklyn.

“It felt a little different,” James said. “Obviously, just wearing a new uniform, but the game is the game.

“We’re still trying to put each other in a position to be successful and complement each other the best way we can out on the floor. But it’s going to take some time.”

– No ‘instant oatmeal’ –

James said people who want quick and easy camaraderie will be disappointed.

“They want instant oatmeal,” James said. “If you want to do something special, it takes time, every single day doing things you may not want to do, because it’s the same thing over and over and over and over.

“For us to be great we have to do things that are just not comfortable. We have to be comfortable being uncomfortable. That’s the best way to expedite being great.

“I didn’t leave my family to lose in the second round I know that for sure. Work needs to be done and I’m ready to put the work in.”

World.title: Knicks face tall task in NBA championship repeat bid
World.content:
Los Angeles – Jalen Brunson and the New York Knicks say they’re starting from scratch as they aim for an elusive NBA championship repeat with the San Antonio Spurs spearheading a host of rivals as the 2026 season tips off on Tuesday.

“We just have to find a way to turn the page and move on,” NBA Finals Most Valuable Player Brunson said as the Knicks began their preparations in September three months after ending the storied franchise’s 53-year title drought with an epic defeat of San Antonio.

The Knicks return their starting five, but a sour note has already been sounded in the pre-season as star center Karl-Anthony Towns said he was “extremely disappointed” by the Knicks’ public announcement that they were pausing contract extension talks with him and Josh Hart.

Additionally, no team has won back-to-back titles since the Golden State Warriors in 2018, and Victor Wembanyama’s Spurs are just one of the clubs tipped to keep it that way.

The Oklahoma City Thunder, led by two-time reigning MVP Shai Gilgeous-Alexander, are eager to reassert themselves after the Spurs ended their title repeat bid in the Western Conference finals.

Closer to home in the Eastern Conference the Knicks will contend with a retooled Philadelphia 76ers squad now featuring all-time leading scorer LeBron James and Jaylen Brown, who earned Finals MVP honors with the Boston Celtics in 2024.

Four-time champion James, still a force at 41, agreed to slash his salary in his quest for a fifth ring.

Along with Brown he’ll team with former MVP big man Joel Embiid, All-NBA point guard Tyrese Maxey and 21-year-old phenom VJ Edgecombe.

The 76ers will be out to make an early statement when they take on the Knicks at Madison Square Garden on Tuesday, part of a three-game opening day slate.

The Miami Heat have also added star power in the shape of two-time MVP Giannis Antetokounmpo. Antetokounmpo, who led Milwaukee to the crown in 2021, arrived from the Bucks in a blockbuster trade and could form a lethal partnership with Bam Adebayo — who poured in 83 points in one game last season.

But nowhere are the expectations higher than in San Antonio. The Knicks were still celebrating their Finals victory when Wembanyama started counting the days to the 2027 championship series.

San Antonio used the disappointment of their 2013 Finals loss to Miami to fuel their run to the 2014 title, and Wembanyama says the current Spurs squad is determined to bounce back in the same way.

– Spurs eye summit –

“We’re fighting for the top spot of the mountain,” says the towering French center, who reached his first NBA Finals in only his third season.

At just 22 Wembanyama is a bona fide star. He was the 2026 Defensive Player of the Year and finished third in MVP voting. An abundance of other talented players at coach Mitch Johnson’s disposal includes Dylan Harper, who emerged as a consistent threat at the rim in the playoffs after being limited by injuries in the regular season.

The annual pre-season survey of league general managers saw the Spurs tipped to take it all.

Gilgeous-Alexander and the Thunder expect to have something to say about that.

Oklahoma City took the Spurs to seven games in last season’s Western Conference finals despite the injury struggles of key offensive contributors Jalen Williams and Ajay Mitchell during the series.

With Williams and Mitchell healthy the Thunder are poised to maintain their offensive efficiency while All-Star big man Chet Holmgren and Isaiah Hartenstein return to anchor the league’s best defense.

The Minnesota Timberwolves, who reached the Western Conference finals in 2024 and 2025, are counting on the arrival of LaMelo Ball to team with Anthony Edwards to ramp up their challenge to the Spurs and Thunder.

In Los Angeles, Slovenian star Luka Doncic and Austin Reaves spearhead the new-look Lakers, aiming to forge a new identity after the departure of James in free agency.

World.title: ‘Protocol, not power’: Ex-IMF director rebuts Pakistan’s 'historic milestone' claim over 2027 leadership
World.content:
NEW DELHI: Former International Monetary Fund (IMF) executive director Krishnamurthy V Subramanian has challenged Pakistanâs claim that its appointment to chair the IMF and World Bank Boards of Governors in 2027 marks a return to global financial leadership, calling the role âprotocol, not powerâ.

In a post on X, Subramanian said the chairmanship was ceremonial and rotated annually, arguing that it should not be equated with leadership of a major global economic forum.

âClaim: âPakistan is heading back to the top table of global finance after 74 years!â Reality: Pakistan will chair the IMF-World Bank Annual Plenary in 2027. This chair is purely ceremonial & rotates annually: Paraguay this year, Cabo Verde in 2025.

It's protocol, not power,â he wrote.

Pakistan was recently named chair of the Boards of Governors of the IMF and the World Bank Group for 2027. The country will take up the position for the first time since 1953, with Pakistanâs Minister for Economic Affairs and World Bank governor, Ahad Khan Cheema, set to assume the role, according to an Islamabad statement.

Pakistanâs Ministry of Economic Affairs described the appointment as a âhistoric milestoneâ, saying it would give the country an opportunity to contribute to global economic and development discussions and facilitate dialogue among member nations.





What Krishnamurthy Subramanian said

In another post, Subramanian rejected comparisons between Indiaâs presidencies of the G20 and BRICS and Pakistanâs rotating chairmanship of the IMF-World Bank Annual Plenary, calling them a false equivalence.

World.title: 6 in 10 men over 45 unaware of their prostate cancer screening status: Survey
World.content:
NEW DELHI:

Nearly six in 10 Indian men aged 45 and above do not know whether they have ever been screened for prostate cancer, while only around one in six report having undergone screening, a survey by NGO Heal Foundation has found.

The survey of 1,036 men across Delhi-NCR, Tamil Nadu, Karnataka, Telangana and Maharashtra points to significant gaps in awareness of prostate cancer risk factors, screening and when to seek medical advice. Nearly 69% of respondents could not name a single risk factor, while only 13.2% recognised family history as one. Around three-fourths believed prostate cancer monitoring should begin only at age 50 or later.

The findings highlight a disconnect between routine healthcare and prostate-specific awareness. Although 62% of respondents said they underwent annual health check-ups, 60.8% did not know their prostate cancer screening status and only about 16% reported having ever been screened.

Awareness of the prostate-specific antigen (PSA) blood test was also limited. Only around 31% had heard of PSA as a marker, and just 14% had specifically requested the test.





âThese findings point to a fundamental awareness gap around prostate cancer,â said Dr Devavrat Arya, vice-chairman, medical oncology, Max Healthcare, Delhi. He said awareness of risk factors, screening and when to consult a doctor needed to become a more visible part of routine health conversations among men over 45.

The survey found that 59.5% of men were uncomfortable discussing screening or treatment with doctors, while only 18% would initiate the conversation themselves.

Although 67% trusted doctors and hospitals, just 36% identified a urologist as the appropriate specialist. Meanwhile, 84% searched online or on social media for health information.

The biggest barriers to screening were believing it was unnecessary (34%), having no symptoms (28%) and not receiving a doctor's recommendation (22%). Cost (19%), embarrassment or privacy concerns (17%), fear of diagnosis (14%) and not knowing where to go (11%) were other reasons.

Gaps widened with age: around 72% of men aged 65 and above were unsure of their screening status, while 80% reported low treatment knowledge. Overall, 71.2% had limited knowledge of treatment options, only 10% felt confident across the treatment pathway, and 44% wanted a second opinion before treatment.

Dr Nitesh Rohatgi, principal director of medical oncology at fortis memorial research institute, said symptoms in older men were often dismissed as ageing, delaying diagnosis, while awareness of advanced treatments such as radioligand therapy remained limited even after diagnosis.

The findings highlight the need for greater risk awareness and informed discussions with doctors. However, the survey reflects self-reported awareness and screening experiences, not prostate cancer prevalence or screening rates among all Indian men.

World.title: AIIMS removes uterus of 98-cm-tall woman through keyhole surgery
World.content:
NEW DELHI: A 44-year-old woman, just 98 cm tall and weighing 22 kg, has undergone laparoscopic hysterectomy at

, with doctors adapting the surgical approach to minimise fracture risks from severe osteoporosis and address anaesthesia challenges linked to her exceptionally small stature.

The woman, who has been living with osteoporosis, or fragile bones, since 2019, had suffered from extremely painful menstrual periods for nearly a year. The pain disrupted her daily life, forcing her to rely frequently on painkillers. Investigations revealed deep pelvic endometriosis and adenomyosis, a condition in which tissue similar to the uterine lining grows outside the uterus or within its muscular wall.

Prof Neena Malhotra, head of Obstetrics and gynaecology said that the patient recovered well and was discharged on the third day after surgery.

Given her age, bone fragility and high blood pressure, hormonal treatment was not considered feasible.

Doctors recommended removing the uterus to relieve her symptoms. Teams from gynaecology, endocrinology and anaesthesia jointly assessed the risks before proceeding with minimally invasive surgery.





âMinimally invasive surgery is now routine for most hysterectomies, but operating on an adult woman of this size, with severe bone weakness and hypertension, poses unusual challenges,â said Prof K Aparna Sharma from the department of obstetric and gynaecology.

A major concern was positioning the patient. The conventional lithotomy position, in which the legs are raised and supported, could have exposed her lower back and thigh bones to fractures.

âDue to short stature along with severely fragile bones, standard lithotomy position for hysterectomy could have put her at risk of lower back and thigh bone fractures. There was a need for utmost care in proper positioning and cushioning during surgery,â said Prof Rajesh Khadgawat of the endocrinology department.

Join conversation Commentsâ Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful Â· TOI community guidelines

At the request of the patient and her family, the team opted to perform the procedure with her lying flat on her back, taking precautions to minimise injury.

âThe uterus was enlarged due to adenomyosis, and the uterus and ovaries were stuck to the adjacent intestines, while the space in her abdomen was very limited. We were able to complete the hysterectomy successfully through the laparoscopic route in around 90 minutes,â said Prof Reeta Mahey, who performed the surgery.
