But we cannot simply say, ‘You know, there are difficulties, so we will not pursue this.’ We will approach our friends in the most friendly manner possible, but these issues must be resolved,” he stressed.

What Armenia’s prime minister and the head of Russian Railways discussed

The previous day, Pashinyan received a delegation led by Russian Railways CEO Oleg Belozerov.

According to the Armenian prime minister’s office, Pashinyan stressed that his government aims to integrate Armenia’s railway network with those of neighbouring countries. The meeting covered:

Opportunities arising from regional developments;

Measures to improve the competitiveness of Armenia’s railways and integrate them into international transport routes;

Railway reconstruction projects, particularly the Gyumri–Akhurik–Turkish border line and the Yeraskh–Nakhchivan line, as well as the opportunities these projects would create;

Infrastructure development carried out by South Caucasus Railway under the concession agreement;

Management efficiency, existing problems and possible solutions.

Comment

Political analyst Samvel Meliksetyan believes Russia proposed setting up an Armenian-Russian working group on the railway issue to delay the process and buy time.

In his view, Russia intends to maintain its presence in Armenia’s railway network. He explains that Moscow wants to take advantage of the expected reopening of regional transport links and secure a political role in the process.

“This matters to Russia economically, in terms of its image and in terms of its geopolitical presence in Armenia. Moscow does not want to lose a very important lever of influence as the region’s transport links reopen.”

Meliksetyan believes the Armenian authorities are trying to act constructively and avoid escalating tensions with Russia. In this context, he recalled the “instruments of blackmail” that Russia openly uses.

At the same time, the political analyst does not rule out the possibility of Russian investment in Armenia’s railways.

“The scale of this investment would not pose a significant problem for Russia. We are talking about just tens of millions of dollars. Even amid Russia’s current crisis, that is a very small sum. Its daily military spending runs into billions of dollars.”

According to Meliksetyan, three months of work by the Armenian working group are unlikely to persuade Russia to relinquish the concession.

“Formal decisions or partial amendments to the concession agreement in Armenia’s favour are possible. However, this is a political issue. In the near future, I do not see a political solution that would not lead to a further deterioration in Armenian-Russian relations.”

Russia seeks to keep Armenia railway concession

World.title: Fidan says ‘everything is fine’ in Baku, but relations remain strained
World.content:
Strained relations between Turkey and Azerbaijan

Turkey’s Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan arrived in Baku on the evening of 14 October. The official reason for his visit was the seventh summit of the Conference on Interaction and Confidence-Building Measures in Asia (CICA), where Fidan represented Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan. However, the visit came amid worsening relations between the two countries in recent weeks, putting every detail under close scrutiny.

Azerbaijan’s Youth and Sports Minister Farid Gayibov greeted Fidan at Heydar Aliyev International Airport. The decision to assign him to welcome the Turkish foreign minister prompted mixed reactions on social media in both Azerbaijan and Turkey. On 15 October, Fidan met Azerbaijani President Ilham Aliyev. Later that day, during the summit, he left the hall along with representatives of several other delegations when Israeli President Isaac Herzog began his speech.

After his meeting with Aliyev, Fidan said relations between the two countries remained strong and unbreakable. However, his remarks also acknowledged that disagreements existed between Baku and Ankara.

One of the main factors behind the deterioration in relations has been the de facto ban on wearing the hijab in Azerbaijani schools. JAMnews examined the issue in detail in an earlier article. This time, however, the focus is on a different question:

What is happening in relations between Baku and Ankara, and how serious is the growing chill between them?

Fidan’s message: “There are disagreements, but…”

Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan at a dinner hosted by Azerbaijani President Ilham Aliyev in Baku to mark the seventh CICA summit. Photo: president.az

Speaking to journalists in Baku, Fidan said relations between the two countries had stood the test of wars and crises, while their leaders shared an “unbreakable friendship and brotherhood”. He added that Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan had given him special instructions before the trip.

At the same time, the minister openly acknowledged that the two countries might hold different positions on certain issues. Fidan stressed that neither side should allow these disagreements to damage their strategic relationship:

“We are a people with an ancient history. We must resolve our problems as befits a people with such a past: by sitting down at the negotiating table and discussing them in a civilised manner.”

The minister also said the two sides should not turn their differences into a propaganda tool on social media. He said his conversation with Aliyev had followed this approach, with the Turkish side hearing the Azerbaijani president’s position and his assessment of the situation.

Fidan did not explicitly mention the hijab issue, Israel or Aliyev’s speech on 2 October. However, his references to “our problems”, “differences in approach” and the “use of disagreements” suggest that Ankara acknowledges the existence of tensions but prefers to address them through diplomatic channels rather than in public.

Meanwhile, photographs from the visit attracted the most attention on social media. Some users analysed Fidan’s body language, noting that he appeared relaxed both at the airport and during his meeting with the president, as though relations between the two countries faced no problems. Although such assessments are subjective, they show how closely the public watches every gesture by representatives of Baku and Ankara.

However, the most notable moment of the visit came during Israeli President Isaac Herzog’s speech. At the summit in Baku, Fidan refused to listen to Herzog and left the hall. Just a month earlier, the decision by an Azerbaijani representative to remain in the hall during Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s speech at the UN General Assembly had drawn sharp criticism in Turkey.

What triggered the tensions?

A series of events over the past three weeks has heightened tensions between Baku and Ankara:

23 September — Speaking at the UN General Assembly, Erdoğan described bans on headscarves in schools in “some countries” as an infringement of women’s rights. During the same session, Azerbaijan’s representative remained in the hall while Netanyahu delivered a speech in which he called Erdoğan a “tyrant”.

— Speaking at the UN General Assembly, Erdoğan described bans on headscarves in schools in “some countries” as an infringement of women’s rights. During the same session, Azerbaijan’s representative remained in the hall while Netanyahu delivered a speech in which he called Erdoğan a “tyrant”. 2 October — Speaking at a congress of the ruling New Azerbaijan Party (YAP), Aliyev said, without naming anyone in particular, that everyone should “know their place” and that nobody had the right to interfere in the Azerbaijani people’s way of life. He stressed that Azerbaijan had achieved its military victories without foreign patronage and had bought weapons with its own money (JAMnews).

— Speaking at a congress of the ruling New Azerbaijan Party (YAP), Aliyev said, without naming anyone in particular, that everyone should “know their place” and that nobody had the right to interfere in the Azerbaijani people’s way of life. He stressed that Azerbaijan had achieved its military victories without foreign patronage and had bought weapons with its own money (JAMnews). 9–12 October — Azerbaijani schools began inspections during which officials barred female pupils and teachers wearing hijabs from attending classes. The measures sparked protests and led to the detention of 37 people (JAMnews).

— Azerbaijani schools began inspections during which officials barred female pupils and teachers wearing hijabs from attending classes. The measures sparked protests and led to the detention of 37 people (JAMnews). 12 October — Erdoğan’s chief adviser Oktay Saral called on Azerbaijan to “correct this mistake” as soon as possible. Leyla Şahin Usta, deputy chair of the parliamentary group of the Justice and Development Party (AKP), made a similar statement.

— Erdoğan’s chief adviser Oktay Saral called on Azerbaijan to “correct this mistake” as soon as possible. Leyla Şahin Usta, deputy chair of the parliamentary group of the Justice and Development Party (AKP), made a similar statement. 13 October — YAP’s press service criticised Saral and AKP MPs, naming them individually. Its statement called on the AKP to abandon its “harmful policy” and also referred to “hegemonic ambitions” (Yeni Azerbaijan).

— YAP’s press service criticised Saral and AKP MPs, naming them individually. Its statement called on the AKP to abandon its “harmful policy” and also referred to “hegemonic ambitions” (Yeni Azerbaijan). 14–15 October — Fidan arrived in Baku and met Aliyev.

Against this backdrop, AKP spokesperson Ömer Çelik limited his response to saying that the two countries’ leaders shared a “genuinely brotherly relationship”.

Why relations are cooling: Israel, Russia and claims to the role of “big brother”

All the experts JAMnews interviewed before Fidan’s visit believe the hijab issue represents just one manifestation of deeper problems in relations between Azerbaijan and Turkey.

“The need to choose between two rivals”

Araz Aliyev | Photo: Third Republic Platform

Politician Araz Aliyev, one of the founders of the Third Republic Platform, told JAMnews that he linked the current tensions to Azerbaijan’s foreign policy.

In his view, Baku has begun to see itself as “a major geopolitical player”. However, unlike the US or China, Azerbaijan lacks the capacity to maintain close relations with two rival states at the same time:

“Over the next ten years, Turkey and Israel will be the two main rivals in the Middle East. At the same time, Azerbaijan is a strategic ally of both countries. When Netanyahu speaks, the Turkish delegation leaves the hall, while the Azerbaijani delegation cannot do the same, even if it wants to. Israel also invests in Azerbaijan and supports it. Naturally, this causes resentment in Turkey.”

Araz Aliyev notes that Azerbaijan first felt the negative consequences of its “multi-vector policy” after it backed Pakistan in its confrontation with India. According to the politician, India blocked Azerbaijan’s accession to the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation, while trade between the two countries — worth as much as $2 billion — suffered a setback.

Aliyev identifies Russia as a second factor. In his view, Baku has been pursuing closer relations with Moscow since August. He sees the resolution of disagreements over the crash of an AZAL aircraft as one sign of this rapprochement. Historically, he notes, closer ties between Azerbaijan and Russia have gone hand in hand with a degree of distancing from Turkey.

Araz Aliyev also links these changes to the domestic political situation in the US. In his view, Baku’s foreign policy strategy, which has largely relied on Donald Trump’s administration, could come under threat if Republicans lose the US midterm elections in November. The politician believes concerns about this scenario are pushing the Azerbaijani authorities to seek alternative foreign policy partners.

“I don’t depend on you”

Ömer Faruk Gergerlioğlu | Photo: Grand National Assembly of Turkey

Ömer Faruk Gergerlioğlu, a member of Turkey’s parliament representing Kocaeli province and the Peoples’ Equality and Democracy Party (DEM), told JAMnews that he sees Aliyev’s 2 October speech as a rejection of Turkey’s claim to the role of “big brother”.

“Turkey has always seen itself as the big brother of Central Asian countries and Azerbaijan. Aliyev, however, disagrees. His message is: I don’t depend on you; I need you only as much as you need me. We have mutual interests, but ours is not a relationship between an older and a younger brother.”

In the MP’s view, Baku sees cooperation with Israel as a “lifeline” that helps it preserve its authoritarian system of government, and it has no intention of making concessions on this issue.

Gergerlioğlu also points to what he sees as contradictions in Erdoğan’s position. The Turkish president sharply criticises Israel but turns a blind eye to oil shipments from the Turkish port of Ceyhan to Israel. The oil reaches the port through the Baku-Tbilisi-Ceyhan pipeline. The MP claims he has repeatedly presented the government with documentary evidence of these shipments.

“If tensions between Turkey and Israel escalate, I think Aliyev will openly side with Israel. For him, the principle of ‘one nation, two states’ takes a back seat. He views the world primarily through the lens of preserving his own power.”

Against this backdrop, Fidan’s decision to walk out rather than listen to Israeli President Isaac Herzog’s speech in Baku takes on particular significance. This time, Ankara demonstrated its differences with Azerbaijan over Israel directly in the Azerbaijani capital.

Growing discontent in Turkish society

Джавид Ага | Фото: личный архив

Journalist and analyst Javid Agha notes that discontent with Azerbaijan in Turkish society extends beyond the hijab issue.

According to him, Turkish businesspeople have complained for years about the difficulties of doing business in Azerbaijan, demands for unofficial payments by tax authorities and deliberate delays affecting lorries at the Georgian-Azerbaijani border.

“Turkish society has accumulated numerous grievances against Azerbaijan. However, people have only begun expressing them more openly and actively since the summer. Previously, Erdoğan’s inner circle kept this discontent in check through groups it funded, which fell silent at the president’s first signal. Now I see posts supporting protests in Azerbaijan on Instagram, TikTok and even platforms where I would never have imagined seeing such things before.”

The hijab factor: a sensitive issue for Turkey

The de facto ban on wearing the hijab in Azerbaijani schools has provoked a particularly strong reaction in Turkey. According to Gergerlioğlu, bans on headscarves remained one of the most hotly debated issues in Turkish society from the 1980s until the 2010s. Today, even voters who support the secular Republican People’s Party (CHP) consider the issue “a thing of the past”.

“Footage showing girls in headscarves being turned away from school brings back painful memories for Turkish society. Supporters of the ban argued that without it, Turkey would become a state governed by Sharia law. But the ban was lifted, and Turkey still did not become a Sharia state.”

The MP also clashed with Azerbaijani lawmakers over the issue. He said that during an online meeting of the Parliamentary Assembly of Turkic States (TURKPA), he criticised the ban. Azerbaijani MP Hikmet Mammadov then claimed that no such ban existed in the country and accused him of lying. However, according to Gergerlioğlu, a lawmaker from Turkey’s ruling Justice and Development Party (AKP), who attended the meeting, chose to remain silent.

Araz Aliyev believes Ankara’s reaction was inevitable. In his view, under Erdoğan, Turkey presents itself as a defender of “moderate Islam” and Muslims, while religious voters form one of the ruling party’s main support bases. “In this situation, Baku’s decision could not go unanswered,” he says.

Javid Agha, meanwhile, points out that Leyla Şahin Usta was among those whom Azerbaijan’s ruling New Azerbaijan Party (YAP) criticised in its statement. In the late 1990s, a headscarf ban prevented her from continuing her studies in Istanbul. Şahin Usta later lost her case against Turkey at the European Court of Human Rights and completed her education in Vienna.

“These bans did not stop her. Today, she is among those who govern Turkey. The authors of the statement should at least have familiarised themselves with her biography,” Agha says.

Sheikh-ul-Islam: “Consultations could have taken place, but they did not”

Allahshukur Pashazade, chairman of the Caucasus Muslims Board, has also commented on the situation. In an interview with Real TV, he acknowledged that the authorities had not consulted the religious organisation he heads before making the decision:

“I deeply regret that consultations could have taken place on this issue in advance, but they did not.”

At the same time, Pashazade supported the government’s position. He said the school uniform regulations do not mention the word “hijab” and that the country has no ban on wearing it. Children can study in hijabs at madrasas, he added, “but a different decision was taken regarding state schools”.

The Sheikh-ul-Islam stressed that “religion is separate from the state, and school is separate from religion”. He also accused certain “internal and external forces” of politicising the issue and trying to turn citizens against the state.

Araz Aliyev sees Pashazade’s statement as evidence that the authorities made the decision hastily:

“If the decision had been carefully considered and prepared over many years, the authorities should have consulted someone. It appears they made the decision in haste.”

For more on the legal aspects of the hijab ban, protests at schools and detentions, see JAMnews’ earlier report.

How will relations develop?

None of the experts interviewed expects Azerbaijan and Turkey to break off their alliance. However, they all believe the chill between the two countries will persist for some time.

Araz Aliyev believes the tensions will remain at the political level and gradually ease:

“Turkey needs Azerbaijan, while Azerbaijan needs Turkey even more in terms of national security, the economy and defence. Companies close to the leadership in both countries may face pressure from one another, but I do not believe their alliance will be threatened. After some time, we will hear declarations of brotherhood again.”

He notes that the two countries have weathered similar crises in the past. In particular, tensions in the late 2000s, when Turkey and Armenia were discussing protocols to normalise relations, led to Turkish flags being taken down in Baku. Aliyev believes the summit of the Organisation of Turkic States, which is expected to take place in Turkey at the end of the month, could indicate the direction in which relations between Baku and Ankara will develop.

Gergerlioğlu also does not expect Erdoğan to distance himself from Baku solely over the hijab issue. He says Ankara places much greater importance on revenue from the Baku-Tbilisi-Ceyhan pipeline, Turkey’s ambition to play a leading role in the “Turkic world” and the support of its nationalist-conservative electorate.

“Behind closed doors, they will probably say politely: ‘Wouldn’t it have been better not to introduce such a ban?’ However, if Aliyev begins openly supporting Israel, Turkey will also start signalling its discontent with the relationship more openly.”

The MP also points to declining electoral support for the ruling party. He claims that some voters dissatisfied with the AKP’s “two-faced” policy towards Israel backed the New Welfare Party in the last election. In his view, the hijab issue could deepen this discontent further.

Javid Agha reaches a similar conclusion. He believes that no matter how often Erdoğan repeats the slogan “one nation, two states”, he will have to take into account the views of the religious-conservative electorate that forms the foundation of his political support and adjust his position accordingly.

Fidan’s statements in Baku also offer insight into this diplomatic strategy. Ankara does not deny that problems exist, but seeks to move discussions about them out of the public arena and into closed-door diplomatic channels. So far, however, there are no signs that Baku intends to make concessions either on the hijab issue or on its relations with Israel.

Strained relations between Turkey and Azerbaijan

World.title: Uzbekistan allocates $12.9M to compensate families for energy costs
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 19. Uzbekistan allocated 156.6 billion soums (about $12.9 million) in compensation payments to more than 470,000 families in 2025 and the first nine months of 2026 to help households cover electricity and natural gas costs during energy tariff reforms, according to information presented at a meeting in Tashkent on October 15.

This was reflected in the statement by the Uzbekistan's National Agency for Energy Efficiency.

The event, held on October 15, focused on social protection measures and energy efficiency under the World Bank’s Innovative Carbon Resource Application for Energy Transition (iCRAFT) project, which supports energy sector reforms in Uzbekistan.

The session was organized in cooperation with the Center of Green Economy Projects under the Ministry of Economy and Finance, the National Agency for Social Protection, the National Agency for Energy Efficiency and the Yuksalish Movement. Government officials, nongovernmental organizations, businesses and media representatives attended.

Madina Azizova, chief specialist at the National Agency for Social Protection, outlined existing compensation mechanisms and proposals to expand assistance for vulnerable households.

Under the current arrangements, eligible families can receive monthly compensation of up to 37,500 soums (around $3,10) for electricity and between 135,000 (approx. $11,18 ) and 225,000 soums (about $18,63) for natural gas, depending on the season.

Participants also discussed proposed measures for the 2026–2027 autumn and winter season. These include a one-time payment of 1 million soums (around $82,79) to each of 1.017 million families, raising the income eligibility threshold for compensation from 1.5 times to twice the minimum consumer expenditure level, and extending social assistance to an additional 166,000 families.

Other proposals include extending electricity and natural gas compensation through April 1, 2028, covering costs associated with coal and liquefied gas purchases, and increasing the baseline electricity consumption allowance from 200 to 350 kilowatt-hours during the heating season in areas with limited or no access to natural gas.

Obid Ahmedov, head of department at the National Agency for Energy Efficiency, presented existing financial incentives for households and businesses adopting energy-efficient technologies.

Under current support programs, households can receive full reimbursement for residential energy audits, compensation for 20% of solar panel costs and up to 40% of heat pump costs. Businesses can also access financial incentives for renewable energy technologies and energy audits.

Shohijahon Xurramzoda, head of division on the iCRAFT project team, highlighted the importance of cooperation among government agencies, civil society and other stakeholders in implementing social support and energy efficiency measures.

Participants also raised practical challenges in accessing assistance and discussed ways to improve public awareness of available programs.

The session underscored the importance of balancing energy sector reforms with targeted social assistance while expanding household access to energy-efficient technologies.

Well-known singers and music groups will create a festive autumn atmosphere on Baku Boulevard with afternoon and evening performances.

The festival will give Baku residents and visitors an opportunity to explore olive products, enjoy live music outdoors and spend quality time with family and friends.

World.title: Kazakhstan, Lithuania discuss Middle Corridor development
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 19. Kazakhstan and Lithuania have discussed the development of the Trans-Caspian International Transport Route (Middle Corridor) and ways to improve international road transport, according to the Kazakh Ministry of Transport.

The issues were discussed at a meeting between representatives of Kazakhstan's Ministry of Transport and the Lithuanian business community.

The parties focused on the digitalization of transport permits, improving conditions for international road transport, and developing the Middle Corridor.

They also emphasized the need to introduce digital solutions, reduce administrative barriers in customs administration, and strengthen cooperation between Kazakhstan and Lithuania in the transport and logistics sector.

Following the meeting, the parties agreed to continue joint work on the issues discussed and reaffirmed their mutual interest in expanding cooperation in road transport.

The Middle Corridor is a multimodal transport route connecting Asia and Europe through Central Asia, the Caspian Sea, Azerbaijan, Georgia and Türkiye. It starts in China, crosses Central Asia and the Caspian Sea, and continues through Azerbaijan, Georgia and Türkiye to European markets.

According to the Kazakh Ministry of Transport, freight traffic along the Middle Corridor increased by 30% in January-September 2026 compared to the same period last year. Transit container traffic on the China-West route rose by 64%.

World.title: Tajikistan, China hold talks on economic cooperation
World.content:
Photo: Press Service of the President of Tajikistan

BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 19. President of Tajikistan Emomali Rahmon met with Chinese Premier of the State Council Li Qiang at the Palace of the Nation in Dushanbe on October 19 to discuss ways to expand economic cooperation between the two countries.

This was reported by the press service of the President of Tajikistan.

Li Qiang is visiting Tajikistan officially and attending the 25th meeting of the Council of Heads of Government of the Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) member states.

At the beginning of the meeting, Rahmon emphasized that Tajikistan consistently attaches great importance to strengthening and expanding cooperation with China.

Li Qiang, in turn, said China was ready to continue supporting Tajikistan’s development and prosperity and to assist in implementing priority joint projects.

The sides discussed ways to expand economic cooperation, including bilateral trade, which exceeded $2.5 billion in January–August 2026.

Particular attention was paid to implementing new mutually beneficial joint projects in industry, energy, transport, infrastructure and agriculture.

The discussions also covered the application of modern technologies, including artificial intelligence, as well as job creation and personnel training.

The sides also exchanged views on a broad range of issues related to the comprehensive strategic partnership between Tajikistan and China, as well as international and regional affairs.

World.title: Navy member stood down with pay after recording device found
World.content:
An Australian navy member who allegedly planted a recording device in a female-only cabin on a ship has been stood down with pay.

The device was discovered in a women's bathroom on HMAS Leeuwin while it was docked in Cairns on October 11.

An investigation was launched, and a person of interest was identified on October 15.

Recording device found in cabin of navy ship The recording device was discovered in female "shower facilities" on board the HMAS Leeuwin while it was stationed near Cairns.

Today, Chief of Navy Vice Admiral Matthew Buckley confirmed that person had been stood down. He said the decision for the member to continue to receive pay was "normal convention" during an investigation.

There were initially concerns that the footage taken from the device may have been shared online.

However, Vice Admiral Buckley said the investigation has not found any evidence of that happening.

"I can't go into any specific details about the investigation, but I've seen no evidence of any sharing of that information," he said.

"As I said, the investigation is ongoing, and it's important that we don't compromise that, such that we can take the appropriate actions needed."

Vice Admiral Matthew Buckley confirmed the person would be stood down with pay. (ABC News: Gavin Coote)

After the incident, the navy conducted an audit of all of its ships and found no other devices.

Defence Industry Minister Pat Conroy said the behaviour was "reprehensible".

"[It] undermined the dignity and privacy of Royal Australian Navy personnel. It was completely unacceptable, and it has no place in the modern Australian Defence Force," he said.

The investigation into the incident is being led by the Joint Military Police Unit and Defence and is receiving assistance from the Australian Federal Police.

World.title: Aussie seamer Darcie Brown cut down by back injury
World.content:
Darcie Brown's bid to feature in the inaugural T20 Women's Champions Trophy in India has suffered a huge blow after she was ruled out of the upcoming WBBL season with a back injury.

The Adelaide Strikers' pace ace was diagnosed with a disc injury following her participation in the Australia A tour of India last month.

It was initially hoped a period of de-loading would allow Brown to recover in time for the WBBL season, which runs from October 29 to December 5.

But Cricket Australia confirmed on Monday the injury had not healed sufficiently to allow Brown to resume training.

The news is a big blow to Brown, who was dropped ahead of this year's T20 World Cup and was looking to win back her spot in time for the T20 Champions Trophy in India from February 14-28.

The back injury also ruled the 23-year-old out of Australia's recent 3-0 ODI clean sweep of Bangladesh.

Brown has played six Tests, 30 ODIs and 41 T20s for Australia, and will be a huge loss for the Strikers this WBBL season.

"Darcie is a quality player who will be missed on the field, but she remains a hugely important part of our squad," Strikers coach Luke Williams said.

"She brings outstanding experience, professionalism and leadership, and those qualities will continue to have a positive influence on our group throughout WBBL 12."

Australia are 1-0 up in their three-match T20 series against New Zealand after posting a tense two-wicket win at North Sydney Oval on Sunday.

Games two and three will be held at North Sydney Oval on Tuesday and Thursday.

World.title: St Kilda AFL player Charlie Banfield accidentally runs over friend with car
World.content:
St Kilda AFL player Charlie Banfield accidentally ran over his close friend with a car on a private property in Western Australia earlier this month.

The ABC was contacted by two separate sources who said the accident occurred at a party at a rural property in Yallingup, in the state's south-west.

The ABC has been told that the victim was hospitalised with broken bones.

But despite the severity of the injuries, the ABC understands emergency services were not called to the scene.

Do you know more? Contact Jessica Halloran at Halloran.Jessica@abc.net.au

If you require more secure communication, please choose an option on the confidential tips page.

St Kilda confirmed the accident occurred and said in a statement: "The St Kilda Football Club is aware of an incident involving Charlie Banfield on a rural private property in Western Australia.

"Our thoughts are with Charlie and the injured individual, who we understand will make a swift and full recovery.

"The club has already spoken to Charlie about this incident and will continue to support him through the matter."

It is understood the pair are close friends and no legal action would be taken against Banfield, as it was being treated as an accident.

A WA Police spokesperson said it had not received any reports regarding the incident, while St John Ambulance said it did not have a record of attending the area that night.

Charlie Banfield with his mother Amber and his father Drew ahead of him making his AFL debut in May. (Instagram: @stkildafc)

The 19-year-old midfielder grew up in WA and made his AFL debut this year.

The ABC contacted Banfield's mother, Amber, who did not wish to comment.

Amber Banfield spent six years on the board of the West Australian Football Commission, while his father, Drew Banfield, was a two-time premiership player for the West Coast Eagles.

The teenager was picked up by the Saints after the Eagles decided not to match their bid in last year's national draft.

Banfield was recruited from the Claremont Colts in the WAFL, winning the Mel Whinnen Medal as best on ground in the 2025 WAFL Colts Grand Final.

He was also vice-captain at his prestigious Perth private school, Scotch College.

The AFL has been contacted for comment.

World.title: Report into department's handling of Kumanjayi Little Baby to be released
World.content:
An independent review into the Northern Territory's Department of Children and Families (DCF) in the wake of Kumanjayi Little Baby's alleged murder will be tabled in parliament tomorrow.

Children and Families Minister Robyn Cahill told the ABC the review by former NSW Police Commissioner Karen Webb and longtime NT public servant Greg Shanahan "clearly articulates the structural deficiencies" in the department.

"[Kumanjayi Little Baby] is not an isolated incident and there very much is a systemic issue in the way in which child protection legislation has been applied," she said.

"That comes down to the manner in which previous governments have been providing direction to the department about what their expectations are in this space."

Jefferson Lewis, 47, was charged with the five-year-old girl's murder in May following a five-day manhunt.

He is yet to enter a plea and will return to the Alice Springs Local Court in December.

Robyn Cahill says Kumanjayi Little Baby's case was not the only one of its kind. (ABC News: Marcus Kennedy)

Ms Cahill said the review's 40 recommendations would be "extensive", "practical" and "very clear".

"I think the changes will really be around making sure that the people who are working in this incredibly difficult space are provided with the frameworks and clarity around what the expectations are," she said.

"There are some significant issues around how things have been done and a lack of leadership has left the department struggling."

Child protection controversy

In late April, the body of the missing five-year-old girl, now referred to as Kumanjayi Little Baby for cultural reasons, was found on the outskirts of the Old Timers town camp in Alice Springs.

A week later, reports emerged in the media that the little girl had been subject to child protection notifications prior to her disappearance, with Ms Cahill announcing shortly after that three NT child protection workers had been stood down.

At least two of those workers were later reinstated.

At the time, Secretariat of National Aboriginal and Islander Child Care chief executive Catherine Liddle urged the minister to investigate "the leaking of information", which she said "only served to demonise a mother trying to keep herself and her children safe".

Catherine Liddle raised concerns earlier this year about the leaking of child protection information. (ABC News: Marcus Kennedy)

While the review received support, including from federal Labor MP Marion Scrymgour, concerns were raised by then-NT Children's Commissioner Shahleena Musk about the NT government's lack of communication with her and her offer to lead a board of inquiry into the child protection system.

Ms Musk said such an inquiry would allow her to examine "interconnected systems" impacting vulnerable families, including housing, family violence, criminal justice and policing, as well as any progress on recommendations from previous inquiries.

Shahleena Musk resigned in July as NT Children's Commissioner citing her "effective sidelining" by the NT government. (ABC News: Michael Donnelly)

Separately, the NT government introduced child protection reforms which prompted protests from legal services and domestic violence organisations who argued the bill would lead to more child removals.

Ultimately, the laws passed the parliament in mid-July.

The interim review

On the same day the child protection amendments passed, an interim review of Kumanjayi Little Baby's case was tabled in parliament.

Ms Webb and Mr Shanahan's interim report revealed all of the child protection notifications related to Kumanjayi Little Baby were "based on alleged domestic violence perpetrated primary by her father on her mother".

Kumanjayi Little Baby review finds departmental failings Nearly three months since the death of Kumanjayi Little Baby, an interim report into her family circumstances prior to the tragedy has been handed down.

But Ms Webb and Mr Shanahan said in the report they were "not able to draw a nexus between the matters referred to DCF and the circumstances leading to [Kumanjayi's] abduction".

The interim report also flagged "systemic issues", including the department's failure to respond in a "timely manner" to family violence.

Ms Webb and Mr Shanahan made seven interim recommendations, including the need for a "comprehensive reset of the DCF operating model".

World.title: Man who traded fake gold bars for e-bike ordered to repay $7.5k
World.content:
A man who traded fake gold bullion for a mountain bike in order to pay off debts to drug dealers will serve a two-year community correction order.

David Robert Meade appeared before Batemans Bay Local Court today, after he pleaded guilty in August to one count of dishonestly obtaining financial advantage by deception.

In November 2023, the 40-year-old contacted a man selling an electric mountain bike for $7,500 on Facebook Marketplace, and asked to trade the bike for three gold bullions.

Meade met the victim at their house the next day in Batemans Bay, bringing with him three gold bars in separate cases.

Court documents state each of the bars had a serial number and were branded with "Credit Suisse".

After the victim weighed each of the bars, which all came in as one ounce each, the trade was made and Meade left with an electric Norco Sight mountain bike.

The court heard Meade is currently on parole for a previous offence of a similar nature. (ABC News: Holly Tregenza)

In January 2024, the victim contacted Meade asking for the gold's authentication papers but he never received a response.

The victim kept the bars in a safe until November 2025, when he saw a social media post that identified Meade as someone who had previously sold fake gold bullion.

The victim then brought the gold to the police, where it was determined that the bars were fake.

'Not the same desperate man'

The court heard Meade is currently on parole for a previous offence of a similar nature and was released from custody.

His lawyer, Vanya Hampel, said that Meade was dealing with a methamphetamine and opioid addiction at the time of the offending and had "significant debts to drug dealers".

She went on to say that since being released from custody, he had completed his own rehab and was engaging in treatment, and he had found stable housing.

During sentencing, Judge Doug Dick acknowledged that he was part of Meade's previous sentencing but that the "man I'm looking at today is not the same desperate man I was looking at before".

The now-Queanbeyan local was given a two-year community corrections order and ordered to pay back the cost of the bike and a $1,500 fine.

World.title: Voluntary assisted dying uptake in WA far higher than predicted
World.content:
Almost 3 per cent of deaths in Western Australia are now due to patients using voluntary assisted dying (VAD), and authorities expect growth to continue.

The annual report into the operations of WA's VAD legislation has found the uptake has increased significantly since the law came into effect in July 2021.

"In the 25/26 year, we had 541 deaths, which is about a 12 per cent increase on the previous year, and about a 181 per cent increase since we started the whole process five years ago," Colin Holt, chair of the VAD board, told 102.5 ABC Perth.

Colin Holt says awareness is growing that VAD is an option if someone has a terminal diagnosis. (ABC News: Andrew O'Connor)

The numbers are far greater than were predicted when the law came into effect, and account for 2.9 per cent of all deaths in Western Australia annually.

Mr Holt says the increase is likely due to more people becoming aware of the option to use VAD if they have a terminal diagnosis.

This has put increasing pressure on the small number of doctors who are authorised to provide VAD services. The annual report notes that eight doctors did 53 per cent of all practitioner-administered deaths last year.

"We need more of those incredible people who participate as practitioners to come forward and be involved in the process," he said.

" The feedback we get from practitioners is that it's an incredibly rewarding field to be participating in. "

Mr Holt said the board is also looking at whether the current time restrictions, which mean patients can only apply if they have a condition that is expected to cause death within six months, or 12 months for neurodegenerative conditions, are too restrictive.

Debate over dementia continues

Stephen Walker, president of Dying with Dignity WA, said he was not surprised by the popularity of VAD since the law was introduced.

Stephen Walker says Dying with Dignity WA would like people with dementia to be able to access VAD. (ABC News: Emma Wynne)

His organisation now wants to see the legislation extended to allow people with dementia to access VAD, and said experiences in the Canadian province of Quebec showed it was possible to design laws that allowed for it.

"In Quebec, people can sign a particular form of advance health directive while they still have capacity," Mr Walker said.

"They have to do it in consultation with a doctor who also signs it.

"When the person reaches the stage or condition that they have carefully stipulated in their advance health directive, carers or family members can report that apparent state of the patient to doctors.

"Two doctors assess the patient, and they can, but importantly, they don't have to, terminate that person's life."

Mr Holt said the question of euthanasia for people who may lave lost capacity was an issue the board received ongoing feedback on from the community.

"I think there's a bit to learn from some of the Canada stuff and Quebec in particular, but I don't think we've completely solved the issue around retaining decision-making capacity throughout the whole process," he said.

"When you've got advanced dementia, when you're nearing death, you often lose capacity to make those decisions."

World.title: ‘A bad call’: Greens rift deepens over Steele-John allegations
World.content:
PoliticsFederalGreens ‘A bad call’: Greens rift deepens over Steele-John allegations Nick Newling, James Massola and Hamish Hastie October 19, 2026 — 6:21pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Greens leader David Shoebridge has insisted Jordon Steele-John agreed to take leave during an investigation into his conduct, contradicting the senator and deepening a rift within the Greens over allegations about his behaviour towards women. The dispute follows Steele-John’s decision to post a near 2400-word open letter on social media on Sunday night, which detailed his own version of events and accused factions within the WA Greens of weaponising rumours for political advantage. Senator Jordon Steele-John at Parliament House in Canberra in 2023. Alex Ellinghausen Last week, this masthead revealed that Shoebridge had ordered an independent investigation after seven Greens members wrote to him expressing concern over “multiple allegations” against Steele-John between 2017 and 2025. This masthead also reported the existence of a 47-page secret dossier that catalogued allegations against Steele-John and set out ways to shut down media coverage and monitor members who raised concerns on social media.



Shoebridge said last Thursday that Steele-John had chosen to take leave during the investigation. However, in his social media post on Sunday night, Steele-John said he was not on leave and strongly denied all allegations. The senator criticised Shoebridge for saying he had requested time off “because I knew it would be read as validating a story where there isn’t one”. “It was a bad call from David,” Steele-John wrote. In a statement released on Monday afternoon, a spokesperson for Shoebridge said the leader understood that leave was agreed. “Senator Shoebridge remains of the opinion that leave is appropriate under the circumstances and reiterates that this in no way prejudges any of the matters being referred to an inquiry commissioned by the WA Greens,” the spokesperson said.



“Senator Shoebridge firmly believes this matter must be resolved with a fair, timely and independent process as is being commissioned by the WA Greens, and he has worked to ensure this occurs. This process must include procedural fairness for all involved, with the key findings made public.” Related Article Exclusive

Political leadership How to kill a story: The secret dossier the Greens used to protect Steele-John Steele-John on Sunday said the letter to Shoebridge had not detailed any allegations against him – the authors only said they were aware that allegations existed – and claimed it was motivated by factionalism. “It is my opinion that this is an attempt to influence forthcoming party pre-selections by deliberately leaking out of context or misleading information to smear potential candidates and myself,” he wrote. Steele-John also responded to a reference the letter made to the party receiving a complaint of serious sexual misconduct in 2025 that involved the senator and a former partner.



In his statement, Steele-John said he had been interviewed by WA Police after a former partner accused him of removing a condom during sex on multiple occasions – an act known as stealthing. He denied the allegations and said he offered to be interviewed by police. “The report made to the police was of sexual assault – that I had, on multiple occasions, removed condoms without her knowledge while she was on top, facing me,” he wrote. “This is just not true. I volunteered to be interviewed and spent hours answering every question – including detailing which sex positions are possible for me as a Disabled man.” Steele-John has cerebral palsy and uses a wheelchair. He said WA Police closed the investigation and did not lay any charges, and that he was granted a family violence restraining order against his former partner earlier this year based on her excessive attempts to call and message him after he ended the relationship. WA Police declined to comment or confirm whether an investigation took place. Steele-John’s former partner was approached for comment.



The statement released by Steele-John on Sunday evening shocked and upset many members of the Greens in WA, who believed he was trying to pre-empt or shape the outcome of the independent inquiry before it had even begun. Related Article Exclusive

Workplace culture Greens senator takes leave after letter raises allegations of inappropriate comments to women “A fifteen-slide statement released in the middle of an investigation reads as an attempt to win the verdict in public before the process has a chance to deliver one,” said one member of the WA Greens on the condition of anonymity. “He cast the people who signed the letter as a faction chasing preselection. That framing sends a message to every future complainant about what awaits them if they speak up. The respectful choice was to let the investigation do its work in silence.” Some supporters of Steele-John in the disability community have rallied around the senator, who has long championed their needs and defended the NDIS in the face of cuts by the Labor government.



Amid growing divisions within the party, Steele-John’s length statement attracted more than 6000 “likes” and comments in less than 20 hours. Steele-John liked several comments underneath his Instagram post from users who thanked him for speaking out and apologised for the situation he was facing. In his statement, Steele-John said he had been thinking about how to “make sure people who’ve been harmed are believed, while also making sure everyone is treated fairly”. He said the investigation into matters relating to him provided a “safe way for anyone to raise concerns”. Cut through the noise of federal politics with news, views and expert analysis. World.title: Melbourne Assembly live: World-leading thinkers spark crucial conversations about the city’s future
World.content:
Professor Diane Kerr, known as Aunty Di, gives a Welcome to Country.

Acknowledging the traditional owners of the land, Kerr says the people of Melbourne need to have a safe city, saying we can understand each other, our children, and “live in harmony”.

“We need to look at what we need in the future, but it won’t work unless we have a safe city,” she says.

“How do we do that? I don’t know.

“All I do is ask people every day to talk to someone that you don’t know and share your story about who you are and where we come from. We have beautiful cultures in Melbourne.”

World.title: The pubs define my suburb. I had a night so wild in one of them I feared for my life
World.content:
Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Forty years. From a student shack in my 20s to working here for the last 20 years. Surry Hills, this wicked and wonderful ’hood has wowed and wooed me. A few kilometres from the CBD up the big incline from Central train station, it paints a broad-brush stroke. Low life, high life, underclass, upper class. Eccentrics and degenerates. A protester mocks police officers as protesters gather around the Surry Hills Police Station. Audrey Richardson Commuters head towards Central Station. Jeremy Piper For as long as I’ve been here, people have been saying the place has been gentrified. Licks of paints, fancy panes of glass, fine providores. The advertising agency my partners and I started occupies the smartly restored old Crown Street Women’s Hospital, once the largest maternity hospital in Australia. Sometimes a client leans in, smiles and says, “I was born here you know?” The floors have ears. The pubs here define this place more than most. People gather at The Clock hotel on Crown Street to watch the AFL grand final. Audrey Richardson The Shakespeare Hotel in 1999. Brendan Esposito



“The Shakey” (Shakespeare Hotel) was a journo haunt for years. “The Crix” (The Cricketer’s Arms) which is sports-day headquarters because of its proximity to the SCG. And a great French bistro upstairs. The Hollywood, an art deco gem where now departed and Hollywood showgirl Doris Goddard was one of the first in the 1960s to let women drink in front bars. “The Carro” (The Carrington) once flaunted a transvestite bar out back but now it’s got a flashy dog-friendly menu. You can also have a beer outside at The Forrester’s and play “spotto” – watching the punters walking through the subtle red-light door at Australia’s most famous brothel, A Touch More Class. We also have the special tiny arthouse cinema The Golden Age; the Belvoir St Theatre where Cate Blanchett once plied her trade; and the recently renovated Brett Whiteley Studio where the artist once lived and worked. Cate Blanchett in The Blind Giant Is Dancing in 1995 at the Belvoir St Theatre. Steven Siewert Indeed, Surry Hills has discarded her old frock – working class, a band in every pub, every night – and shaken off that heroin and street hooker look. She plays to a different beat for sure, but with plenty of bass notes of old. The most explosive gig of my life was in the early 80s when a young Nick Cave and his band The Birthday Party played the legendary Sydney Trade Union Club – “the People’s Palace” – in Foveaux Street. A night so wild I feared for my life. In those days, “the Tradies” stayed open until 5am proffering acts such as INXS and Violent Femmes. It’s now wannabe New York-style loft apartments spruiked by travel influencers. Coral Renee gears up for the Cowgirl Boots Writers Round event at Low 302. Audrey Richardson Yum Club Steven Siewert



I’ve watched the grumpy old kebab man get replaced by a pricey (and delicious) ice cream store. Joe the Grocer went too, subbed for a communal space with digital nomads ordering $9 iced matchas. Speaking of subs, the S&M bondage store is now a Korean instafamous destination cafe. And spot Taylor Swift dining at Pellegrino 2000 when she comes to town. But roots run deep in postcode 2010, despite the seeds of change. Ruth Park’s book Harp in the South, written in the 1940s tells of life as an Irish Catholic immigrant raising a family in Surry Hills – then an inner-city slum – complete with her drunken husband Hughie and the minutiae of hard lives. Outlines of that raw portrait remain to this day. The old hobos still thread the streets, the pub habitues still glower or bawl, a domestic or two spills into the streets from clusters of run-down terraces. Surry Hills street scene, 1944. Ernest Bowen Street scene, Surry Hills in 1944. Ernest Bowen Auction of 112 Arthur Street, Surry Hills, 2026. James Brickwood



Along Surry Hills’ main artery, Crown Street, the Salvation Army’s Oasis centre takes in kids who can no longer live at home or are displaced too young by life’s other misfortunes. Generous pockets of public housing thread the area and poke through the eye-pleasing distractions of the street. For the local housos, the street is their living room and playground. Like recently departed Chris. who sat near the Clock Hotel with his boom box and his trusty hat-wearing dog Sauvignon Blanc (Sav for short). He would cheerfully greet passers-by dispensing genuine happiness. I was sad when his spot went vacant. He brightened everyone’s day. (I hear Sav is ok). Then there’s Peter, “the Bird Man of Surry Hills”. He struts around with Caesar on his shoulder, a brazen bright-green parrot who dares you with his cocky pebble eyes. When Queen Camilla came to tour community food hub OzHarvest, one of her entourage asked him: “Would Caesar like to meet the Queen?” Peter said, “Why not?” Footage of the parrot and the Queen snared front-page news. Queen Camilla meets Peter the Bird Man and his parrot. Matthew Clark, owner of The Barberia, does a regular customer’s hair during a busy Saturday afternoon. Audrey Richardson Coffee enthusiasts wait for tables at Single O cafe. Jeremy Piper Cleveland Street, which separates Redfern from Surry Hills. Audrey Richardson

World.title: ‘We crash and burn together’: Meet the SNL UK hosts pushing the show to its limit
World.content:
Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

When SNL UK premiered in March, it did so with a monologue from host Tina Fey, former head writer of the flagship American comedy series. In a back and forth with Irish actor Nicola Coughlan, playing the classic SNL role of “celebrity audience plant”, Fey said she got the gig because “none of you f---ers would do it” – immediately signalling that this new version of the notoriously censored original would have a little more bite. Local talent probably avoided the gig, Coughlan remarked because “British people tend to root for the failure of others.” Halfway through the show’s second season, nothing could be further from the truth. Related Article Opinion

Comedy A US comedian’s jokes amid the Cornell rape scandal have set off a firestorm Katy Hall Age deputy state topic editor The spin-off, executive produced by SNL creator Lorne Michaels, has not just found its stride but is running laps around its American counterpart, which is having a run of dire, lethargic episodes and is in the headlines for the sexist monologue from most recent host, comedian Shane Gillis. While he was issuing an apology for accidentally swearing on last week’s episode, the UK version made the most of their “lawless” standards for cursing – and got a few of their own shots in. SNL UK’s sketches and impressions skewering local celebrities and news with a distinctly British flavour are only picking up steam. In a cold open that’s racked up more than 2 million views on YouTube, King Charles meets with socially inept American tech billionaires who have created an AI assistant for him. The Deeply Intelligent Autonomous Neurokinetic Android – or D.I.A.N.A. – wears a revenge dress, decides she “shan’t be taking orders any more” and goes full Terminator. It’s material that would work anywhere, but is right at home in the world of non-rhotic accents. “People kept asking us how are we going to do a British spin on [SNL]? But actually, we’ve been doing sketch [comedy] in this country forever,” Paddy Young tells me over Zoom. He and Ania Magliano are two stand-ups who, after rounds of auditions she describes as “a series of live gigs to audiences and then also screen tests to complete silence in these vast TV studios”, were paired up behind the desk as co-anchors of the Weekend Update segment.



They describe the format of the show as a skeleton, one that mimics the specific structure of its source material, with fleshy bits they build out fresh each week. Every Friday it feels impossible to pull off. But as Michaels famously said: “The show doesn’t go on because it’s ready; it goes on because it’s 11.30.” On Sunday, it’s done, and on Monday, you start building out the guts all over again. Live from London, it’s Saturday night: The cast of Saturday Night Live UK. HBO Max While every cast member pulls their weight and finds their niche, Weekend Update anchors are the ones who do it in their voice. Ever since the inaugurator uttered the words, “I’m Chevy Chase, and you’re not” in 1975, the anchors are also the only SNL cast members to announce themselves by name on live TV every week. The dynamic between a pair of hosts is its own specific alchemy. Fey and Jimmy Fallon gave off a teacher’s pet holding down the fort next to a practical joker. Seth Meyers was the straight man to Amy Poehler’s most base instincts. The current co-anchors, Colin Jost and Michael Che, have a fratty frenemies quality. “At the beginning, before the first season, we were talking more explicitly about our dynamic,” Magliano says. “Is this something we need to create and decide? But then when Seth Meyers was over visiting, he said to us, ‘You don’t need to plan any of this. Literally just focus on telling the jokes and the right stuff will come out’. It’s really useful to have some people … who can just be confident for you when we didn’t necessarily have the experience to be fully confident in it.” “The moment you try and shock or pull people’s heartstrings, that’s not the game. All we’re worried about is being funny.” Paddy Young Paddy Young and Ania Magliano, hosts of Weekend Update. HBO Max



As two gigging comics, Young and Magliano know what it feels like to be alone on stage as a joke thuds in the room, or to not have anyone to pat you on the back after a particularly stellar show. “It is nice that we’re up there together,” Magliano says. “When you do stand-up and you’re up there on your own, you’re sort of like, ‘Here we go. This is a judge of my character and my soul, whether I’m good enough on a fundamental level’. But when we’re doing it as a team, if it goes badly, we’re crashing and burning together.” The show’s overnight ratings on Sky One and streaming service NOW average about 140,000 viewers on Saturday nights, but it’s a show built for catch-up and online audiences. In April, Deadline reported the show had more than 86 million views of individual clips on Instagram Reels and YouTube. The cottage industry of streamers and tiny-microphone reaction accounts further boosted the status of the show recently, thanks to Weekend Update’s ruthless teardown of Ed Sheeran after he bowed to pressure from billionaire stadium owner Robert Kraft. While its American contemporaries covering the story barely went further than a gag about Macklemore’s music being bad, Magliano and Young left nothing in the tank. During the segment’s two-minute run, Magliano pointed out the hypocrisy of Sheeran being an advocate for “causes that are allowed” like the war in Ukraine. “Genuinely though, this crisis is the worst thing that’s happened to Ed Sheeran fans since their head injury,” she said biting back a smile, while Young joked that Jeffrey Epstein “had himself killed” to avoid being associated with “wealthy corpsemaxxer” Kraft. “I think the moment you try and shock or pull people’s heartstrings or whatever, that’s not the game,” he says. “All we’re worried about is being funny and being funny in as many ways as possible.” And if there are any hard lines holding them back from going too far? “We just let other people tell us what the limits are. We just try and make everything as funny as we can.”



By the time the clips started getting traction online, they were already at their desks trying to work new jokes about Prince Andrew’s bodily fluids into the next weekend’s packet of punchlines. Jeff Goldblum (right) hosts an episode of Saturday Night Live UK. HBO Max “When we did that Ed Sheeran thing, we were really proud of it, and we heard that people liked it, but we were back in the office on Tuesday worrying about the next thing,” Young says. Magliano adds that the job can be like a hamster in a wheel, with little time to pause and reflect on its impact. “There’s a thing in stand-up … you only feel as good as your last gig. And so I do think the threat of the looming week does mean you can’t spend too much time being self-congratulatory about what did work, or being self-negative about what didn’t.” Editor's pick Australian TV Why this ‘unhinged’ killer gnome comedy took 10 years to bring to life With James Norton and Cynthia Erivo announced for the next two episodes at the time we speak, I ask Magliano and Young for the names on their dream list of SNL UK hosts. Magliano’s picks? Hugh Grant, Diane Morgan and mentalist Derren Brown. “I’m really into magic at the moment. I think it’s fantastic … Imagine an SNL where there’s also a lot of magic in it.”

World.title: ‘Dismantling decades of trust’: Melbourne health provider to close clinic
World.content:
NationalVictoriaHealthcare ‘Dismantling decades of trust’: Melbourne health provider to close clinic Gemma Grant October 19, 2026 — 5:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

A prominent community health organisation will close the doors of its major clinic in St Kilda this week, forcing vulnerable clients to instead travel to Prahran or South Melbourne for help. Better Health Network (BHN) formed in 2022 following the voluntary amalgamation of three smaller community health organisations. Today, it provides primary and allied care to those experiencing homelessness, socioeconomic disadvantage or complex health needs. The Better Health Network clinic on Fitzroy Street in St Kilda will close at the end of October. Simon Schluter The St Kilda clinic at 22-28 Fitzroy Street offers alcohol and drug programs, counselling, and housing support services – as well as the Resourcing Health & Education program, which services the local street-based sex work community. The Age has spoken to five former and current Better Health Network staff who criticised the St Kilda closure – set to take place on October 23 – and raised concerns regarding wider management decisions throughout the organisation.



Former BHN case manager Alana Lewis, who left the provider in May, called the closure “deeply concerning,” and said moving the services would erode trust within the St Kilda community. “These relationships and connections don’t happen overnight. They take years to build, particularly with communities that still and have historically experienced stigma and discrimination when accessing services,” Lewis said. Former Better Health Network case manager Alana Lewis. Joe Armao “Closing Fitzroy Street isn’t simply relocating a service. It’s dismantling decades of trust, community connection and accessible support.” Details of the closure of the site were communicated to staff in an internal announcement last month, which was authorised by chief operating officer Wayne Merritt and seen by The Age.



Among the reasons given were issues securing a suitable lease and structural building changes required by the landlord, described as being “outside [the] control” of the organisation. The current lease expires on October 30. “To enable us to sustainably continue delivering services in suitable environments, we continue to review how we use our buildings and spaces,” the document explains, adding that clients will be redirected to nearby clinics in Prahran and South Melbourne. Another former BHN staff member, who wished to remain anonymous to protect their reputation within the industry, said the closure meant the provider was effectively dislocating itself from the community it is supposed to be serving. Although clients will be referred to other clinics, the former employee said the type of travel being put forward as a solution is unrealistic for many vulnerable or complex clients.



“That’s a middle-class view of mobility … a lot of people can’t travel in those sorts of ways. Even though people say it’s just a tram ride … it’s actually about being intimate within your own community,” they said. Related Article Exclusive

Healthcare A minister’s aide probed cohealth’s issues, then ended up working for them “If you’re in community health, you can’t take community out.” As well as the upcoming clinic closure, Lewis and other current and former BHN employees have expressed concern about transparency and accountability regarding staffing at the not-for-profit provider. Last December, two BHN clinics in Clarinda and in Bentleigh permanently closed. Chief executive Andrea McLeod told The Age at the time there were no planned redundancies as part of last year’s changes, and staff would be redistributed to nearby clinics.



“We’ve committed to continuing to provide essential health and wellbeing services to our communities, but we need to deliver them more effectively to operate within the funding we receive,” McLeod said at the time. But a current BHN employee, who wished to remain anonymous to protect their job, described a dynamic of “near-continuous” restructuring, including a high turnover of senior leadership and multiple redundancy rounds. An internal document from January seen by this masthead details a lengthy “realignment” of client services leadership within the organisation. It refers to 23 program leaders being made redundant, 17 new leadership positions being created and a range of title and role description changes. In response to questions from The Age, a spokesperson for BHN said the organisation was committed to providing client-facing services in St Kilda. They said they were in the final stages of negotiating a lease for a new clinic in the suburb, but declined to provide a specific timeframe as to when that could open.



In the interim, they said clients would be supported with the relocation to the Prahran and South Melbourne clinics, and to access services at partner organisations. “We are committed to supporting continuity of care and giving clients choice about where they access services, based on their needs and preferences,” they said. Better Health Network also leases an administrative office at the Victorian Pride Centre in St Kilda. John Gollings The not-for-profit will continue to lease its administrative office at the Victorian Pride Centre in St Kilda, as well as housing offices for senior leadership, but which is not permitted to provide client-facing services. Another former BHN staff member, who also wished to remain anonymous to protect their reputation within the industry, said maintaining the organisation’s “dream factory” within the suburb’s centre was an example of the “corporatisation of community health”.



“There’s a real divide between leadership and corporate and the [operations] people … they’re just shooting for dollar outcomes, not client outcomes,” they said. Related Article Exclusive

Healthcare How Shane’s botched eye surgery exposes Victoria’s record $254 million hospital payout crisis The BHN spokesperson said the Victorian Pride Centre site was “an important base for a range of frontline teams,” including those who coordinate support by phone. “With a significant forecasted operating deficit for the 2025/26 financial year, the organisation must focus on achieving cost efficiencies that can support our need for financial sustainability,” the document explains. The BHN employee said they had raised concerns to management regarding the impact of these major restructuring processes, but was met with a “tokenistic response”.



“Speaking up within BHN no longer feels possible. Those who have raised concerns have been minimised or driven out of the organisation,” the staff member said. “BHN claims its values are accountability, purpose, courage and respect … [but] BHN’s actions are fundamentally at odds with the very values it claims to uphold.” The BHN spokesperson said they recognise organisational change that impacts people’s employment is challenging. “BHN has undergone organisational change to support the organisation’s long-term sustainability and continued delivery of accessible health and wellbeing services to the community,” they said.

World.title: A visit to the zoo in a wheelchair and alcoholic drinks: Inside the HSC maths exams
World.content:
NationalNSWEducation A visit to the zoo in a wheelchair and alcoholic drinks: Inside the HSC maths exams Emily Kowal October 19, 2026 — 5:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

If you are visiting a steep zoo in a wheelchair, what is the best path to see the lions from the penguin exhibition? What time would you need to leave to make it for feeding time? It’s a question HSC standard maths student Darnish Noori struggled with: “I did not manage to finish it.” Renuka Parmesh, Nithya Potlakayala, Darnish Noori and Mayukh Mandala have just sat their HSC exams at Parramatta High School. Janie Barrett The Parramatta High student was one of 31,698 students who tackled the HSC standard maths 2 exam on Monday, wrestling with questions about zoos, the probability of students wearing the correct uniform, and how long it took for a 72-kilogram man to consume three drinks, based on a formula and the time it took for his blood alcohol level to return to zero. Parramatta High student Nithya Potlakayala described the zoo question as one of the easiest in the test, once you got past the scenario.



The three-part question was designed to test students’ understanding of networks: their ability to use graph theory to model, analyse and optimise real-world systems. Students were presented with two network images of a zoo – one showing the lengths of paths between exhibits and another presenting the gradient of each path. Advised that the zoo visitor – Nikolai – was in a wheelchair that could only traverse gradients below a certain threshold, students had to explain why the best path for Nikolai was not necessarily the shortest, what the best path was, and the latest time he could leave to watch the lion feeding. Maths students Darnish Noori, Renuka Parmesh, Nithya Potlakayala and Mayukh Mandala sat their HSC exams at Parramatta High School. Janie Barrett “I really hate these questions – they are easy, but my brain doesn’t process the information,” Potlakayala said. She skipped the question, heading to the harder ones and circling back to it later. She finds it is best to blur out the scenario; only the numbers matter and what they represent. The advanced maths exam has previously come under fire from teachers for being too wordy and overloading students with unnecessary information.



Both Potlakayala and Noori used artificial intelligence to prepare for their exams, feeding chatbots past papers to generate new practice questions. “I used it to generate more challenging and more specific questions. It was able to actively accommodate whatever I am struggling with,” Noori said. Renuka Parmesh and Mayukh Mandala were part of the more than 16,000 year 12 students who completed the advanced maths exam, describing it as “a little less complicated” than last year’s. A question about loan repayments had both Parmesh and Mandala scratching their heads.



Related Article HSC ‘I haven’t seen that before’: Surprise wording in the HSC modern history exam “It was significantly harder than anything I’ve really encountered,” Parmesh said. “In this particular question, there were were a couple of extra steps you had to do before determining the sequence you had, and it was not very clear where to really start off. That’s what really threw me off, and that’s what I feel like threw a lot of people off as well.” Mandala said he was scrambling at the end. “The fact that we had to balance so much in such less time, and especially towards the end ... that was very pressurising.” Maths teacher Deepti Asija said it was a good exam: “It was achievable but not impossible – it was designed to reward hard work.” HSC exams continue until November 5.
