World.content:
Australia’s Test bowling attack ranks among the best in the world over the last 50 years, having broken new ground as a quartet and taking an unprecedented number of wickets as a four-man unit.

Statistically, Pat Cummins, Mitchell Starc, Josh Hazlewood and Nathan Lyon sit comfortably in the same pantheon as some of the best West Indian attacks from the late ’70s.

Loading

Michael Holding, Andy Roberts, Joel Garner, Malcolm Marshall and Colin Croft combined hostility with control. People have described facing them as like facing an execution squad, offering no respite from either end.

In Durban against South Africa last week, Australia out-bowled, out-batted and out-fielded their opponents and deserved their decisive victory. Central to the win was the attack.

World.title: ‘A bad call’: Greens rift deepens over Steele-John allegations
World.content:
PoliticsFederalGreens ‘A bad call’: Greens rift deepens over Steele-John allegations Nick Newling, James Massola and Hamish Hastie October 19, 2026 — 6:21pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Greens leader David Shoebridge has insisted Jordon Steele-John agreed to take leave during an investigation into his conduct, contradicting the senator and deepening a rift within the Greens over allegations about his behaviour towards women. The dispute follows Steele-John’s decision to post a near 2400-word open letter on social media on Sunday night, which detailed his own version of events and accused factions within the WA Greens of weaponising rumours for political advantage. Senator Jordon Steele-John at Parliament House in Canberra in 2023. Alex Ellinghausen Last week, this masthead revealed that Shoebridge had ordered an independent investigation after seven Greens members wrote to him expressing concern over “multiple allegations” against Steele-John between 2017 and 2025. This masthead also reported the existence of a 47-page secret dossier that catalogued allegations against Steele-John and set out ways to shut down media coverage and monitor members who raised concerns on social media.



Shoebridge said last Thursday that Steele-John had chosen to take leave during the investigation. However, in his social media post on Sunday night, Steele-John said he was not on leave and strongly denied all allegations. The senator criticised Shoebridge for saying he had requested time off “because I knew it would be read as validating a story where there isn’t one”. “It was a bad call from David,” Steele-John wrote. In a statement released on Monday afternoon, a spokesperson for Shoebridge said the leader understood that leave was agreed. “Senator Shoebridge remains of the opinion that leave is appropriate under the circumstances and reiterates that this in no way prejudges any of the matters being referred to an inquiry commissioned by the WA Greens,” the spokesperson said.



“Senator Shoebridge firmly believes this matter must be resolved with a fair, timely and independent process as is being commissioned by the WA Greens, and he has worked to ensure this occurs. This process must include procedural fairness for all involved, with the key findings made public.” Related Article Exclusive

Political leadership How to kill a story: The secret dossier the Greens used to protect Steele-John Steele-John on Sunday said the letter to Shoebridge had not detailed any allegations against him – the authors only said they were aware that allegations existed – and claimed it was motivated by factionalism. “It is my opinion that this is an attempt to influence forthcoming party pre-selections by deliberately leaking out of context or misleading information to smear potential candidates and myself,” he wrote. Steele-John also responded to a reference the letter made to the party receiving a complaint of serious sexual misconduct in 2025 that involved the senator and a former partner.



In his statement, Steele-John said he had been interviewed by WA Police after a former partner accused him of removing a condom during sex on multiple occasions – an act known as stealthing. He denied the allegations and said he offered to be interviewed by police. “The report made to the police was of sexual assault – that I had, on multiple occasions, removed condoms without her knowledge while she was on top, facing me,” he wrote. “This is just not true. I volunteered to be interviewed and spent hours answering every question – including detailing which sex positions are possible for me as a Disabled man.” Steele-John has cerebral palsy and uses a wheelchair. He said WA Police closed the investigation and did not lay any charges, and that he was granted a family violence restraining order against his former partner earlier this year based on her excessive attempts to call and message him after he ended the relationship. WA Police declined to comment or confirm whether an investigation took place. Steele-John’s former partner was approached for comment.



The statement released by Steele-John on Sunday evening shocked and upset many members of the Greens in WA, who believed he was trying to pre-empt or shape the outcome of the independent inquiry before it had even begun. Related Article Exclusive

Workplace culture Greens senator takes leave after letter raises allegations of inappropriate comments to women “A fifteen-slide statement released in the middle of an investigation reads as an attempt to win the verdict in public before the process has a chance to deliver one,” said one member of the WA Greens on the condition of anonymity. “He cast the people who signed the letter as a faction chasing preselection. That framing sends a message to every future complainant about what awaits them if they speak up. The respectful choice was to let the investigation do its work in silence.” Some supporters of Steele-John in the disability community have rallied around the senator, who has long championed their needs and defended the NDIS in the face of cuts by the Labor government.



Amid growing divisions within the party, Steele-John’s length statement attracted more than 6000 “likes” and comments in less than 20 hours. Steele-John liked several comments underneath his Instagram post from users who thanked him for speaking out and apologised for the situation he was facing. In his statement, Steele-John said he had been thinking about how to “make sure people who’ve been harmed are believed, while also making sure everyone is treated fairly”. He said the investigation into matters relating to him provided a “safe way for anyone to raise concerns”. Cut through the noise of federal politics with news, views and expert analysis. World.title: The pubs define my suburb. I had a night so wild in one of them I feared for my life
World.content:
Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Forty years. From a student shack in my 20s to working here for the last 20 years. Surry Hills, this wicked and wonderful ’hood has wowed and wooed me. A few kilometres from the CBD up the big incline from Central train station, it paints a broad-brush stroke. Low life, high life, underclass, upper class. Eccentrics and degenerates. A protester mocks police officers as protesters gather around the Surry Hills Police Station. Audrey Richardson Commuters head towards Central Station. Jeremy Piper For as long as I’ve been here, people have been saying the place has been gentrified. Licks of paints, fancy panes of glass, fine providores. The advertising agency my partners and I started occupies the smartly restored old Crown Street Women’s Hospital, once the largest maternity hospital in Australia. Sometimes a client leans in, smiles and says, “I was born here you know?” The floors have ears. The pubs here define this place more than most. People gather at The Clock hotel on Crown Street to watch the AFL grand final. Audrey Richardson The Shakespeare Hotel in 1999. Brendan Esposito



“The Shakey” (Shakespeare Hotel) was a journo haunt for years. “The Crix” (The Cricketer’s Arms) which is sports-day headquarters because of its proximity to the SCG. And a great French bistro upstairs. The Hollywood, an art deco gem where now departed and Hollywood showgirl Doris Goddard was one of the first in the 1960s to let women drink in front bars. “The Carro” (The Carrington) once flaunted a transvestite bar out back but now it’s got a flashy dog-friendly menu. You can also have a beer outside at The Forrester’s and play “spotto” – watching the punters walking through the subtle red-light door at Australia’s most famous brothel, A Touch More Class. We also have the special tiny arthouse cinema The Golden Age; the Belvoir St Theatre where Cate Blanchett once plied her trade; and the recently renovated Brett Whiteley Studio where the artist once lived and worked. Cate Blanchett in The Blind Giant Is Dancing in 1995 at the Belvoir St Theatre. Steven Siewert Indeed, Surry Hills has discarded her old frock – working class, a band in every pub, every night – and shaken off that heroin and street hooker look. She plays to a different beat for sure, but with plenty of bass notes of old. The most explosive gig of my life was in the early 80s when a young Nick Cave and his band The Birthday Party played the legendary Sydney Trade Union Club – “the People’s Palace” – in Foveaux Street. A night so wild I feared for my life. In those days, “the Tradies” stayed open until 5am proffering acts such as INXS and Violent Femmes. It’s now wannabe New York-style loft apartments spruiked by travel influencers. Coral Renee gears up for the Cowgirl Boots Writers Round event at Low 302. Audrey Richardson Yum Club Steven Siewert



I’ve watched the grumpy old kebab man get replaced by a pricey (and delicious) ice cream store. Joe the Grocer went too, subbed for a communal space with digital nomads ordering $9 iced matchas. Speaking of subs, the S&M bondage store is now a Korean instafamous destination cafe. And spot Taylor Swift dining at Pellegrino 2000 when she comes to town. But roots run deep in postcode 2010, despite the seeds of change. Ruth Park’s book Harp in the South, written in the 1940s tells of life as an Irish Catholic immigrant raising a family in Surry Hills – then an inner-city slum – complete with her drunken husband Hughie and the minutiae of hard lives. Outlines of that raw portrait remain to this day. The old hobos still thread the streets, the pub habitues still glower or bawl, a domestic or two spills into the streets from clusters of run-down terraces. Surry Hills street scene, 1944. Ernest Bowen Street scene, Surry Hills in 1944. Ernest Bowen Auction of 112 Arthur Street, Surry Hills, 2026. James Brickwood



Along Surry Hills’ main artery, Crown Street, the Salvation Army’s Oasis centre takes in kids who can no longer live at home or are displaced too young by life’s other misfortunes. Generous pockets of public housing thread the area and poke through the eye-pleasing distractions of the street. For the local housos, the street is their living room and playground. Like recently departed Chris. who sat near the Clock Hotel with his boom box and his trusty hat-wearing dog Sauvignon Blanc (Sav for short). He would cheerfully greet passers-by dispensing genuine happiness. I was sad when his spot went vacant. He brightened everyone’s day. (I hear Sav is ok). Then there’s Peter, “the Bird Man of Surry Hills”. He struts around with Caesar on his shoulder, a brazen bright-green parrot who dares you with his cocky pebble eyes. When Queen Camilla came to tour community food hub OzHarvest, one of her entourage asked him: “Would Caesar like to meet the Queen?” Peter said, “Why not?” Footage of the parrot and the Queen snared front-page news. Queen Camilla meets Peter the Bird Man and his parrot. Matthew Clark, owner of The Barberia, does a regular customer’s hair during a busy Saturday afternoon. Audrey Richardson Coffee enthusiasts wait for tables at Single O cafe. Jeremy Piper Cleveland Street, which separates Redfern from Surry Hills. Audrey Richardson

World.title: ‘We crash and burn together’: Meet the SNL UK hosts pushing the show to its limit
World.content:
Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

When SNL UK premiered in March, it did so with a monologue from host Tina Fey, former head writer of the flagship American comedy series. In a back and forth with Irish actor Nicola Coughlan, playing the classic SNL role of “celebrity audience plant”, Fey said she got the gig because “none of you f---ers would do it” – immediately signalling that this new version of the notoriously censored original would have a little more bite. Local talent probably avoided the gig, Coughlan remarked because “British people tend to root for the failure of others.” Halfway through the show’s second season, nothing could be further from the truth. Related Article Opinion

Comedy A US comedian’s jokes amid the Cornell rape scandal have set off a firestorm Katy Hall Age deputy state topic editor The spin-off, executive produced by SNL creator Lorne Michaels, has not just found its stride but is running laps around its American counterpart, which is having a run of dire, lethargic episodes and is in the headlines for the sexist monologue from most recent host, comedian Shane Gillis. While he was issuing an apology for accidentally swearing on last week’s episode, the UK version made the most of their “lawless” standards for cursing – and got a few of their own shots in. SNL UK’s sketches and impressions skewering local celebrities and news with a distinctly British flavour are only picking up steam. In a cold open that’s racked up more than 2 million views on YouTube, King Charles meets with socially inept American tech billionaires who have created an AI assistant for him. The Deeply Intelligent Autonomous Neurokinetic Android – or D.I.A.N.A. – wears a revenge dress, decides she “shan’t be taking orders any more” and goes full Terminator. It’s material that would work anywhere, but is right at home in the world of non-rhotic accents. “People kept asking us how are we going to do a British spin on [SNL]? But actually, we’ve been doing sketch [comedy] in this country forever,” Paddy Young tells me over Zoom. He and Ania Magliano are two stand-ups who, after rounds of auditions she describes as “a series of live gigs to audiences and then also screen tests to complete silence in these vast TV studios”, were paired up behind the desk as co-anchors of the Weekend Update segment.



They describe the format of the show as a skeleton, one that mimics the specific structure of its source material, with fleshy bits they build out fresh each week. Every Friday it feels impossible to pull off. But as Michaels famously said: “The show doesn’t go on because it’s ready; it goes on because it’s 11.30.” On Sunday, it’s done, and on Monday, you start building out the guts all over again. Live from London, it’s Saturday night: The cast of Saturday Night Live UK. HBO Max While every cast member pulls their weight and finds their niche, Weekend Update anchors are the ones who do it in their voice. Ever since the inaugurator uttered the words, “I’m Chevy Chase, and you’re not” in 1975, the anchors are also the only SNL cast members to announce themselves by name on live TV every week. The dynamic between a pair of hosts is its own specific alchemy. Fey and Jimmy Fallon gave off a teacher’s pet holding down the fort next to a practical joker. Seth Meyers was the straight man to Amy Poehler’s most base instincts. The current co-anchors, Colin Jost and Michael Che, have a fratty frenemies quality. “At the beginning, before the first season, we were talking more explicitly about our dynamic,” Magliano says. “Is this something we need to create and decide? But then when Seth Meyers was over visiting, he said to us, ‘You don’t need to plan any of this. Literally just focus on telling the jokes and the right stuff will come out’. It’s really useful to have some people … who can just be confident for you when we didn’t necessarily have the experience to be fully confident in it.” “The moment you try and shock or pull people’s heartstrings, that’s not the game. All we’re worried about is being funny.” Paddy Young Paddy Young and Ania Magliano, hosts of Weekend Update. HBO Max



As two gigging comics, Young and Magliano know what it feels like to be alone on stage as a joke thuds in the room, or to not have anyone to pat you on the back after a particularly stellar show. “It is nice that we’re up there together,” Magliano says. “When you do stand-up and you’re up there on your own, you’re sort of like, ‘Here we go. This is a judge of my character and my soul, whether I’m good enough on a fundamental level’. But when we’re doing it as a team, if it goes badly, we’re crashing and burning together.” The show’s overnight ratings on Sky One and streaming service NOW average about 140,000 viewers on Saturday nights, but it’s a show built for catch-up and online audiences. In April, Deadline reported the show had more than 86 million views of individual clips on Instagram Reels and YouTube. The cottage industry of streamers and tiny-microphone reaction accounts further boosted the status of the show recently, thanks to Weekend Update’s ruthless teardown of Ed Sheeran after he bowed to pressure from billionaire stadium owner Robert Kraft. While its American contemporaries covering the story barely went further than a gag about Macklemore’s music being bad, Magliano and Young left nothing in the tank. During the segment’s two-minute run, Magliano pointed out the hypocrisy of Sheeran being an advocate for “causes that are allowed” like the war in Ukraine. “Genuinely though, this crisis is the worst thing that’s happened to Ed Sheeran fans since their head injury,” she said biting back a smile, while Young joked that Jeffrey Epstein “had himself killed” to avoid being associated with “wealthy corpsemaxxer” Kraft. “I think the moment you try and shock or pull people’s heartstrings or whatever, that’s not the game,” he says. “All we’re worried about is being funny and being funny in as many ways as possible.” And if there are any hard lines holding them back from going too far? “We just let other people tell us what the limits are. We just try and make everything as funny as we can.”



By the time the clips started getting traction online, they were already at their desks trying to work new jokes about Prince Andrew’s bodily fluids into the next weekend’s packet of punchlines. Jeff Goldblum (right) hosts an episode of Saturday Night Live UK. HBO Max “When we did that Ed Sheeran thing, we were really proud of it, and we heard that people liked it, but we were back in the office on Tuesday worrying about the next thing,” Young says. Magliano adds that the job can be like a hamster in a wheel, with little time to pause and reflect on its impact. “There’s a thing in stand-up … you only feel as good as your last gig. And so I do think the threat of the looming week does mean you can’t spend too much time being self-congratulatory about what did work, or being self-negative about what didn’t.” Editor's pick Australian TV Why this ‘unhinged’ killer gnome comedy took 10 years to bring to life With James Norton and Cynthia Erivo announced for the next two episodes at the time we speak, I ask Magliano and Young for the names on their dream list of SNL UK hosts. Magliano’s picks? Hugh Grant, Diane Morgan and mentalist Derren Brown. “I’m really into magic at the moment. I think it’s fantastic … Imagine an SNL where there’s also a lot of magic in it.”

World.title: ‘Dismantling decades of trust’: Melbourne health provider to close clinic
World.content:
NationalVictoriaHealthcare ‘Dismantling decades of trust’: Melbourne health provider to close clinic Gemma Grant October 19, 2026 — 5:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

A prominent community health organisation will close the doors of its major clinic in St Kilda this week, forcing vulnerable clients to instead travel to Prahran or South Melbourne for help. Better Health Network (BHN) formed in 2022 following the voluntary amalgamation of three smaller community health organisations. Today, it provides primary and allied care to those experiencing homelessness, socioeconomic disadvantage or complex health needs. The Better Health Network clinic on Fitzroy Street in St Kilda will close at the end of October. Simon Schluter The St Kilda clinic at 22-28 Fitzroy Street offers alcohol and drug programs, counselling, and housing support services – as well as the Resourcing Health & Education program, which services the local street-based sex work community. The Age has spoken to five former and current Better Health Network staff who criticised the St Kilda closure – set to take place on October 23 – and raised concerns regarding wider management decisions throughout the organisation.



Former BHN case manager Alana Lewis, who left the provider in May, called the closure “deeply concerning,” and said moving the services would erode trust within the St Kilda community. “These relationships and connections don’t happen overnight. They take years to build, particularly with communities that still and have historically experienced stigma and discrimination when accessing services,” Lewis said. Former Better Health Network case manager Alana Lewis. Joe Armao “Closing Fitzroy Street isn’t simply relocating a service. It’s dismantling decades of trust, community connection and accessible support.” Details of the closure of the site were communicated to staff in an internal announcement last month, which was authorised by chief operating officer Wayne Merritt and seen by The Age.



Among the reasons given were issues securing a suitable lease and structural building changes required by the landlord, described as being “outside [the] control” of the organisation. The current lease expires on October 30. “To enable us to sustainably continue delivering services in suitable environments, we continue to review how we use our buildings and spaces,” the document explains, adding that clients will be redirected to nearby clinics in Prahran and South Melbourne. Another former BHN staff member, who wished to remain anonymous to protect their reputation within the industry, said the closure meant the provider was effectively dislocating itself from the community it is supposed to be serving. Although clients will be referred to other clinics, the former employee said the type of travel being put forward as a solution is unrealistic for many vulnerable or complex clients.



“That’s a middle-class view of mobility … a lot of people can’t travel in those sorts of ways. Even though people say it’s just a tram ride … it’s actually about being intimate within your own community,” they said. Related Article Exclusive

Healthcare A minister’s aide probed cohealth’s issues, then ended up working for them “If you’re in community health, you can’t take community out.” As well as the upcoming clinic closure, Lewis and other current and former BHN employees have expressed concern about transparency and accountability regarding staffing at the not-for-profit provider. Last December, two BHN clinics in Clarinda and in Bentleigh permanently closed. Chief executive Andrea McLeod told The Age at the time there were no planned redundancies as part of last year’s changes, and staff would be redistributed to nearby clinics.



“We’ve committed to continuing to provide essential health and wellbeing services to our communities, but we need to deliver them more effectively to operate within the funding we receive,” McLeod said at the time. But a current BHN employee, who wished to remain anonymous to protect their job, described a dynamic of “near-continuous” restructuring, including a high turnover of senior leadership and multiple redundancy rounds. An internal document from January seen by this masthead details a lengthy “realignment” of client services leadership within the organisation. It refers to 23 program leaders being made redundant, 17 new leadership positions being created and a range of title and role description changes. In response to questions from The Age, a spokesperson for BHN said the organisation was committed to providing client-facing services in St Kilda. They said they were in the final stages of negotiating a lease for a new clinic in the suburb, but declined to provide a specific timeframe as to when that could open.



In the interim, they said clients would be supported with the relocation to the Prahran and South Melbourne clinics, and to access services at partner organisations. “We are committed to supporting continuity of care and giving clients choice about where they access services, based on their needs and preferences,” they said. Better Health Network also leases an administrative office at the Victorian Pride Centre in St Kilda. John Gollings The not-for-profit will continue to lease its administrative office at the Victorian Pride Centre in St Kilda, as well as housing offices for senior leadership, but which is not permitted to provide client-facing services. Another former BHN staff member, who also wished to remain anonymous to protect their reputation within the industry, said maintaining the organisation’s “dream factory” within the suburb’s centre was an example of the “corporatisation of community health”.



“There’s a real divide between leadership and corporate and the [operations] people … they’re just shooting for dollar outcomes, not client outcomes,” they said. Related Article Exclusive

Healthcare How Shane’s botched eye surgery exposes Victoria’s record $254 million hospital payout crisis The BHN spokesperson said the Victorian Pride Centre site was “an important base for a range of frontline teams,” including those who coordinate support by phone. “With a significant forecasted operating deficit for the 2025/26 financial year, the organisation must focus on achieving cost efficiencies that can support our need for financial sustainability,” the document explains. The BHN employee said they had raised concerns to management regarding the impact of these major restructuring processes, but was met with a “tokenistic response”.



“Speaking up within BHN no longer feels possible. Those who have raised concerns have been minimised or driven out of the organisation,” the staff member said. “BHN claims its values are accountability, purpose, courage and respect … [but] BHN’s actions are fundamentally at odds with the very values it claims to uphold.” The BHN spokesperson said they recognise organisational change that impacts people’s employment is challenging. “BHN has undergone organisational change to support the organisation’s long-term sustainability and continued delivery of accessible health and wellbeing services to the community,” they said.

World.title: Chris Hipkins challenges Christopher Luxon to debate on health
World.content:
Labour leader Chris Hipkins has challenged National leader Christopher Luxon to a debate on health.

It comes after Luxon denied the healthcare system was in crisis, even as a number of professionals sound the alarm about the state of the sector.

In a video on social media, Hipkins spoke directly to the camera, saying: "Christopher Luxon doesn't want to talk about it, but everyone else does."

"So today, I'm challenging Christopher Luxon: come and debate me on health."

Hipkins said the health system was "in crisis."

"That's one of the major issues we should be debating in this election campaign. Let's hear from the people who are being denied the healthcare they deserve. Let's hear from the medical professionals in our health system who are right at breaking point. Now let's answer their questions.

"I'm up for it. I challenge Christopher Luxon to join me."

He said New Zealanders deserved "straight answers about the state of their health system and what the future holds".

World.title: Gloriavale School board defends response to allegation of historic sexual assault
World.content:
Audio player for " Future of Gloriavale's school debated in court " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._f0.YIZs2-J2FpwgcBcJJb29s1vXmFAWHLh_p1oUyv-l-RA/education/2024693%2Fgloriavale-school-board-defends-response-to-allegation-of-historic-sexual-assault

Future of Gloriavale's school debated in court Checkpoint Download MP3 4m

The Gloriavale school board has defended its response to an allegation of an historic sexual assault involving a staff member.

Opening arguments have been made in the High Court at Wellington over the future of the West Coast Christian community's school.

The judicial review followed the decision by the Secretary of Education to cancel the private school's registration, over serious concerns that the school is not a physically and emotionally safe place for students.

On Monday, Gloriavale counsel Richard Raymond KC told a courtroom packed with supporters the decision was unlawful and flawed to such an extent it should be dismissed.

Gloriavale counsel Richard Raymond KC. RNZ / Samuel Rillstone

He said closing a school was a last resort and the decision to cancel Gloriavale's registration was rushed and disproportionate.

Secretary for Education Ellen MacGregor-Reid told school leaders in December that she was cancelling its registration, but the 80-student school has remained open pending the High Court challenge by the board.

She again confirmed the move in September, after considering the findings of a special Education Review Office (ERO) report, with the ministry applying to lift interim court orders preventing the school's closure.

It was revealed in court on Monday, the Ministry of Education had been critical of the school board's response to an allegation of an historic sexual assault.

The Court suppressed any names and identifying details related to the matter.

Raymond argued the board acted appropriately when the complaint surfaced and took "all reasonable steps to obtain information" about the nature of the allegation.

Gloriavale. (File photo) RNZ / Jean Edwards

"Your honour will be well-aware, I'm sure... there are situations where someone wants information and you simply can't get it.

"There are charges before the court or there's a disciplinary inquiry pending, and it's not in the interests of the person under investigation to disclose it."

He told Justice Karen Grau there had been a factual error and false assumption by the ministry that something more could have been done.

"And with respect, your honour, it's quite telling that the ministry fails to articulate what could have been done. And I say the answer to that is simple. They can't identify it."

A Ministry of Education spokesperson confirmed to RNZ that, "how the board responded to a recent complaint was one of the aspects considered by the Secretary."

Raymond also took issue with earlier information provided to, and reported by, RNZ under the Official Information Act.

In June, RNZ reported a letter from ERO to Oranga Tamariki stating that Gloriavale's school "knowingly employed staff with prior convictions unsuitable for work with children" and "in at least one instance, the school failed to act when behaviours placing students at risk were identified".

Raymond said the information was false, and sought a correction from the Court arguing it had the jurisdiction and responsibility to correct matters in the public domain that had caused reputational damage.

"There are at least two government departments with this incorrect information.

"There has never been anyone employed by the Gloriavale school board who's had prior convictions that would make them unsuitable to teach children and it's incorrect, therefore, to say that when it was discovered that the board basically did nothing about it.

"It's a heinous, serious, highly damaging, very upsetting allegation that the school has had to deal with and we seek to remedy that."

Oranga Tamariki and ERO declined to comment as the matter was before the Court.

The judicial review continues on Tuesday.

World.title: Large vegetation fire which sent smoke billowing across Auckland's Upper Harbour Motorway under control
World.content:
A large vegetation fire which sent smoke billowing across Auckland's Upper Harbour Motorway is now out.

Fire and Emergency NZ said the smoke could be seen between Westgate and Brigham Creek on Monday afternoon.

The fire was in Whenuapai in the Trigg Rd area, it said.

Do you know more? Email iwitness@rnz.co.nz

A large number of firetrucks and firefighters responded to the scene, it said.

By 6.30pm the fire was out, Fire and Emergency NZ said, but three fire crews were still on site to dampen hot spots along with a water tanker.

It said no buildings had been damaged by the blaze.

Fire and Emergency's shift manager Colin Underdown earlier said eight fire crews were attending as well as a special command unit and water tankers.

Underdown said calls began coming in about the blaze at 4.10pm.

World.title: Kyle Whorrall trial: Supermarket run led to unprovoked murder, court told
World.content:
Kyle Whorrall had just made a routine night-time visit to the supermarket and was walking home when he sat down at a bus stop in the Auckland suburb of Meadowbank.

While he was at the bus stop, the Crown says the 33-year-old American PhD student was brutally murdered in an unprovoked attack in April 2025.

Four teens pleaded not guilty to his murder and aggravated robbery in the High Court at Auckland on Monday.

Jurors heard a fifth teenager had earlier pleaded guilty to both charges.

None of the young people can be named.

In his opening address, Crown prosecutor Taniela-Afu Veikune laid out the case and said Whorrall was making his way home from the shops, when the four teens drove past in a car.

"[The car] and its occupants drove past him again, and again, and again, five times, four U-turns going back and forth past Mr Whorall..."

Veikune said two people got out of the car, armed with a machete.

They robbed Whorrall and struck him in the head with the machete, splitting his skull.

"The defendants then left the scene with Mr. Whorrall's wallet, driving away in [the car], leaving him crumpled on the bench in the bus stop, dying from a catastrophic and ultimately fatal injury," Veikune said.

Audio player for " Teens on trial after pleading not guilty to murder of Kyle Whorral " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._f0.YIZs2-J2FpwgcBcJJb29s1vXmFAWHLh_p1oUyv-l-RA/crime-and-justice/2023162%2Fkyle-whorrall-trial-supermarket-run-led-to-unprovoked-murder-court-told

Teens on trial after pleading not guilty to murder of Kyle Whorral Checkpoint Download MP3 2m

The trial was less about the murder, and more about the extent of the actions of those involved, Veikune said.

He said the Crown did not have to prove who struck the fatal blow, only that those in the car knew what could have happened.

"The Crown says that the defendants agreed to target Mr Whorrall to rob him, and it would have been known to each of the four defendants, as it would be to any reasonable person, that the robbery could well result in the use of the machete."

Lawyers for the teenagers also gave opening remarks.

Paul Borich KC told the court with all the evidence, and with 18 months of detective work, the Crown still could not say who wielded the machete.

"You might think: 'Well, if the case is going to be proved beyond a reasonable doubt, and the Crown don't know, how can we as jurors know?'," he said.

Borich said it was the person who had already pleaded guilty who was the murderer.

"He used the machete, he is your murderer, the evidence will show that he is the person who did that."

Defence lawyer Harvena Cherrington said there were three questions the jury would need to answer for her client: Was he there, who got out of the car, and what knowledge did he have?

She said the jury should focus on the matters in front of them at trial and not other incidents the Crown referenced.

Veikune had earlier told jurors two of the defendants - Cherrington and Borich's clients - had previously been involved in robberies with a machete.

Another lawyer - Oscar Hintze - acknowledged the Whorrall family.

"We recognise the grief of the Whorrall family," he said.

"Their loss is real and permanent, nobody on this side of the courtroom disputes that Kyle died a terrible and senseless death, or whoever caused it did a grave wrong."

Hintze said feeling sympathy for Kyle and his family was natural, but reminded jurors those feelings had to be put to one side.

"When a young man is killed in a public place, there is an understandable urge for someone to pay, that urge is instinct for revenge," he said.

"You're not here to satisfy that, you're here to do justice, that is something much different and much harder."

Meanwhile, defence lawyer Marie Taylor-Ciphers said there was no evidence her client got out of the car that night.

She cautioned jurors that what they had heard earlier was just the Crown's version of events.

"That's what the prosecution say happened," she said.

"You must make your mind up once you've heard all of the evidence.

The four appeared before Justice Simon Mount, who reminded jurors it was up to the Crown to prove the charges against the group.

World.title: Police use of external AI systems raises 'high risks' of data breaches - expert
World.content:
Using external AI systems for criminal cases raises the risk that cases could be compromised and witnesses could be identified, says a privacy law expert.

Police investigators took evidence home and loaded it into unsecured artificial intelligence (AI) services on their own devices, in breach of police policy.

Documents released to RNZ have detailed some of the AI breaches and risks within the ranks.

Police have a detailed generative AI policy, and did successfully use the Whisper AI tool in the Gulf Harbour body-in-the-bag investigation in 2024.

But one investigator used Google Translate to decipher 350,000 lines of intercepted Chinese language audio. Documents also suggest that sensitive files have been uploaded to unsecured cloud services.

Audio player for " Police investigators uploaded evidence to AI against policy " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._f0.YIZs2-J2FpwgcBcJJb29s1vXmFAWHLh_p1oUyv-l-RA/crime-and-justice/2023450%2Fpolice-use-of-external-ai-systems-raises-high-risks-of-data-breaches-expert

Police investigators uploaded evidence to AI against policy Checkpoint Download MP3 7m

Barrister and privacy law expert Kathryn Dalziel told Checkpoint it was "absolutely unacceptable" that police were taking data home and loading it up into open source systems.

"There are high risks that a police officer is putting confidential information into their own environment, it opens themselves up to attack if that becomes known to cyber criminals, it opens up questions about integrations with police internal systems when that information is obtained and then put back into police systems.

"I can see a significant amount of high risk issues around taking things home to work on them."

Employment and privacy lawyer Kathryn Dalziel. Stephanie Defregger

Dalziel said using external AI systems could compromise evidence or an entire case.

"It might provide information or result in information getting out into the public that means it compromises the controls that a court might have over the evidence. If it's made public and jury members get to see it beforehand it could compromise a case; if there are ways to mitigate what's happened or to cover up what's happened, which prevents the police from doing their job."

There was also the possibility that witnesses could be identified.

"If, for example, we are looking at 350,000 lines of audio data, I'm anticipating that there might be a number of witnesses that could be involved in there and that could put them under threat.

Dalziel said there needed to be good policies, procedures and systems to ensure this kind of thing did not result in data breaches, including potentially personal details, legal case information and financial data.

She said police should have these systems available to them.

"We're in a data age, there is nothing new about that and it surprised me when I heard that police officers were going to Google Translate, rather than having a proper system internally to help them.

"I understand the problem for the police was that their internal systems were not assisting them. They had significant controls over Whisper AI that didn't allow them to use other languages and they had 350,000 lines of audio data in Chinese that needed to be quickly assessed in order to know where to direct their attention."

She said urgent resourcing was needed for tools that police could use and would be secure, internal and controlled.

The Privacy Act applies to agencies handling personal information, including when using AI tools. These agencies are expected to have an AI policy and to ensure staff are complying with it.

The office of the Privacy Commissioner says uploading personal information to platforms like Google Translate may be a disclosure under the Privacy Act.

Where sensitive personal information has been disclosed without authorisation, they expect the agency to consider whether it is likely to cause serious harm and requires notification to its office.
